entry.summary: BERT written in PyTorch from scratch and loaded with Google's weights: why reading in both directions needed a mask, what BERT knows and what its attention heads do, and a detector of personal data in long financial documents, against regular expressions.

entry.title: How accurate is Polymarket? Calibration, longshot bias and a volume trap

link.title: How accurate is Polymarket? Calibration, longshot bias and a volume trap

entry.content:
In short

Polymarket’s prices are good probabilities where people actually trade. A week before the close, markets with real trading are off by under two percentage points on average, and a day before the close they remove 82% of the error of a forecaster who knows only the base rate.

The famous accuracy figures say less than they seem, because most questions resolve No. What mispricing is left sits at the tails, cheap longshots a little too dear and near-certain favourites a little too cheap, and it is about the size of the spread.

1.8points between price and outcome, on average, a week before the close
77%right for a forecaster who answers No to every question
−39%average return on contracts bought at 2 to 5 cents

On the last evening of October I opened Polymarket to look at one number. The US midterm elections were three days away, and the market on which party would control the Senate had taken $13.5 million of bets.

A share that pays a dollar if Democrats win the Senate cost 71.5 cents. The House was hardly a contest by the market’s account: 94.5 cents for Democrats.

A week earlier the same kind of number had been wrong in public. Going into Brazil’s presidential runoff on 25 October, Polymarket and Kalshi gave Flávio Bolsonaro about an 80% chance of beating Lula, and Lula won[1]. Semafor’s headline that week was that prediction markets had “blown three big elections”[2].

By the time you read this you probably know how the Senate went, and I don’t. Suppose Republicans keep it. Was 71.5 wrong?

Suppose they lose it. Was it right? Neither follows, and Brazil does not prove the 80% wrong either.

A forecast of 71.5% claims something only about many situations like this one: that roughly seven in ten of them end the way the market leaned, and three in ten don’t.

So the question in the title cannot be settled by any one market, however famous. It can be settled by many. I downloaded the record of every market Polymarket resolved from 2024 on, almost three million of them, took the price histories of about 150,000 and checked what the prices said against what then happened.

This post is about what came out: how good the prices are as probabilities, where they are systematically off, a trap in the most natural way to slice the data, what the “accuracy” figures in the press leave out, and what a trader can and cannot do with any of it.

What a Polymarket price is, and why it should be a probability

Polymarket sells shares in outcomes. A share of “Yes” pays one dollar if the event happens and nothing if it does not; a share of “No” pays a dollar in the opposite case.

Since April 2026 the dollar is pUSD, Polymarket’s own token backed by the USDC stablecoin; before that it was USDC itself[3]. One Yes and one No together always pay exactly a dollar, so their prices add up to about a dollar too.

Every market is binary. A question with many answers, such as who wins a prize, is a set of Yes/No markets, one per candidate.

Shares trade in an order book, as on a stock exchange: buyers post bids, sellers post asks, and a trade happens when they meet.

The price the site shows, the number the press calls “the odds”, is the midpoint between the best bid and the best ask, or the last trade if the gap between them is wider than ten cents[4].

Why should that price be a probability? Because of a simple argument about money. If you believe Democrats win the Senate with probability \(q\), a Yes share bought at price \(p\) is worth \(q \cdot 1 + (1 - q) \cdot 0 = q\) to you on average.

You buy when \(q > p\) and sell when \(q < p\). The price stops moving where nobody with money left is willing to push it either way.

That argument has holes, and economists have spent twenty years mapping them. The price is a compromise between traders, not anyone’s belief.

With logarithmic utility it equals the traders’ average belief, and for other reasonable preferences it stays close to it between about 20 and 80 cents[5]; for risk-neutral traders with different beliefs, a price of 75 cents is compatible with an average belief anywhere from 56% to 94%[6].

Money tied up in a bet until December could have earned interest. Since March 2026 most categories charge the taker a fee[7]. And the dollar arrives only if the event is resolved the way you expect, by a process with its own failures.

Whether the price works as a probability despite all that is an empirical question, and the rest of this post answers it with data.

How to check a forecaster

Calibration

A forecaster who said 70% is not wrong when the event fails to happen, but a forecaster who says 70% a thousand times should see about seven hundred of those events happen. That property is called calibration.

Weather services have been checked this way for seventy years: on the days a calibrated service gives a 30% chance of rain, it rains on about 30% of them.

The picture that shows calibration is the reliability diagram. Take all the forecasts, group them by value (all forecasts between 60% and 70%, say), and for each group plot the average forecast against the share of events that happened. A calibrated forecaster’s points fall on the diagonal.

If you have ever trained a classifier and checked whether its predicted probabilities can be trusted, you have drawn this picture already; modern neural networks are famously overconfident on it[8], and how to bin the forecasts is a small science of its own[9].

Calibration is not enough. A forecaster who always announces the base rate, the share of all events that happen, is perfectly calibrated and perfectly useless. About 34% of Polymarket’s markets resolve Yes, so saying “34%” about every market is calibrated: of all the markets you said it about, 34% happened.

What a good forecaster adds is resolution, forecasts that move away from the base rate in the right direction, high for the events that happen and low for those that don’t.

The Brier score

The Brier score measures both at once. For \(N\) forecasts \(p_i\) of events with outcomes \(y_i\) (1 if it happened, 0 if not), it is the mean squared error

\[\mathrm{BS} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (p_i - y_i)^2 .\]

A forecast of 70% scores \(0.3^2 = 0.09\) if the event happens and \(0.7^2 = 0.49\) if it does not. A forecaster who always says 50% scores \(0.25\), and a clairvoyant scores zero. Glenn Brier’s original score summed the error over both outcomes and ran from 0 to 2, so it is twice this one[10].

The score splits into a part for calibration, called reliability, a part for resolution, and a part that belongs to the questions rather than the forecaster. The skill score says how much of the worst honest score, that of the base-rate forecaster, a forecaster removes.

The Brier score in three parts: Murphy's decomposition

Allan Murphy showed that the score splits into three parts[11]. Group the forecasts into bins \(k\), each holding a share \(n_k / N\) of them, with average forecast \(\bar p_k\) and observed frequency \(\bar y_k\), and let \(\bar y\) be the overall base rate:

\[\mathrm{BS} \approx \underbrace{\sum_k \frac{n_k}{N} (\bar p_k - \bar y_k)^2}_{\text{reliability}} \;-\; \underbrace{\sum_k \frac{n_k}{N} (\bar y_k - \bar y)^2}_{\text{resolution}} \;+\; \underbrace{\bar y (1 - \bar y)}_{\text{uncertainty}} .\]

Reliability is the calibration error, the squared distance of the points from the diagonal, and should be small. Resolution is how far the groups’ outcomes spread away from the base rate, and should be large. Uncertainty belongs to the questions, not the forecaster: it is the score of the base-rate forecaster. The skill score \(1 - \mathrm{BS} / \bar y(1 - \bar y)\) says what share of that score a forecaster removes.

Three forecasters on the same markets

The three charts below put this on real data. All three forecasters see the same 18,157 markets a week before they closed. The first is Polymarket’s prices.

The second is a bolder copy that doubles the prices’ log-odds, so that 70% becomes 84% and 30% becomes 16%. The third is a timid copy that halves them, so that 70% becomes 60%. The grey square is the base-rate forecaster.

The market’s own prices score 0.079. Both copies score worse, 0.084 for the bold one and 0.089 for the timid one, and they fail in opposite ways.

The bold copy’s points lie above the diagonal on the left and below it on the right: when it says 5%, the event happens more often than that, because it took a modest forecast and inflated its confidence.

The timid copy bends the other way. Neither copy knows anything the market didn’t, and that is the point of the exercise. Distorting a calibrated forecaster in either direction only makes its score worse.

The base-rate forecaster says 25% about everything, the share of these markets that resolved Yes, and scores 0.186, more than twice the market’s error.

Why one election proves nothing

The case people quote as proof is the 2024 US presidential election. On the eve of the vote Polymarket priced a Trump win at 59 cents, while 538’s final model gave Kamala Harris 50 chances in 100[12]. Trump won all seven swing states.

The market’s best-known trader that year, a Frenchman the press called Théo, had bet more than $30 million on Trump across several accounts.

He told the Wall Street Journal he had “absolutely no political agenda”[13], and later turned out to have commissioned his own polls, asking people not whom they would vote for but whom their neighbours would[14]. He made tens of millions of dollars, and he was right.

Think about what that shows. A forecaster who put 59% on the winner scores \(0.41^2 \approx 0.17\) for that election; one who put 50% scores \(0.25\).

A single draw from a coin that lands heads 59% of the time says almost nothing about the coin, and the same arithmetic run on Brazil a week ago says almost nothing in the other direction. One outcome cannot separate a good forecaster from a lucky one.

Thousands can.

Three million markets, and which of them are forecasts

Polymarket publishes everything needed to check it. Its Gamma API lists every event and market with its question, its tags, the dollars traded and the final outcome; its order-book API returns the price history of every outcome token.

I took every event that closed from 2024 to the end of October 2026 with at least $1,000 traded: 2,959,534 binary markets that resolved cleanly to Yes or No. (The API records only a few thousand markets before 2024, and I leave them out of the counts.)

About 0.4% of markets with more than $10,000 traded resolved 50-50, the platform’s answer to a question that turned out ambiguous, and I set those aside.

What Polymarket has become

Polymarket in 2026 is mostly a sports book. One football match can carry a dozen markets (the winner, the handicap, the total goals), and sports make up 73% of all the markets that closed this year.

Next come the short crypto markets that ask whether Bitcoin will be higher at the end of the next fifteen minutes, hour or day, 11%, and science and weather questions, 6%. Politics, the subject of nearly every article about prediction markets, is 2% of the count.

Downloading the price history of three million markets is not practical, so I sampled about 150,000 of them, and how to sample turned out to matter more than anything else in this study.

Big markets were drawn more often than small ones, and every pooled figure is weighted back to the whole population; a later section shows what goes wrong without that.

How the markets were drawn and weighted

I made two independent random draws. The first takes a share of the markets in each topic, whatever their size: 1.7% of sports, 11% of politics, 16% of economics, 20% of culture, 5.5% of crypto, 3.5% of science and weather.

The second takes every market with more than $100,000 traded (every sports market with more than a million) and a share of the smaller ones above $10,000. Together they hold 153,602 markets in 80,320 events.

Every market had a known chance of being drawn, and when I pool markets each counts in inverse proportion to that chance, so the pooled figures describe all resolved markets rather than my sample; statisticians call this the Horvitz–Thompson estimator[15].

Drawing big markets more often is harmless as long as the weights undo it. Leaving markets out, or grouping them by size, is not. Uncertainty comes from a bootstrap over events rather than markets, because the twenty candidates of one election are not twenty independent questions.

Market lists come from the Gamma API (events/keyset), prices from the order-book API (prices-history, an hourly series for the last two weeks of a market and a 12-hour one for its whole life), and trades from the data API (trades).

What counts as a forecast

The forecast I score is the price of a market’s first outcome (Yes, in a Yes/No market) a fixed time before the market closed: a week, mostly, and a day, a month or three months where I compare horizons.

The close comes after the outcome is known, typically hours after a match ends or a day or two after an election, so a week before the close is before the event itself.

A market counts as a forecast only if at least $1,000 had been traded in it in the week before. This matters more than it sounds. Most markets on Polymarket are created, barely traded and resolved, and the price history of such a market is the middle of an almost empty order book.

One football market in my sample, on whether a Bundesliga match would have five goals or more, stood at 48 cents a week before the game; most matches end with fewer, this one did too, and over its whole life the market traded $134. That price is not a forecast of a high-scoring game.

A bid at one cent and an ask at 95 cents would give it. The test uses only what was known at the time, the trades of that week, which I took from Polymarket’s public trades API.

Calibration: a week out, prices are off by 1.8 points

Here is the main result.

The points sit close to the diagonal. Of the 18,157 markets with real trading a week before the close, those priced around 25 cents resolved Yes 28% of the time and those around 75 cents 82%.

The average gap between price and frequency is 1.8 percentage points, and the reliability term of the Brier score is 0.001, a hundredth of the resolution term, 0.108. A weather service would be pleased with that.

When a liquid market says 70%, read it as about 70%, and remember that 70 means it fails three times in ten.

The small deviations have a shape. Between 55 and 85 cents events happened a little more often than priced (60% of the markets at 55 cents, 82% of those at 75), while contracts at 2 to 5 cents happened less often than priced, 2.3% of the time against a price of 3.2. The prices are slightly compressed toward the middle: favourites a little too cheap, longshots a little too dear.

That is the pattern economic theory predicts for traders who like long shots or dislike tying up money, and it is what a Princeton thesis on 188,509 Polymarket markets found too[16].

The right panel shows something just as important: where the forecasts are. Almost half of these markets are priced below 5 cents a week before they close.

Most questions on Polymarket are of the form “will this specific thing happen”, most of them don’t happen, and the market knows. Those confident, correct and uninteresting forecasts are a large part of every headline accuracy figure.

Accuracy against a forecaster who always says no

Polymarket advertises its record on a page titled “How accurate is Polymarket?”: 98.7% accurate four hours before resolution, 90.3% a month before[17]. Accuracy there means the share of markets where the leading outcome won.

It sounds like a hard bar to clear. The same page notes that 78.3% of its markets resolve No, and explains why: “There are usually more ways for something not to happen than to happen in one exact way”.

A forecaster who answers “No” to every question without reading it is therefore 78% accurate on Polymarket’s own sample. The left half of the next chart shows what that does to the comparison on mine.

The chart uses the 5,420 markets that had real trading a month, a week and a day before they closed, so the same questions are scored at every horizon.

The favourite won 87% of them a month before the close, 93% a week before and 96% a day before. A forecaster who says No to everything gets 77% right on these markets at every horizon, since only 23% of them resolved Yes.

The honest comparison is skill: the market removes 48% of the base-rate forecaster’s Brier score a month out, 70% a week out and 82% a day out. On the questions still in doubt at the time, priced between 2 and 98 cents, it removes 40%, 54% and 57%.

Key point

Accuracy flatters any forecaster whose questions mostly resolve one way. Ask for skill: the share of the base-rate forecaster’s error that is gone. On Polymarket it is 70% a week before the close, and 54% on the questions still in doubt.

Those are the numbers to keep in mind the next time anyone, a platform or a pundit, advertises 90% accuracy.

How the forecast sharpens as the close approaches

Information arrives over time. The Brier score of markets that lived at least two months traces how quickly.

Sixty days before the close, the 3,492 markets that lived that long and were traded a month out already score 0.084, well below the base rate’s 0.150.

The score falls steadily, to 0.056 a month out and 0.033 a week out, and drops again in the last days, when scheduled events (a vote, a match, a data release) take place.

The lower panel counts the markets already priced at the extremes, below a cent or above 99 cents: a quarter of them at sixty days, more than half a week out, three quarters at the end. A market at 99.5 cents is not a forecast any more; it is a receipt waiting to be cashed.

The volume trap: why big markets seem to underprice longshots

The obvious next question is whether big markets forecast better than small ones, and the obvious way to answer it is to group markets by the dollars traded. Polymarket’s accuracy page does exactly this. It is a trap, and I walked into it first.

My first sample took every market with more than $100,000 traded and a share of those between $10,000 and $100,000, the way one naturally filters out dead markets.

In that sample, contracts priced between 10 and 20 cents a week before the close returned 25% on average, and the bigger the market, the more the longshots won.

It looked like the reverse of everything the racetrack literature says, and a trading strategy in one line. Here are the longshots of the sample drawn by topic, grouped two ways.

On the left, grouped by the dollars a market traded over its whole life, contracts priced 2 to 20 cents won about half as often as priced in markets under $1,000 (a ratio of 0.49) and twice as often in markets of $1–10 million (2.14).

On the right, the same contracts grouped by the dollars traded in the week before the forecast show nothing of the kind: 0.72 in the thinnest markets, 0.87 and 0.96 as trading grows. Favourites mirror it, from 1.05 to 0.88 on the left and flat at about 1.0 on the right.

The left panel is an artefact, and the reason is in what volume counts. A market’s total volume includes all the trading after the forecast, and nothing makes people trade like a surprise.

When a 10-cent candidate starts winning, the market fills with buyers, sellers, hedgers and spectators, and its volume jumps; when the favourite wins as expected, the market stays quiet and small.

a longshot starts winningeveryone trades itits volume grows"big markets underprice longshots"

So sorting markets by total volume quietly sorts them by whether the unlikely happened. In statistics this is selection on a consequence of the outcome, the same family of error as look-ahead bias in a backtest, which I wrote about in the post on AI crypto trading bots. Polymarket’s own accuracy page breaks its Brier scores down by volume in exactly this way.

Trap

Never filter, group or weight markets by their total volume, or by anything else that is counted after the forecast. Use what was known when the price was set: the dollars traded in the week before, the order book at the time, the topic.

The right panel is the honest version, because the week before a forecast is over when the forecast is made. It says something useful.

In thin markets longshots are overpriced, and the more a market trades, the closer to fair they become. That is why the rest of this post, like the calibration above, uses the test of $1,000 traded in the week before and never groups markets by their total volume.

Longshots lose, favourites earn a little

Calibration is an average, and averages hide the tails. The tails are where traders make or lose money, and economists have known for seventy years where to look: at the racetrack, bettors overpay for longshots and underpay for favourites[18].

In six million American horse races, betting on horses at 100 to 1 or longer lost about 61% of the stake, while betting on the favourite in every race lost only 5.5%[19]. On Kalshi, contracts bought below 10 cents lost over 60% of the money put into them[20].

To look for it on Polymarket, I treated both sides of every market as a contract: a Yes at the price \(p\) and a No at \(1 - p\). Buying a contract at price \(p\) that pays \(y \in \{0, 1\}\) returns \(y / p - 1\) on the stake. If prices were exact probabilities, the average return in every price band would be zero.

The bias is there, and it lives at the extremes. Contracts priced between 2 and 5 cents a week before the close won 2.1% of the time while costing 3.2 cents on average, so buying them lost 39% of the stake, with a 95% interval from −53% to −22%.

The cheapest band, under 2 cents, lost 22%, with an interval wide enough to include zero.

At the other end, contracts at 95 to 98 cents won 97.8% of the time and returned 1.15% in the week, and those at 98 to 99.5 cents returned 0.35%; both intervals stay above zero. Between 5 and 95 cents the averages cannot be told apart from zero.

Longshots under 5 cents lose a quarter to two fifths of the stake; favourites above 95 cents earn a fraction of a percent a week, before costs.

How the returns are counted, and why the weighting matters

How contracts are weighted matters for this kind of result. A study of 588 million Polymarket trades found that buys under 10 cents lost 19.3 cents per dollar when weighted by the money traded, 6.3 cents when each contract counted once, and gained 4.1 cents when related contracts were first grouped by event[21].

My numbers count each market once, weighted to the population of markets, with uncertainty from resampling whole events.

A return here is that of one contract bought at the mid price a week before the close and held to the end, averaged over contracts in a price band with the population weights; the interval resamples whole events 400 times.

A favourite at 97 cents that earns a percent in a week sounds like free money, and it is not. The bars are mid prices, and nobody buys at the mid.

The downside is a total loss on the rare occasion the favourite fails, and the 50-50 resolutions I excluded would cost a favourite buyer half the stake; at about 0.4% of markets they take back up to 0.2 points of that return.

What the spread and the fees take

The price shown is the middle of the order book, but a buyer pays the ask. On the last night of October I recorded the best bid and ask of all 124,068 open markets, 57,468 of them with orders on both sides, and measured what buying at the ask costs above the middle, as a share of the price paid.

For contracts between 40 and 95 cents the median cost is about 2% of the price. Below 20 cents it explodes: 13% for contracts at 10 to 20 cents, 29% at 5 to 10, and about two thirds of the price under 5 cents.

A two-cent contract with a bid at one cent and an ask at three costs a full cent above its middle, half of what it is worth on paper. At the other end, near-certain contracts above 98 cents are cheap to buy, 0.6% of the price.

On top of the spread comes the fee. Since 30 March 2026 a taker on most categories pays \(r \cdot p(1 - p)\) per share, where \(p\) is the price and the rate \(r\) is 0.04 for politics, 0.05 for sports and most other categories and 0.07 for crypto; makers pay nothing, and geopolitical markets are free[7].

As a share of the money paid that is \(r(1 - p)\): about 5% of the stake for a 5-cent sports contract, a quarter of a percent for a 95-cent one.

Many of the busiest markets ran with the fee switched off on the day I looked, so the rate has to be checked market by market.

Put together, a longshot buyer who crosses the spread gives up between a tenth and two thirds of the stake before the event even happens.

A favourite buyer gives up a couple of percent, more than the whole edge the previous chart found: after half the spread the 95–98 cent band goes from +1.15% to −0.9% a week, and the 98–99.5 cent band from +0.35% to −0.3%. The diamonds on that chart show it.

For traders

The longshot discount and the favourite premium are real, but they are about the size of what it costs to trade them, which is why they survive. Selling longshots and buying near-certainties works only for those who post limit orders and let others cross the spread.

Topics: politics is calibrated best

A week before the close, markets with real trading are skilled in every topic, from about 53% of the base rate’s error removed in sports and crypto to 70% in science and weather.

Politics, with 8,929 markets the largest group, is also the best calibrated, with an average gap of 1.9 points; sports and science have the largest gaps, 4.4 and 4.1, with crypto close behind at 3.9. Sports here means the markets traded a week before the close, mostly season futures (who wins the league, who wins the award) rather than single games, which are listed only days before kick-off.

Crypto markets resolve together

Crypto deserves a chart of its own, because its errors have a cause that has nothing to do with the traders’ judgement.

Most crypto markets ask about one number, the price of Bitcoin or Ether on a date. Take the close calls, markets priced between 30 and 70 cents a week out, and orient each so that Yes means the price went up.

In the months when Bitcoin rose, the bet on rising prices won 63% of the time; in the months when it fell, 32%. Its price a week before was about 50 cents in both. Across fifteen months, the share of winning bullish bets and Bitcoin’s monthly return have a correlation of 0.78.

The market was not wrong in any useful sense: a week before the close nobody knew which way Bitcoin would go, and 50 cents was a fair price for a coin toss. But a dozen such markets in one month are not a dozen tosses. They are one toss recorded a dozen times.

A calibration chart of crypto markets mostly shows whether the period studied was a good one for Bitcoin. Calibration needs independent questions, which is why I resample whole events rather than markets, and why even that understates the uncertainty for crypto.

Long-dated favourites and the price of waiting

A market that resolves in six months has to pay its traders for waiting. A No share at 95 cents on a question that will almost certainly resolve No pays 5 cents on 95 after half a year, about 10.8% a year, if it pays at all; three-month US Treasury bills paid 4.07% on average in 2025 and 3.71% so far in 2026[22].

Traders who could earn interest elsewhere will not bid near-certain long-dated contracts all the way to a dollar, and the people with the most money to commit, favourite buyers, drop out first.

Page and Clemen found the result on the old Intrade exchange: markets far from expiry were poorly calibrated, with prices “systematically biased toward 0.50”[23].

Polymarket noticed. Since September 2025 it has paid interest on positions in a short list of long-dated markets “to keep long-term pricing accurate”, 4% a year at launch and 3.25% since June 2026[24].

The list holds about eighteen events, the 2028 presidential race and the midterms among them. Every other market pays nothing for waiting.

Polymarket shows the same thing. Contracts priced between 90 and 95 cents a month before the close won 94.3% of the time against a price of 92.6, and those at 95 to 98 cents won 98.4% against 96.6.

Held to the end, both earned about 1.8% in a month, which compounds to roughly 25% a year, six times what a Treasury bill paid.

Three months out, the same two bands earned 6 to 9% a year and the most expensive band lost money; six months out the samples are small and the results noisy.

A month before the close, favourites at 90 to 98 cents paid about 25% a year at mid prices: the price of waiting, not of ignorance.

The pattern fits Page and Clemen: near-certain long-dated contracts are a little too cheap, and the discount is about what impatient money charges. It is not free money either.

These are mid prices, a single failure costs the whole stake, and a trader who buys favourites a month out is lending to the market at a rate that has to cover the risk that the near-certain doesn’t happen.

A two-number correction that doesn’t help

An engineer looking at the calibration chart will ask the obvious question: if the market is slightly off in a systematic way, can a model correct it? This is the same move as calibrating a classifier. Fit two numbers, \(a\) and \(b\), so that a corrected probability

\[\hat q = \sigma\big(a \cdot \operatorname{logit}(p) + b\big), \qquad \operatorname{logit}(p) = \ln \frac{p}{1 - p}, \quad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}},\]

fits the outcomes better. With \(b = 0\), a slope \(a > 1\) means the prices should have been bolder, longshots cheaper and favourites dearer, and \(a < 1\) means they should have been more timid. This is Platt scaling, a standard way to recalibrate a classifier[25].

A Princeton thesis that fitted it to 188,509 Polymarket markets found a slope of 1.112[16], and a study of Kalshi and Polymarket found political markets “compressed toward 50%” in the same sense[26].

The interesting question is whether such a correction helps on markets it has not seen. I fitted \(a\) and \(b\) only on markets that closed before July 2025 and scored the correction on markets that closed after.

Fitted on the markets that closed before July 2025, the correction has a slope of 1.12 a week before the close and 1.18 a month before: the prices should have been a little bolder, the same compression the calibration chart showed, and close to Walker’s 1.112.

Applied to the 13,618 markets that closed later, it changes the Brier score a week out by −0.0001, with a 95% interval from −0.0009 to +0.0008, and a month out by −0.0003. In other words, nothing.

The bias is real on average, but too small and too unstable over time for a formula to turn it into a better forecast, let alone a profit after the spread.

For engineers

The same discipline applies to any recalibration of a model: fit it on the past, score it on the future, and report the difference with its interval. Here a correction that every in-sample diagnostic recommends turns out to be worth nothing.

Insiders: when the market knows too early

The most impressive forecasts on Polymarket are sometimes not forecasts at all.

The Nobel Peace Prize

The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the 2025 Peace Prize at 09:00 UTC on 10 October. For months María Corina Machado had traded at a cent or two. Shortly after midnight in Oslo her price started to climb, passed 43 cents before one in the morning and reached 73 by two[27].

In the price history I downloaded she was still at 67 cents five minutes before the announcement. An account created days earlier bought early and made tens of thousands of dollars.

The director of the Norwegian Nobel Institute said, “We take this very seriously”[28]. In January the institute concluded that the winner’s name had most likely leaked through “the digital domain” and that it could not say who was behind it[29].

Maduro, the Iran strikes and Google

That was not the only case. On the night of 2 January 2026, hours before Donald Trump announced the capture of Nicolás Maduro, a weeks-old account bet about $33,000 that Maduro would be out by the end of the month and made about $400,000.

In April the Justice Department charged a Special Forces master sergeant who had helped plan the operation, and the CFTC called it the first insider-trading case it had ever brought over event contracts[30, 31]. He has pleaded not guilty.

Hours before the US strikes on Iran on 28 February, six freshly funded wallets bought Yes on the strike market and made about a million dollars[32].

In May a Google engineer was charged over about $1.2 million made on markets about Google’s “Year in Search” lists, using, according to Google, marketing material he could see at work[33].

Polymarket’s chief executive once put it plainly to CBS[34]:

Insiders having an edge to the market is a good thing.

Shayne Coplan, chief executive of Polymarket

For accuracy, in a narrow sense, he is right: the price moved to the truth before the public knew it. It is not prediction, though, and it is no use to an ordinary trader, who is the one on the other side of each of those trades.

The company now says it referred the Maduro trader to the Justice Department itself. In Congress, one bill would bar officials and their staff from trading on government decisions[35], and another would ban markets on elections, sports and military action altogether[36].

Resolution: when the truth is decided by a vote

A share pays a dollar if the event happens, but someone has to say whether it happened. On Polymarket that someone is usually UMA’s optimistic oracle. A proposer posts an outcome with a bond, typically $750, and from there it is a chain of deadlines[37]:

a proposaltwo hours to dispute ita second disputea vote of UMA holders, two days

Most markets resolve in two hours without a dispute. The ones that don’t are where prediction becomes a governance problem.

In March 2025 a $7 million market on whether Ukraine would agree to a minerals deal with the US before April resolved Yes, although Ukraine had not agreed; a single large token holder was accused of swinging the vote, and Polymarket called the situation “unprecedented” but paid no refunds, since “this wasn’t a market failure”[38].

That summer a market with hundreds of millions of dollars traded asked whether Volodymyr Zelensky would be photographed in a suit; he appeared at a NATO summit in a black jacket and matching trousers that many outlets called a suit, and UMA’s voters decided it was not[39].

In May 2026 Bloomberg found that nine wallets held about half of the UMA votes cast in Polymarket disputes over three years[40].

The platform has been narrowing the problem: since September 2025 only whitelisted proposers can propose outcomes, which cut disputes by two thirds in the first month[41], crypto price markets now settle from Chainlink prices without a vote, and a new contract system that can combine several oracles is due to switch on for new markets this week[42].

For a trader, resolution risk is a cost like the spread, small on most markets and large on exactly the ones with ambiguous wording.

Wash trading: volume that isn’t

Volume is the number every article about Polymarket leads with, and it is the least reliable number on the platform.

Researchers at Columbia classified nearly 25% of Polymarket’s historical volume as consistent with wash trading, traders buying from and selling to themselves without changing their position; it peaked at nearly 60% of weekly volume in December 2024, and in sports markets it reached 45% of all-time volume[43].

Separately, Paradigm showed in December 2025 that most dashboards counted every trade twice, once for each side[44].

Neither changes the prices this post studies: a wash trade moves money in a circle, not the price. But together with the trap above, they are good reasons not to read a market’s volume as a measure of how much it knows.

What a Polymarket price is worth

As a probability, a Polymarket price on a market people actually trade is about as good as public forecasts get.

A week before the close the prices were calibrated to within 1.8 percentage points on average, and on the markets open for at least a month they removed 70% of the base-rate forecaster’s error a week out and 82% a day out.

When a liquid market says 70%, the honest reading is “about 70%”, give or take a few points.

That is a statement about many markets, not about one. The Senate at 71.5 cents is a single draw, and so was Brazil at 80. A calibrated price is still wrong three times in ten when it says 70, which is what 70 means.

The weak spots are where theory and the data agree they should be. Thin markets are not forecasts at all, and in them longshots are overpriced. Prices months before the close drift toward 50 cents, because waiting costs money and Polymarket pays for the wait on only a handful of markets.

Crypto price markets share one driver and resolve together, so a bad month for Bitcoin looks like miscalibration. Insiders sometimes move prices before the news, which makes the forecast right and the trade unfair. And the dollar arrives only if the oracle agrees that the event happened.

For a trader the useful findings are modest and specific. The mispricing that survives is at the tails: contracts under 5 cents lose a quarter to two fifths of the stake on average, and near-certain favourites earn a fraction of a percent a week, more when they are bought a month or more before the close.

It is about the size of the spread and the fee, which is why it survives. Nothing in the data suggests a general bias that a formula could exploit, and a two-number correction fitted on the past made the future no better.

The people who make money on Polymarket, according to a study of 588 million trades, are mostly the ones who post limit orders and let others cross the spread; the top 1% of profitable accounts took 76.5% of the profits[45].

For an engineer the lessons are the ones from evaluating any model, sharpened by a market’s habits. Accuracy flatters when the classes are unbalanced, and most questions resolve No. Comparisons across horizons are confounded by which questions exist at each horizon, so they have to be made on the same questions.

And a filter on anything that depends on the outcome, a market’s total volume included, manufactures effects that aren’t there. The trap that caught my first sample is the most transferable thing in this post.

entry.summary: Polymarket's prices checked against what happened across almost three million resolved markets: how well calibrated they are, what accuracy figures hide, where longshots and favourites are mispriced, insiders, oracles and the cost of trading

entry.title: AI crypto trading bots: what machine learning and LLMs can and can’t do

link.title: AI crypto trading bots: what machine learning and LLMs can and can’t do

entry.content:
In October 2025 a small lab called Nof1 gave six of the strongest language models $10,000 each and let them trade crypto perpetual futures on Hyperliquid with real money.

Every two or three minutes each model received the same prompt with prices and indicators for six coins and answered with a trade: the coin, long or short, the size, the leverage and a plan for getting out[1].

Seventeen days later Qwen3-Max was up 23% and DeepSeek V3.1 up 5%, while Claude Sonnet 4.5, Grok 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT-5 had lost between a third and two thirds of their money. Bitcoin ended the period where it began.

The results went around social media as a ranking of which model “can trade”. The chart says something more modest.

The grey bands show where a trader with no skill at all, taking the same risk as the models, would end up: two times in three inside the darker band, nineteen times in twenty inside the lighter one.

Every model finished inside the bands, and the winner’s lead is a third of what luck alone would typically give.

Nof1 said as much before the season ended: “We do not expect any of the models to do well, and early successes may be the result of luck.”

Its founder summed up the season with a sentence that is more useful than the leaderboard: “LLMs don’t really handle numerical time series data very well, but that’s all the context we gave them”[2].

Meanwhile, AI has become part of how people trade crypto. In a survey that the exchange MEXC ran among its users in September 2026, 84.8% had used AI for research or trading in the previous six months, and 13% had tried an agent connected to their exchange account[3].

Binance, OKX and Kraken now ship toolkits that let a language model place orders, and regulators keep charging schemes that sold AI trading bots where, in the words of one SEC release, “there were no AI trading bots”[4].

This post tries to separate what models can do in crypto trading from what they are sold for.

I ran the experiments myself on six years of Binance’s public data: gradient boosting that predicts the next hour, a volatility model, almost 800 backtested strategies and 20,000 random ones, two foundation models for time series, and seven open language models asked about Bitcoin’s past.

For ML engineers it explains what makes markets unlike other prediction problems; for traders, what the models actually learn and where the numbers in their marketing come from.

What a model sees in crypto prices

A trading model learns from returns, the relative changes of price from one bar to the next. An hourly return of Bitcoin is \(r_t = \ln(P_t / P_{t-1})\), where \(P_t\) is the price at the close of hour \(t\); for small moves it is the percentage change.

Two facts about these numbers shape everything that follows, and both are easy to see in Binance’s public data.

The first is the shape of their distribution. Measured in standard deviations, most hours are quiet, and a few are wild in a way a normal distribution does not allow:

From January 2021 to the end of October 2026 Bitcoin had 51,057 hours, and 96 of them moved more than six standard deviations. Under a normal law with the same mean and spread, a six-sigma hour happens about once in 58,000 years. Ether and Solana look the same, with 108 and 109 such hours.

For a model this means that a handful of hours carry a large share of the total movement, and a loss function that squares errors is pulled around by them. It also means that any test period without a crash is missing the hours that decide whether a leveraged strategy survives.

The second fact is about memory. The autocorrelation of a series at lag \(k\) is its correlation with itself \(k\) steps earlier. For returns it is close to zero at every lag; for the size of the returns, their absolute value, it is not:

The direction of the last hour says almost nothing about the direction of the next one, but a violent hour is likely to be followed by another violent hour, and that memory lasts for days.

The bumps at 24, 48 and 72 hours are the daily rhythm of trading. The same hours are busy every day: in the hour from 14:00 UTC, around the opening of stock trading in New York, Bitcoin moves 56 bp on average, against 29 bp in the hour from 04:00 (a basis point, bp, is 0.01%).

These two curves are the plan of this post in miniature. Direction is close to unpredictable, so a model that predicts it will be right only a little more often than a coin, and the question is whether that little survives the costs of trading.

Volatility is predictable, and that is where machine learning earns its keep without anyone writing about it.

Predicting the next hour

The experiment is the one a newcomer to quantitative trading usually runs first, done carefully.

Every hour, a model sees what a trader’s screen shows at the close of that hour for Bitcoin, Ether and Solana: returns over the last 1, 2, 4, 8, 24, 72 and 168 hours, Bitcoin’s returns as a market factor, volatility measured from 5-minute candles, volume against its weekly norm, the share of volume bought by takers (traders who cross the spread and pay for immediacy), the range of the last hour, the hour of the day, the day of the week and which coin it is.

Twenty features in all.

It predicts the probability that the next hour closes higher. The model is gradient boosting, LightGBM with shallow trees, the default choice for tabular data and a strong one.

The test has to respect time. Shuffling hours into random training and test sets would let the model learn from the future, so the evaluation is walk-forward:

Every month from January 2022 to October 2026 gets its own model, trained on every hour before that month except the last day, which is kept out so that no training target overlaps the test. The 58 months of predictions, 42,142 hours per coin, form one long out-of-sample record that no model saw while it was trained.

The result is better than I expected. The model calls the direction of Bitcoin’s next hour correctly 53.9% of the time, against 50.5% for always saying “up”; for Ether 53.8%, for Solana 52.9%.

The area under the ROC curve is 0.555 for Bitcoin. Over 42,142 hours a hit rate this far from a coin toss is not luck: its standard error is a quarter of a percentage point.

A result like this deserves suspicion before celebration. The usual cause of a good backtest is a leak, a feature that quietly contains the future. Here the hourly closes rebuilt from 5-minute candles match Binance’s own hourly candles to the cent, and the pattern the model found, described next, survives when the last five minutes before each forecast are skipped.

The feature that carries most of the signal is the simplest: the return of the last couple of hours, with a negative sign. Crypto hourly returns tend to be partly taken back in the next hour.

The rank correlation between consecutive hourly returns of Bitcoin is −0.06 over the test period, small but steady, and it shows plainly in how often an hour moves the same way as the hour before:

A mean-reverting wiggle like this is what liquidity providers are paid for. When an impatient trader pushes the price by buying a lot at once, someone has to sell to them, and that someone expects the price to drift back. The effect was strongest in 2022 and 2023 and weaker in 2025 and 2026.

Where the edge goes

A model that is right 53.9% of the time sounds like a money machine, and this is the moment to look at what trading costs.

Every trade pays a fee, and every market order also pays the spread and walks up the order book. Suppose a strategy opens and closes a position on every bar, and the average absolute move over the bar is \(m\).

It earns \(+m\) when right and \(-m\) when wrong, and pays the round-trip cost \(c\) every time. With hit rate \(p\) the expected profit per bar is

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{profit}] = p\,m - (1 - p)\,m - c = (2p - 1)\,m - c,\]

which is positive only if

\[p > \frac{1}{2} + \frac{c}{2m}.\]

The ratio of cost to typical move decides everything. Bitcoin moves 38 bp in an average hour, and a round trip with taker fees on Binance’s futures costs about 10 bp, so an hourly strategy needs to be right 63% of the time. On 5-minute bars, with an average move of 11 bp, it needs 94%:

The fee is only part of the cost. A market order also crosses the spread and, if it is large, eats into the order book.

I took six snapshots of the books of Binance’s perpetual futures, five minutes apart, and measured what a market buy of a given size costs against the mid price, for contracts ranked by their daily turnover:

For Bitcoin and Ether the book is so deep that even a million-dollar order costs a fraction of a basis point: 0.18 bp for Bitcoin, 1.3 bp for Ether. Further down the list the picture changes quickly.

On the 25th most traded contract, a $100,000 order costs 6 bp before any fee; on the 50th, 11 bp; on the 200th, 87 bp, and the visible book cannot fill a million at all.

These snapshots were taken on a Saturday, a day and a half after Binance disclosed a $6.3 billion hack of one of its hot wallets and suspended withdrawals[5], so the books of small contracts may be thinner than on an ordinary weekday.

The point stands on any day: the smaller the coin, the more of a model’s edge goes to the order book.

Now the model’s trades. The plain strategy is long when the model gives the next hour more than even odds to rise and short otherwise, and it pays a fee whenever it switches sides:

Without fees, a dollar traded on Bitcoin’s forecasts from January 2022 grows to about ten. With 2 bp per side, the fee of a market maker on futures, it loses most of its value; with 5 bp, a taker’s fee, it is gone.

The model switches sides 16 times a day, and a 53.9% hit rate does not pay for that.

It is also worse than 53.9% suggests. When the model is right, the hour moves 31.5 bp on average; when it is wrong, 35.6 bp. It is right more often on the small moves and wrong more often on the large ones, so the hit rate overstates the profit, a pattern that every strategy built on small reversals shares.

The obvious fix is to trade less: keep the current position unless the model’s probability crosses a band around one half, say above 0.55 or below 0.45. A wider band means fewer trades and fewer fees, but also acting on fewer of the model’s opinions:

With a band of ±0.05 the Bitcoin strategy trades 6 times a day instead of 16 and still earns 57% a year before costs (here and below, a year’s hourly returns added up, without compounding).

At 1 bp per side 35% remains, at 2 bp 13%, at 5 bp it loses 53%. A wider band loses the edge before it saves enough on fees. Solana, with larger moves, keeps some profit at 2 bp per side, and none at 5.

So the edge is real, and it belongs to whoever pays the least for trading. A market maker who earns a rebate for resting orders, sits next to the exchange and pays a fraction of a basis point can harvest it; a retail trader paying 5 bp per side through an API cannot, however good the model.

This backtest is also generous: it assumes trades at the exact closing price of the hour, with no delay and no slippage beyond the fee. The real numbers would be worse.

What can be predicted: volatility

The other curve of the autocorrelation chart, the one that stayed high, is where forecasting works. Realized variance is the sum of squared 5-minute returns over a day,

\[RV_t = \sum_{i=1}^{288} r_{t,i}^2,\]

a direct measurement of how much the price moved that day. The HAR model of Corsi (2009) forecasts tomorrow’s value from three averages of it: yesterday’s, the last week’s and the last month’s,

\[\ln RV_{t+1} = \beta_0 + \beta_d \ln RV_t + \beta_w \ln RV^{(w)}_t + \beta_m \ln RV^{(m)}_t + \varepsilon_{t+1}.\]

The three terms stand for traders with different horizons, who react to yesterday, to the last week and to the last month. It is a linear regression with four coefficients, and it is hard to beat[6].

I fitted it the same way as the direction model, refitting every month on all earlier days, and next to it fitted the same regression on returns: tomorrow’s return from yesterday’s, the last week’s and the last month’s.

The score is the out-of-sample \(R^2\), the share of the variation of the target that the forecast explains, against the simplest forecast (the historical mean for volatility, zero for returns):

For volatility \(R^2\) is 0.54 for Bitcoin, 0.57 for Ether and 0.63 for Solana. For returns it is below zero for all three: the forecast does worse than saying “zero” every day.

A volatility forecast is not a trading signal by itself, but it decides how large a position should be. A position scaled by the inverse of forecast volatility keeps its risk roughly constant, small when the market is wild and larger when it is calm:

Holding Solana from 2022 to October 2026 meant a realized volatility of 93% a year and a worst fall of 94.5% from a peak. Scaling the position to a target of 50% held the realized volatility at 48% and cut the worst fall to 72%.

For Bitcoin it raised the Sharpe ratio, the return per unit of volatility, from 0.21 to 0.31. It does not make a bad asset good, but it makes the risk of a strategy predictable, and in a market with six-sigma hours that matters more than a percent of hit rate.

This is the part of machine learning that professional crypto firms use every day and rarely write about: forecasting volatility and liquidity, sizing positions, setting quotes, managing risk. The models are less glamorous than price prediction and much more useful.

The backtest that flatters

Every number so far comes from data the models never saw. Most strategies offered to traders, including many sold as AI, come from the opposite procedure: try many ideas on the same history and keep the one that looks best.

Machine learning engineers know this as overfitting to the validation set; in finance it has its own literature and its own name, backtest overfitting.

To see its size, I ran a grid of the rules every trading textbook contains: moving-average crossovers, breakouts of a price channel, and two kinds of mean reversion (RSI and Bollinger bands), each with a range of parameters, on the hourly candles of twelve large coins.

Sixty-six rules on twelve coins make 792 strategies. Each was scored by its Sharpe ratio, the average return divided by its standard deviation and scaled to a year, after a fee of 5 bp per side, once on 2021-2023 and once on 2024 to October 2026:

The ranking in the first period was not useless: its rank correlation with the second is 0.45, mostly because it identifies the rules that trade too often and lose to fees in any period. Mean reversion with RSI and Bollinger bands lost money in both.

The winners are another matter. The 20 best strategies of 2021-2023 had an average Sharpe ratio of 1.56; from 2024 on, their average was 0.19, and 6 of the 20 lost money. They kept about an eighth of what the backtest promised.

The second experiment removes any doubt about what is skill. Each of 20,000 strategies holds a random position, long or short, and flips it at random about once a day; none of them knows anything. Among \(N\) of them, the best one still looks good, and the more of them one tries, the better the best looks:

Bailey and López de Prado (2014) gave the expected best Sharpe ratio among \(N\) independent trials that have no skill:

\[\mathbb{E}\big[\max_N \widehat{SR}\big] \approx \mathbb{E}\big[\widehat{SR}\big] + \sqrt{V}\left((1-\gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}\!\Big(1 - \frac{1}{N}\Big) + \gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\!\Big(1 - \frac{1}{N e}\Big)\right).\]

Here \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{SR}]\) and \(V\) are the mean and the variance of the estimated Sharpe ratios across the trials, \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the inverse of the standard normal distribution function, \(\gamma \approx 0.5772\) is the Euler-Mascheroni constant and \(e\) is Euler’s number. The formula is the expected maximum of \(N\) normal draws, and it grows like \(\sqrt{2 \ln N}\): slowly, but without limit.

Here the average random strategy has a Sharpe ratio of −0.55, because it pays fees for nothing. The best of 10 has 0.32, the best of 1,000 has 1.20, and the best of 20,000 has 1.56, as good as the 20 best real rules looked in their own past. The formula, with the trials’ average added, follows the experiment closely.

Their deflated Sharpe ratio turns this into a test: it asks how likely the best strategy’s true Sharpe ratio is to be above zero, given how many strategies were tried and how long and fat-tailed the record is[7].

Applied to the best rule of my grid, the in-sample Sharpe ratio of 1.81 is below the 2.04 that the best of 792 trials would be expected to reach by luck, given how much their results differ, and the probability that its true Sharpe ratio is above zero comes out at 35%.

That rule, a crossover of 12- and 24-hour averages on Dogecoin, did well afterwards anyway, with a Sharpe ratio of 1.21. A deflated Sharpe ratio is a probability, not a verdict; what it says is that the backtest alone was not evidence.

The same arithmetic applies to every published result. Harvey, Liu and Zhu counted at least 316 factors that academic papers had tested to explain stock returns and concluded that, after so much searching, a new one should have a t-statistic above 3 rather than the usual 2 to be taken seriously[8].

A seller of a trading bot who shows the best of their backtests is showing the maximum of \(N\) draws, and rarely says what \(N\) was.

Language models as traders

Short records have a second problem besides selection: they are too short to tell skill from luck even for one strategy. Under the simplest assumptions, the standard error of an annualized Sharpe ratio estimated from \(D\) days of crypto trading is about

\[\mathrm{SE}\big(\widehat{SR}\big) \approx \sqrt{\frac{365}{D}},\]

so 17 days of Alpha Arena give an uncertainty of about 4.6. A model would have needed an annualized Sharpe ratio above 9 to stand out from zero.

Trading more often does not help: the precision is set by calendar time, not by the number of decisions[9]. To show that a strategy has a Sharpe ratio of 1, the usual level of a good one, takes about four years of daily returns.

The academic benchmarks of LLM traders run into the same wall. AI-Trader tested six models on ten coins for two weeks of November 2025; five of the six did worse than an index of the same coins[10].

In StockBench, thirteen models traded twenty Dow stocks for four months and returned between −2.8% and +2.5%, against +0.4% for simply holding the stocks; in a second test over the falling market of early 2025, every agent did worse than holding[11].

LiveTradeBench found that a model’s rank on general benchmarks says nothing about its returns: the rank correlation was 0.05[12].

The largest record I know of is the least flattering. A company that runs two fleets of LLM agents published six months of their trades; on Hyperliquid, 500 to 600 user-created agents lost money, won 41% of their round trips against 50% for comparable human retail traders, and used a median leverage of 5 regardless of how volatile the market was.

Liquidations were 3.2% of the closed positions and 74% of the gross loss[13]. It is the operator’s own paper, which makes the result harder, not easier, to dismiss.

Longer tests are possible only on history, and history brings in a problem specific to language models. A model trained on text up to some date has read what happened before it. An LLM asked in 2026 whether to buy Bitcoin on 1 March 2020 may simply remember what came next.

To see how much, I asked seven open models released between May 2024 and February 2026 about Bitcoin, from January 2018 to October 2026.

Each model answered three kinds of questions: what Bitcoin closed at on the 1st and the 15th of every month, whether it went up or down over a given month, and whether it went up or down over a given week.

For the up-or-down questions I did not let the models write an answer; I read the probabilities they gave to “up” and “down” as the first word, so that a model that would rather explain that it cannot know still had to lean one way. The models ran on Kaggle’s GPUs, in 16-bit precision and without any tools or web search.

The price answers show where each model’s knowledge ends:

Mistral 7B, released in May 2024, named Bitcoin’s closing price for dates in 2018 to 2022 with a median error of 3 to 5%; for every date after its release it declined to give a number.

Qwen3.5 9B, released in February 2026, was off by 4 to 5% on dates in 2023 and 2024, still close in January and February 2025, and for every date from March 2025 on it answered “0”: its knowledge ends a year before its release.

Olmo 3 7B had a median error of 9 to 10% for 2023 and 2024 and explained, in one of its refusals, that it had no data “beyond my knowledge cutoff in June 2023”, which its own answers contradict.

None of these models was trained to know prices. They picked them up from the internet the way they picked up everything else.

Direction is what a trading backtest needs, and the models remember it too:

Over the months that ended at least a year before a model’s release, the seven models together called the direction right 60.0% of the time, in 525 answers; over the months after their release, 46.8% of 126.

Each model’s answers are split at its own median probability, so that a model that says “up” to everything is judged by how it orders the months.

The newest models have only a few months after their release, so their grey bars are noisy; the pooled numbers are not. For weeks the effect is smaller, 53.3% against 49.0%, probably because far less is written about single weeks than about months.

Now suppose someone builds a trading strategy on these answers and backtests it on 2018-2026, as one would with any signal:

Trading OLMo 2’s monthly answers turns a dollar into 245 between January 2018 and November 2024, while holding Bitcoin turns it into 7. After the model’s release in December 2024 the same strategy loses 19% over 22 months.

Nothing in the backtest is wrong except the one thing that matters: the model had read the answers. Across the seven models, the strategy multiplied money by 8 to 245 before each model’s release and by 0.54 to 1.31 after it.

This is not a curiosity. Lopez-Lira, Tang and Zhu asked GPT-4o for daily levels of the S&P 500: before its training cutoff the error was 0.61%, after it 16.87%.

Telling the model to ignore what it knows did not help, and anonymizing companies did not either: from an earnings call with the names removed, it identified Apple, Meta and Microsoft every time[14].

When five published LLM trading agents were rerun on a period after their model’s cutoff, with a market return similar to their original period, their returns fell by 50 to 72%[15].

Over twenty years of data instead of a few months, holding the stocks beat the two best-known LLM trading agents in every setup[16].

There are fixes. Point-in-time models are trained only on text available up to a given date, one model per year, so that a backtest for 2015 uses a model that has never read 2016[17].

Their authors found the bias modest for one task, ranking stocks by the tone of the day’s news, which is a reminder that the size of the problem depends on what the model is asked.

For anything that names a coin and a date, the only clean test is the one that runs after the model was trained, live, for long enough.

Where language models help

None of this makes language models useless to a trader. They are weak at the job that is easiest to sell, taking prices in and sending trades out, and good at several jobs around it.

The clearest case is research. Man Group, one of the largest quantitative hedge funds, describes a pipeline of LLM agents in which one proposes hypotheses, another writes the code to test them on the firm’s data and a third runs the statistical tests; in their words, “whether generated by human or AI, every strategy entering live trading must pass identical thresholds”[18].

The thresholds matter because a model that writes a hundred strategies an hour is the fastest way yet to make \(N\) in the overfitting formula large.

Code is the second case. Coinbase says that between 95% and 100% of its code is now written by or with LLMs[19].

Data pipelines, backtests, exchange connectors and monitoring are where a trading team spends most of its time, and a model that writes them faster saves more than one that guesses the next candle. Reading is the third: whitepapers, governance proposals, the code of a smart contract.

Anthropic’s red team found that models could write working exploits for half of 405 smart contracts that had been hacked in the past, in simulation, and found two new vulnerabilities in recently deployed contracts[20]; the same skill reviews a contract before one deposits into it, and attacks it for someone else.

News is the case everyone expects to work. The evidence is thin: a 2026 study scored Bitcoin news with ChatGPT and found that the sentiment improved the fit in sample but added nothing significant out of sample[21].

Professional market makers, for their part, still hire for older skills. A recent job advertisement of Wintermute, one of the largest, asks a machine learning researcher to “develop ML-based alpha generation models using high-frequency order book and market microstructure data” and does not mention language models[22].

Forecasting events, rather than prices, is where language models have come furthest. On ForecastBench, a benchmark of questions about the future, several systems were by July 2026 “statistically indistinguishable from superforecaster-level accuracy”, and on questions taken from prediction markets one ranked above the superforecasters’ median for the first time; the human forecasts it was compared with were collected in 2024[23].

The money that bots have demonstrably made in prediction markets comes from something plainer: buying a set of outcomes that must together pay $1 for less than $1. On Polymarket this kind of arbitrage extracted an estimated $40 million in a year[24].

Then there are foundation models for time series, Transformers pretrained on millions of series in the way language models are pretrained on text.

Kronos was trained on more than 12 billion candles from 45 exchanges and reads open, high, low, close and volume as tokens[25]; Chronos-2 is a general forecaster from Amazon[26].

I found no independent test of them on crypto returns, so I ran one: both models, without fine-tuning, forecast every hour of 2026 for Bitcoin, Ether and Solana from the 512 hours before, and Chronos-2 also forecast daily volatility.

Neither model knows the direction of the next hour. Chronos-2 was right 49.2 to 49.6% of the time, slightly worse than a coin, and said “up” in 66 to 75% of the hours: from a series of hourly returns it learned mostly that the average is a little above zero.

Kronos-small was right 49.6 to 52.2% of the time on the hours it forecast; with 1,812 hours per coin, a deviation of one or two points from 50% is within noise.

The gradient-boosting model with its twenty hand-made features did better on the same months, which is what one would expect from a model trained on this very market.

Volatility tells the same story as before. Chronos-2, which has never been trained on crypto in particular, forecast tomorrow’s log volatility with an \(R^2\) of 0.64 to 0.67 against the average of the previous 512 days; the HAR regression with four coefficients scored 0.77 to 0.89 on the same days.

A large pretrained model learned that volatility clusters, and a model built around that fact still knows it better.

Independent tests on stock returns found the same: zero-shot Chronos and TimesFM had negative out-of-sample \(R^2\) on returns, where gradient boosting was close to zero[27], and on realized volatility only a tiny model beat the logarithmic HAR[28].

Agents with keys

In crypto, “AI agent” first meant something other than a trading system. In 2024 a chatbot called Truth Terminal, which posted on X, received a $50,000 research grant in bitcoin from Marc Andreessen and then promoted a memecoin that someone else had launched[29].

Tokens of other “AI agents” followed, and at their peak around the turn of 2025 they were worth about $16 billion together; most have since fallen by more than 90%[30]. In August 2026 the founder of ai16z, a token once worth $2.4 billion, wrote: “The token is dead. Completely”[31].

The agents themselves outlived their tokens, and the interesting question about them is not price but security. A program that reads the internet and can move money is a new kind of target, because everything it reads is text, and a language model treats text as a possible instruction.

The first public demonstration was a game. Freysa was an agent with a wallet and one rule, never to send the money; players paid a rising fee per message to try to talk it into doing so.

After 482 attempts one player convinced it that its transfer function was for receiving funds, offered a donation, and took the prize of $47,316[32].

The real incidents are less elegant. In March 2025 someone with access to the dashboard of AIXBT, an agent that posts market commentary, queued two replies that made it send about 55 ETH, some $100,000, from its wallet; the team said it was “not a result of agent manipulation”, which makes it an ordinary access-control failure with an AI attached[33].

In May 2026 an attacker sent Grok’s wallet a membership NFT that widened what the wallet was allowed to transfer, then posted a message in Morse code; Grok decoded it into an instruction to a trading bot, Bankrbot, which sent 3 billion DRB tokens, worth about $150,000 to $200,000[34]. No key was stolen and no contract had a bug.

Memory makes this worse. Researchers at Princeton showed that an attacker can plant a false instruction in an agent’s long-term memory through an ordinary conversation, and the agent later acts on it when other users make legitimate requests. In their summary, “even the strongest models followed poisoned memories more than half the time”[35].

The tools around the model are a supply chain of their own. Of 2,857 skills in one open marketplace for agents, a security firm found 341 malicious, 163 of them dressed as crypto tools and prediction-market bots[36].

An MCP server published on npm asked for a wallet’s private key to “auto-sign” payments and sent it to a remote server with every call[37].

Of 428 third-party routers that resell access to LLM APIs, researchers found nine that injected malicious code, and one that drained ETH from a key planted as bait[38].

Even the news can be an attack: altering headlines with invisible characters on a single day cut a sentiment-trading system’s annual return by up to 17.7 percentage points[39].

The exchanges’ agent toolkits of 2026 have converged on the same defence. Binance’s lets agents trade from a walled-off sub-account but not move assets to an external wallet[40].

OKX signs orders on the user’s machine, so that “the AI client sends only trading intent”, and offers a mode with simulated funds[41]; Kraken’s command-line tool has a local paper-trading engine[42]. A key that cannot withdraw prevents theft. It does nothing against an agent that loses money by trading.

The design that follows from all this is old-fashioned. The model reads untrusted text and proposes; ordinary code decides, with limits on position size, leverage and daily loss that the model cannot change.

Memory is per user and is treated as untrusted input too. Tools come from sources one has read. And the model never holds a key that can send funds anywhere.

Bots that sell returns

Every claim in the previous sections can be checked against data. The market for “AI trading bots” mostly cannot, and regulators have been warning about it for years.

In January 2024 the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission published an advisory titled “AI Won’t Turn Trading Bots into Money Machines”, with a sentence that could close this post: “AI technology can’t predict the future or sudden market changes”[43].

Its main example was Mirror Trading International, which collected at least 29,421 bitcoin, worth $1.7 billion, from about 23,000 Americans for a trading “bot”[44]. In the advisory’s words, “in reality, very little money was actually traded.” The schemes of 2026 have updated the vocabulary, not the method.

In September the SEC charged two groups that sold access to AI trading bots and signals through WhatsApp; of one of them it wrote that “there were no AI trading bots and deposited funds never were used to earn returns for investors”[4].

On 29 October 2026 it sued a pair of companies that took more than $130 million for trading signals with a claimed accuracy of 99.6% and promised that “the monthly fund return rate is at least 60%”[45].

Sixty percent a month turns $1,000 into $281,000 in a year and into $22 million in three. A strategy that did this would not need investors.

The arithmetic of the earlier sections gives a better sense of scale: a model that is right 54% of the time on the next hour of Bitcoin, close to the best that published studies report, loses money at ordinary fees.

The losses are large. In 2025 Americans reported $7.2 billion lost to crypto investment fraud, the largest category of all in the FBI’s annual report, and more than $632 million in investment complaints where AI was mentioned[46].

Chainalysis found that scam operations that bought AI tools, from face swapping to text generation, earned 4.5 times as much as those that did not[47]. And in a survey by the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, 44% of investors aged 18 to 40 believed that financial information generated by AI is regulated[48].

Strategies that do not need a forecast

Some of the steadiest money in crypto is made without predicting anything. A perpetual future is a contract that tracks a coin and never expires; to keep its price close to the coin’s, the side that is more crowded pays the other side every eight hours.

This payment is the funding rate. When more traders want to be long with leverage, which in crypto is most of the time, longs pay shorts.

Buying a coin and shorting the same amount of its perpetual cancels out the price risk and collects the funding. This is the cash-and-carry trade, and on Binance the rate defaults to 0.01% per eight hours, about 11% a year, when the two prices agree. What it actually paid looks like this:

In 2021 the trade earned 30.6% a year on Bitcoin and 37.5% on Ether, from nothing but other traders’ appetite for leverage. Since then the Bitcoin trade has paid between 4 and 12% a year, and 3.1% in 2026 to the end of October, with a quarter of the payments going the other way.

A study at the BIS found crypto carry averaging more than 10% a year and sometimes reaching 60%[49]; the shrinking yield of recent years is what one would expect once a trade is easy to see and easy to automate.

Market-neutral is not risk-free. On the evening of 10 October 2025, after an announcement of new US tariffs on China, Bitcoin fell 12.6% on Binance in eighty minutes, Ether 14.1% and Solana 17.8%. More than $19 billion of leveraged positions were liquidated across exchanges.

Where insurance funds could not absorb the losses, exchanges closed profitable positions of other traders to cover them, a mechanism called auto-deleveraging, and among the positions closed were the short hedges of market makers[50].

On Hyperliquid alone it closed $2.1 billion of positions in twelve minutes[51]. A hedged trader whose hedge is closed by the exchange is no longer hedged.

The other risk is the exchange itself. A carry position lives on an exchange, and while I was writing this post the largest one stopped withdrawals after the hack mentioned above. A position that is neutral to the price of Bitcoin is not neutral to the solvency of the venue that holds it.

A realistic picture

Put together, the experiments draw a consistent picture, and it is less exciting than the advertising and more useful.

What machine learning does well in crypto is to forecast the things that have memory: volatility, volume, liquidity, the cost of trading.

These forecasts size positions, set quotes, route orders and keep a leveraged book alive through an hour like the evening of 10 October 2025. This is where the firms that make money from crypto markets put their models, and it rarely makes headlines.

Direction is a different matter. Short-horizon patterns exist, like the hourly reversal my model found, and other studies find them too: hit rates of 51 to 56% for Bitcoin from one minute to an hour ahead, with every model losing money once a round trip costs 30 bp[52]; on hourly Bitcoin bars from 2018 to 2026, models that earned 74 to 182% a year before costs lost 64 to 99% after a cost of 10 bp per trade[53].

Such an edge belongs to whoever trades most cheaply, which means market makers, not someone paying taker fees through an API.

Language models are good research assistants, programmers and readers of documents. As autonomous traders they have not shown skill in any test long and clean enough to tell, they remember the history they are tested on, and an agent with keys is a security problem before it is a trading strategy.

For an ML engineer moving into this field, the habits that matter are the ones markets punish for skipping: splitting by time with a gap, putting costs into the evaluation and not after it, counting how many variants were tried, thinking of a Sharpe ratio as an estimate with a standard error, and testing language models only on dates after their training.

For a trader, the same habits turn into questions to ask about any AI product. How many strategies were tried before this one was shown? How long is the live record, and does it include fees?

Were the backtest dates after the model’s training cutoff? Who holds the keys, and can they withdraw? And an offer of a fixed monthly return is not a trading product at all.

There is also a question for the market as a whole. Central banks have started to worry that many traders using the same few models will act alike; the Bank of England warned that more advanced AI trading strategies “could lead to firms taking increasingly correlated positions and acting in a similar way during a stress”[54].

In Alpha Arena, four of the six models, given the same prompt, moved together with hourly correlations between 0.52 and 0.83.

In a market where many agents read the same news with the same model, a crowded trade can form in minutes, and the hour that unwinds it is the kind that sits in the tails of the first chart of this post.
