entry.summary: AI trading bots and LLM agents tested on six years of Binance data: what machine learning predicts, what trading fees eat, and why LLM backtests lie

entry.title: Mixture of experts: why the largest LLMs use a few percent of their weights per token

link.title: Mixture of experts: why the largest LLMs use a few percent of their weights per token

entry.content:
DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion parameters and uses 37 billion of them for each token. Kimi K2 has a trillion and uses 32 billion, gpt-oss-120b uses 5.1 billion of its 117, and some names spell the arithmetic out: Qwen3-235B-A22B has 235 billion parameters, 22 billion of them active.

In every layer of these models a small router looks at the token and picks a few feed-forward networks, the experts, out of dozens or hundreds. Only those are computed. The rest of the weights wait in memory for tokens that need them.

The idea is older than the Transformer. In 1991 Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton described systems “composed of many separate networks, each of which learns to handle a subset of the complete set of training cases”[1].

In 2017 Shazeer and colleagues put a layer of up to 131,072 experts between the layers of an LSTM language model[2], and today the largest open models of DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot, OpenAI, Meta, Zhipu and MiniMax are all mixtures of experts.

This post builds a mixture-of-experts layer in PyTorch, trains it next to dense models of the same cost on English, Russian and Python code, and looks inside: what the router decides, why it has to be kept from playing favourites, what the experts end up specialising in, and what it takes to serve a model whose weights are mostly idle.

Where a Transformer keeps its parameters

A layer of a Transformer has two parts. Attention moves information between tokens: each token looks at the earlier ones and takes what it needs from them.

The feed-forward network then works on every token separately, with the same weights for all of them: it multiplies the token’s vector by a wide matrix, passes the result through a nonlinearity and multiplies it by a second matrix back to the original width. In modern models it is a SwiGLU network with three matrices:

\[\mathrm{FFN}(x) = W_{\text{down}}\big(\mathrm{silu}(W_{\text{gate}}\, x) \odot W_{\text{up}}\, x\big).\]

Here \(x\) is the token’s vector of width \(d\), \(W_{\text{gate}}\) and \(W_{\text{up}}\) map it to a hidden width \(h\), usually three to five times \(d\), the elementwise product \(\odot\) lets one projection switch the other on and off, and \(W_{\text{down}}\) maps the result back to width \(d\).

Most of a model’s weights are in these networks. Qwen3-32B has 64 layers of width 5,120 with feed-forward networks of width 25,600, and its config gives the exact split:

The feed-forward networks hold 25.2 billion of its 32.8 billion parameters, 77%; attention has 6.0 billion and the embeddings 1.6. Qwen3-235B-A22B, a mixture of experts of the same family, turns the picture around. Of its 235 billion parameters a token passes through 22 billion, and 213 billion, 91% of the model, are experts that this token does not use.

Every weight a token passes through costs two operations, a multiplication and an addition, so a dense model of 32 billion parameters spends about 64 billion operations on every token it reads or writes, and most of them in the feed-forward networks.

What do these networks do with so many weights? Geva and colleagues read the two matrices as a memory.

Each row of the first matrix is a key that responds to some pattern in the input, each column of the second is a value added to the output when its key responds, and the network’s output is the sum of the values whose keys fired.

In their words, feed-forward layers “operate as key-value memories, where each key correlates with textual patterns in the training examples”[3].

A memory of 25,600 patterns of which a given token needs a few, read in full for every token, is an obvious candidate for economy. The idea of the mixture of experts is to cut it into many smaller networks and let every token use only some of them.

A layer of experts

A mixture-of-experts layer replaces the one feed-forward network with \(E\) smaller ones, the experts, and adds a router: a matrix \(W_r\) that gives every expert a score for the current token. A softmax turns the scores into probabilities, the token goes to the \(k\) experts with the highest ones, and its output is their outputs added with weights:

\[p = \mathrm{softmax}(W_r\, x), \qquad \mathcal{T} = \text{the } k \text{ largest of } p_1, \dots, p_E, \qquad y = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}} \frac{p_i}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{T}} p_j}\, E_i(x).\]

Term by term: \(W_r\) is an \(E \times d\) matrix, so the router is a single linear layer, tiny next to the experts. \(p_i\) is how much the router trusts expert \(i\) with this token.

\(\mathcal{T}\) is the set of the \(k\) chosen experts; the others are not computed at all, which is the whole point. The weights are the chosen probabilities divided by their sum, so they add up to one, and each \(E_i\) is an ordinary SwiGLU network, only narrower than the dense one.

The models trained below have experts of width 384 and send every token to 2 of 8, so a token passes through 768 hidden units, as in a dense layer of width 768, while the layer holds 3,072.

Here is what the router of one of them, after training, does with the Russian word “президент” in a sentence it has not seen:

The router hesitates over this token. Experts 5 and 6 get 0.36 and 0.32 of the probability, and the other six share the remaining third, expert 4 most of it with 0.10.

The two largest probabilities are kept and divided by their sum, 0.68, which turns them into weights 0.53 and 0.47, so the token’s output is roughly half of what expert 5 computes and half of what expert 6 computes. Experts 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 and 8 never see the token at all.

The router learns with the rest of the model. Its gradient comes through the weights \(p_i / \sum_j p_j\): if expert 3’s output would have lowered the loss more than expert 7’s, the gradient raises \(p_3\) relative to \(p_7\), and the next similar token is more likely to go to expert 3.

Nothing tells the router what an expert should be good at. Specialisation, if any, appears because sending similar tokens to the same expert makes that expert better at them.

In code the layer is a loop over experts, each taking the tokens that chose it:

def moe(x, router, experts, k):
    probs = (x @ router).softmax(dim=-1)              # (tokens, experts)
    top_probs, top_experts = probs.topk(k, dim=-1)    # the k best experts of every token
    weights = top_probs / top_probs.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    out = torch.zeros_like(x)
    for e, expert in enumerate(experts):
        rows, slot = torch.nonzero(top_experts == e, as_tuple=True)   # tokens that chose e
        out[rows] += weights[rows, slot, None] * expert(x[rows])
    return out

Whether this loop is slow depends on how many tokens each expert gets. Every pass launches a few matrix products, and a GPU is efficient only when a product is large enough to keep all of its cores busy.

In training, with thousands of tokens in a batch and a handful of experts, each expert gets plenty of them. With hundreds of experts, or in decoding, where a step has one token per sequence, each expert gets a few rows, and the loop spends its time launching kernels and gathering rows instead of multiplying.

The usual remedy is to sort the token-expert pairs by expert, so that every expert’s tokens lie next to each other, and to run all the experts at once:

My version pads every expert’s queue to the length of the longest, rounded up to a multiple of 256 so that the GPU sees few different shapes, and multiplies all of them by the stacked expert weights in one batched product.

It agrees with a reference that runs every expert on every token and multiplies the unchosen ones by zero, to rounding error.

Production kernels avoid even the padding: MegaBlocks writes the layer as a block-sparse matrix product[4], and DeepSeek’s DeepGEMM library has grouped products that take the experts’ tokens concatenated one after another, each expert’s segment padded only to the kernel’s block size.

Same compute, more parameters

What does a mixture buy? To see it on a small scale, I trained four models on a corpus of three kinds of text: English Wikipedia, Russian Wikipedia and the Python standard library, 8 million tokens of each, with a tokenizer of 8,192 tokens trained on the same mix (code).

All four have 6 layers of width 256 with 4 attention heads, rotary positions and RMSNorm, and differ only in the feed-forward layers.

The dense model has SwiGLU networks of width 768 and 7.2 million parameters in all. The mixture with 8 experts sends every token to 2 experts of width 384: it does the same work per token as the dense model, with 7.2 million active parameters, but holds 17.8 million.

The mixture with 32 experts cuts the same budget finer, 8 of 32 experts of width 96. The fourth model is dense with networks of width 3,072: as many parameters as the mixtures, every one of them used for every token, at about two and a half times the compute.

Each model trained three times, with different seeds, for 3,000 steps of 32 sequences of 256 tokens, about 25 million tokens, on an NVIDIA T4 on Kaggle, with the auxiliary balancing loss described below for the mixtures.

At the same compute per token, the mixture with 8 experts ends with a validation loss of 2.985 on average over the three seeds, against 3.062 for the dense model.

The three seeds of the dense model end within 0.024 of each other and those of the mixture within 0.008, so a gap of 0.077 is not noise, and the mixture is better on each kind of text: by 0.08 on English, 0.10 on Russian and 0.06 on Python.

The dense model with networks four times wider, as many parameters as the mixture and all of them working on every token, reaches 2.948, and until about step 1,750 the mixtures are even ahead of it.

The mixture gets two thirds of the way from the small dense model to the large one while computing as much as the small one.

Compute per token is not the same thing as time. Here is how long one training step takes, with the experts run by the loop shown earlier and by the sorted, batched version:

The mixture with 8 experts takes 31% longer than the dense model that does the same arithmetic, and the one with 32 experts 76% longer: routing, sorting and gathering the tokens are work that a count of multiplications doesn’t show.

The dense model with networks four times wider takes 307 milliseconds, more than twice as long as the narrow one. The loop itself turns out to be harmless here.

With 8 experts a batch of 8,192 tokens gives each expert about 2,000 of them, and the loop is as fast as the batched version, 189 against 188 milliseconds per step; with 32 narrower experts it is 21% slower.

Keeping the experts busy

Left alone, the router has a bad habit. Early in training some expert happens to be a little better than the others, the router sends it more tokens, it trains on more data and gets better still, and the router sends it even more.

The other experts get few tokens, learn little and stay unattractive. Shazeer and colleagues, who brought mixtures of experts to large networks, observed this “self-reinforcing” imbalance and countered it with an extra loss[2].

I trained the mixture with 8 experts in three versions: without any balancing, with the loss described below, and with the bias method that comes after it.

Without balancing, the busiest expert of a layer has 2.6 to 3.1 times its fair share of the tokens by step 200, and nothing ever reverses it.

On held-out text, in three of the six layers of the first of these models a single expert receives 94 to 98% of the tokens, and 9 of the 48 experts get less than a tenth of an even share. They are practically dead: their weights take memory and learn almost nothing.

With the balancing loss, the busiest expert stays at about 1.1 times an even share for the whole run. The unbalanced mixture is still better than the dense model, 3.013 against 3.062, but worse than the balanced one and less predictable: its three seeds end between 2.991 and 3.030.

The balancing loss most models use comes from the Switch Transformer[5]. For a batch of tokens, let \(f_i\) be the share of the token-expert assignments that went to expert \(i\), and \(P_i\) the mean probability the router gave expert \(i\) over the same tokens. The loss is

\[L_{\text{balance}} = \alpha \cdot E \sum_{i=1}^{E} f_i\, P_i ,\]

added to the language modelling loss with a small weight \(\alpha\), 0.01 in the Switch Transformer and in my runs. When the router is perfectly even, \(f_i = P_i = 1/E\) and the sum times \(E\) is 1. When it favours some experts, their large \(f_i\) meet large \(P_i\) and the sum grows.

The two factors play different roles. \(f_i\) is a count of decisions, and a count has no gradient. \(P_i\) is an average of softmax outputs and has one.

So the loss pushes down the probabilities of experts that are already busy, in proportion to how busy they are, and the next tokens drift to the others. Here are both factors in two trained routers, one trained with the loss and one without:

In layer 3 of the router trained without the loss, expert 2 gets 49% of the assignments, and the router’s mean probability for it is 0.58, so the router is not hesitating between experts, it is sure of its favourite.

Experts 1 and 8 get almost nothing. The loss would be 2.68 for this router. For the router trained with it, it is 1.00, and its eight experts all get between 11% and 16% of the assignments.

The extra loss has a cost: its gradient flows into the same weights as the language modelling loss and pulls them towards a goal that has nothing to do with predicting text.

Wang and colleagues at DeepSeek proposed balancing without a loss[6], and DeepSeek-V3 uses their method[7]. Every expert gets a bias \(b_i\) that is added to its score when the \(k\) experts are chosen, and only then:

\[\mathcal{T} = \text{the } k \text{ largest of } p_1 + b_1, \dots, p_E + b_E, \qquad \text{weights from } p_i \text{ alone}.\]

After every training step, the bias of each expert that got fewer tokens than the average goes up by a small step \(\gamma\), and the bias of each one that got more goes down by \(\gamma\).

The biases are not learned by gradient descent and don’t touch the model’s weights; they act like a traffic controller that keeps nudging the queues until they are even. I used \(\gamma = 0.001\), the value DeepSeek-V3 used for most of its training.

The biases start at zero and move by 0.001 a step, so they need time: for the first 200 steps the busiest expert gets one and a half to two times its share.

From about step 500 on, the biases keep the load more even than the loss does, 1.02 times an even share at the end against 1.10 to 1.13.

In quality the two are the same at my scale: 2.981 with the biases and 2.985 with the loss, while the seeds of each spread over 0.014 and 0.008.

DeepSeek’s comparison on models with a billion parameters is hardly more decisive: a validation loss of 2.253 with the biases, 2.258 with a balancing loss computed over each sequence, and 2.253 with one computed over the whole batch, as mine is[7].

A fixed budget per expert

Balancing on average is not enough when the experts sit on different GPUs. Each GPU has to reserve memory for the tokens its experts will receive before it knows how many will come, and the shapes of the arrays on an accelerator are fixed in advance.

The Switch Transformer and GShard therefore give every expert a capacity, a fixed number of slots per batch[8]:

\[C = c \cdot \frac{T\, k}{E},\]

where \(T\) is the number of tokens in the batch, \(T k / E\) is what each expert would get with perfectly even routing, and the capacity factor \(c\), usually between 1 and 2, leaves room for unevenness.

Tokens beyond the capacity are dropped by that expert. A dropped token loses that expert’s contribution; if all its experts are full, it passes through the layer unchanged, carried only by the residual connection.

For the balanced routers a capacity factor of 1 is tight: any unevenness overflows, and 5 to 6% of the assignments are dropped. At 1.25 the share falls to 1% or less, and at 1.5 practically nothing is dropped.

The router trained without balancing is another story. At a capacity factor of 1 it drops a third of the assignments, and even at 2 it drops 15%, because its favourite experts receive nearly four times their share.

The dropped assignments cost more than their share suggests. On the held-out sequences of this analysis, the loss of the mixture with the balancing loss is 2.97 without a limit, 3.21 with 6% of the assignments dropped and 3.01 with 1%. My models were trained without a capacity limit and never learned to do without a missing expert.

A model trained with one adapts: the Switch Transformer saw “typically <1%” of tokens dropped[5], and the ST-MoE study found that models “dropping 10-15% of tokens can perform approximately as well as models that drop <1%”[9].

Dropping tokens is a compromise between quality and the cost of padding, and newer systems avoid it. MegaBlocks computes the experts as one block-sparse product in which every expert gets exactly the rows it was sent[4], and DeepSeek-V3 drops no tokens in training or inference, relying on balancing to keep the load even[7].

What the experts learn

Nobody tells an expert what to specialise in, so it is a fair question whether they specialise at all. My corpus makes it easy to see: a third English, a third Russian, a third Python, three kinds of text that differ in alphabet, vocabulary and structure. If an expert’s tokens are split evenly between the three, it has no preference.

The early layers have little preference. In layers 2 and 3 no expert gets more than about half of its tokens from one kind of text, and the preference grows with depth: three experts of layer 4 lean to one kind, five of layer 5.

In layer 6 the experts have divided the languages between them. Five of the eight get 83 to 96% of their tokens from one kind of text, two from Python, two from Russian and one from English; a sixth leans to English with 59%, and two remain mixed.

The first layer stands apart from its neighbours: one of its experts gets 83% of its tokens from Russian text, another 67% from Python.

Here is the same thing token by token, on three short snippets of held-out text. Each token is coloured by the expert it goes to first:

In the first layer the router sorts tokens by what they look like. Its Russian expert takes президент and most of the pieces into which the tokenizer cut the names Либерии, Чарльз and Кинг: Л, иб, Ч, ар, ль, з, Д, Б, инг.

Python’s =, _, (), try and newlines go to an expert that leans to code. English has no expert of its own in this layer at all. At this depth a token’s vector is still mostly the token itself, and the router has little else to go on.

In the last layer, 10 of the 13 English tokens, 14 of the 17 Russian ones and 9 of the 16 Python ones go to an expert of their own kind.

All the others but one go to the two mixed experts of this layer, and most of them are tokens the three kinds of text share: the numbers 3 and 21, the full stops after the initials Д. and Б., and in Python the brackets, colons, the underscore and newlines.

The last layer prepares the prediction of the next token, and what the next token can be depends first of all on the language.

Specialisation by topic, the kind people usually hope for, is much weaker in large models. Mistral looked for experts on topics in Mixtral and did not find them: “the distribution of expert assignment is very similar for ArXiv papers (written in Latex), for biology (PubMed Abstracts), and for Philosophy (PhilPapers) documents”.

What they found instead was syntax: “in code, the indentation tokens are always assigned to the same experts, particularly at the first and last layers where the hidden states are more correlated to the input and output of the model”[10].

In OLMoE, trained from scratch with 64 small experts per layer, the specialisation is stronger: “for arXiv, which has a very specific distribution with lots of scientific text, the first expert in layer 0 is nearly 100% specialized”, and “vocabulary specialization is higher in later layers”[11].

Languages are a case of their own. The ST-MoE study found that “experts trained on multilingual mixtures do not exhibit language specialization” and blamed the balancing: a group of tokens over which the loss was computed held only one or a few languages, so every expert had to take every language to keep the load even within the group[9].

My batches mix all three kinds of text, and an English expert can stay busy on the English part of every batch.

Smaller experts, and one for everybody

An expert in Mixtral[10] is as wide as the whole feed-forward network of Mistral 7B, whose architecture Mixtral otherwise shares, and a token picks 2 of 8.

DeepSeekMoE argued that this is too coarse: with only 8 experts, each has to cover a broad mix of tokens, and knowledge that all of them need is learned several times over[12]. Their remedy has two parts.

The first is to cut every expert into \(m\) smaller ones and route each token to \(m\) times as many, which keeps the parameters and the compute the same and multiplies the number of combinations a token can choose from: in their example, top-2 of 16 experts allows 120 combinations, top-8 of 64 quarter-size experts “4,426,165,368 potential combinations”.

The second is to set aside shared experts that every token passes through, for what all tokens need, so that the routed experts can specialise.

In my models the finer cut made no difference. The mixture with 32 experts ends at 2.983 and the one with 8 at 2.985, well within the spread of the seeds, and the finer one costs more time, 253 milliseconds per step against 188, because routing, sorting and gathering grow with the number of experts. It does take dropped tokens better.

With a capacity factor of 1 it loses the same 6% of its assignments as the coarse mixture, but its loss rises by 0.10 instead of 0.24: a dropped assignment takes away one of a token’s eight experts instead of one of two.

The case for finer experts was made on larger models. DeepSeekMoE’s smallest comparison is at 2 billion parameters, where “DeepSeekMoE 2B achieves comparable performance with GShard 2.9B”[12], a hundred times the size of my models, trained on far more than my 25 million tokens.

Mixtures in real models

Here are the experts of open models as their config files describe them, in the order the models came out:

Three things changed over these two and a half years. The experts multiplied and shrank. Mixtral has 8 experts of width 14,336 per layer, DeepSeek-V3 256 of width 2,048, Kimi K3 896.

Moonshot measured the effect directly for Kimi K2: at a fixed number of active parameters, “increasing the total number of experts (i.e., increasing sparsity) consistently lowers both the training and validation loss”, and they settled on 8 of 384 as a balance between quality and the cost of the infrastructure[13].

Krajewski and colleagues reached the same conclusion from scaling laws: setting the size of experts to match the dense feed-forward layer “is not optimal at almost any computational budget”[14].

The active share fell accordingly, from 28% in Mixtral to 3–5% in the models of the past year. A model now holds twenty to thirty times as many parameters as it uses for a token.

The shared expert did not convince everyone. DeepSeek, Moonshot, Zhipu and the newer Qwen models use one or two; the OLMoE team found that “sharing an expert performs slightly worse” and left it out[11], and Qwen3 also has none[15].

Not every layer is a mixture either. DeepSeek-V3 keeps its first three layers dense, and Llama 4 Maverick alternates dense and mixture layers, with a token going to 1 of 128 routed experts plus a shared one[16].

Serving a model that is mostly idle

The first cost of a mixture is memory. Every expert has to be at hand, because any token may need any of them, so DeepSeek-V3 needs room for all 671 billion parameters, about 671 GB at one byte per parameter in FP8, more than the 640 GB of a server with eight 80 GB GPUs.

OpenAI made gpt-oss-120b fit on one GPU by storing the experts, which hold “90+% of the total parameter count”, in a 4-bit format, MXFP4: “quantizing these to MXFP4 enables the larger model to fit on a single 80GB GPU”[17].

A model with all its experts in memory reads only a few of them for each token. At a batch of one, the case of a chatbot on a laptop, a decoding step reads the attention weights and \(k\) experts per layer and nothing else.

Decoding is limited by how fast weights come from memory, not by arithmetic, so the step costs about as much as in a dense model of the active size.

This is why models like Qwen3-30B-A3B are popular on laptops: they need the memory of a 30-billion-parameter model but read only about 3 billion parameters per token. llama.cpp even has options to keep the experts in the computer’s main memory while the rest of the model sits on the GPU, --cpu-moe for all of them and --n-cpu-moe N for the first N layers[18]; the GPU then holds what every token needs, and each token reads only its few experts from the slower memory.

A server decodes many conversations at once, and every conversation’s token picks its own experts. If the router spreads tokens evenly, a given expert is skipped by one token with probability \(1 - k/E\), and by all \(B\) tokens of a batch with probability \((1 - k/E)^B\). The expected share of experts a decoding step has to read is therefore

\[1 - \left(1 - \frac{k}{E}\right)^{B}.\]

My router with 8 of 32 experts sits exactly on its curve: a decoding step needs 25% of the experts for one sequence, 90% for 8 and all of them from 32 on, as if every token picked its experts at random.

A model with a smaller share per token holds out longer. DeepSeek-V3, with 8 of 256, reads 3% of its routed experts for one sequence, 40% for 16 and 87% for 64, and from about 128 sequences on, nearly all of them.

So the saving in memory traffic that makes a mixture fast at a batch of one disappears at the batch sizes a server runs at. What remains is the saving in arithmetic: each expert multiplies only the tokens that chose it.

To turn that into speed, a server needs enough tokens per expert to keep each product efficient, and that is what expert parallelism is for: the experts are spread over many GPUs, every GPU holds a few of them, and tokens travel to their experts and back.

DeepSeek described its production setup for V3 and R1 in early 2025. Its reasoning is the same: “the model’s high sparsity necessitates an extremely large overall batch size. This ensures sufficient batch size per expert, enabling higher throughput and lower latency.

Large-scale cross-node EP is essential.” Reading a prompt, one deployment unit spans 4 nodes with 32-way expert parallelism; decoding, it spans 18 nodes with 144-way expert parallelism, each GPU holding 2 routed experts and the shared one, and each node of 8 GPUs writes about 14,800 tokens per second[19].

The price is communication. Every mixture layer sends every token to other GPUs and back, twice per layer and 58 layers per token in DeepSeek-V3, and the exchange has to be hidden behind computation.

DeepSeek overlaps the communication of one batch with the computation of another and, for training, limits every token to experts on at most 4 nodes, because NVLink inside a node is about 3.2 times faster than InfiniBand between nodes[7].

When a mixture is the right choice

A mixture of experts trades memory for compute. For a given quality it needs fewer operations per token than a dense model, and in exchange it keeps all its experts in memory and, served at scale, moves every token between GPUs and back in every layer.

The gain in compute is real and large. The Switch Transformer reached the quality of a dense T5-Base “in one-seventh the time” at the same compute per token[5].

The gain in wall-clock time is smaller, because routing and moving tokens cost time that no operation count shows: the OLMoE team found that their mixture “reaches the performance of the dense model with ∼3× fewer tokens”, but in time “only ∼2× faster”[11].

So the trade pays where compute is the bottleneck and memory is plentiful: training large models, and serving them to many users at once on clusters where every expert sees enough tokens to stay busy. It pays less where memory is the bottleneck or traffic is light.

The authors of GLaM, one of the first large mixtures, noted that sparse models “require a larger number of devices”, which “increases the serving cost especially when the serving traffic is low”[20]. Fine-tuning needs care too.

In the ST-MoE study, sparse models were “prone to overfitting”: on a task with 250 training examples the sparse model did worse than the dense one, and sparse models needed their own fine-tuning settings, smaller batches and a higher learning rate[9].

A laptop with plenty of memory and a modest processor is a case of its own. Its memory can hold all the experts, and at a batch of one each token reads only the few it needs.

References

  1. Jacobs, R. A., Jordan, M. I., Nowlan, S. J., & Hinton, G. E. (1991). Adaptive mixtures of local experts. Neural Computation, 3(1), 79–87. ↩
  2. Shazeer, N., Mirhoseini, A., Maziarz, K., Davis, A., Le, Q., Hinton, G., & Dean, J. (2017). Outrageously large neural networks: the sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer. ICLR 2017. ↩
  3. Geva, M., Schuster, R., Berant, J., & Levy, O. (2021). Transformer feed-forward layers are key-value memories. EMNLP 2021. ↩
  4. Gale, T., Narayanan, D., Young, C., & Zaharia, M. (2023). MegaBlocks: efficient sparse training with mixture-of-experts. MLSys 2023. ↩
  5. Fedus, W., Zoph, B., & Shazeer, N. (2022). Switch Transformers: scaling to trillion parameter models with simple and efficient sparsity. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 23(120), 1–39. ↩
  6. Wang, L., Gao, H., Zhao, C., Sun, X., & Dai, D. (2024). Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing strategy for mixture-of-experts. arXiv. ↩
  7. DeepSeek-AI (2024). DeepSeek-V3 technical report. arXiv. ↩
  8. Lepikhin, D., Lee, H., Xu, Y., Chen, D., Firat, O., Huang, Y., Krikun, M., Shazeer, N., & Chen, Z. (2021). GShard: scaling giant models with conditional computation and automatic sharding. ICLR 2021. ↩
  9. Zoph, B., Bello, I., Kumar, S., Du, N., Huang, Y., Dean, J., Shazeer, N., & Fedus, W. (2022). ST-MoE: designing stable and transferable sparse expert models. arXiv. ↩
  10. Jiang, A. Q., et al. (2024). Mixtral of experts. arXiv. ↩
  11. Muennighoff, N., et al. (2025). OLMoE: open mixture-of-experts language models. ICLR 2025. ↩
  12. Dai, D., et al. (2024). DeepSeekMoE: towards ultimate expert specialization in mixture-of-experts language models. ACL 2024. ↩
  13. Kimi Team (2025). Kimi K2: open agentic intelligence. arXiv. ↩
  14. Krajewski, J., et al. (2024). Scaling laws for fine-grained mixture of experts. ICML 2024. ↩
  15. Qwen Team (2025). Qwen3 technical report. arXiv. ↩
  16. Meta (2025). The Llama 4 herd: the beginning of a new era of natively multimodal AI innovation. Blog post. ↩
  17. OpenAI (2025). gpt-oss-120b & gpt-oss-20b model card. arXiv. ↩
  18. llama.cpp (2025). llama : add –n-cpu-moe option. Pull request #15077. ↩
  19. DeepSeek-AI (2025). Day 6: one more thing, DeepSeek-V3/R1 inference system overview. GitHub. ↩
  20. Du, N., et al. (2022). GLaM: efficient scaling of language models with mixture-of-experts. ICML 2022. ↩
entry.summary: A mixture-of-experts layer in PyTorch trained next to dense models: the router, load balancing, dropped tokens, what experts learn, and serving

entry.title: Hybrid attention: why new LLMs keep full attention in only a few layers

link.title: Hybrid attention: why new LLMs keep full attention in only a few layers

entry.content:
Qwen3-32B, a dense model from April 2025, keeps 32 GiB of keys and values for one conversation of 128 thousand tokens, about half of what its weights take. Qwen3-Next, released by the same team a few months later, keeps 3 GiB at the same length. It doesn’t compress its cache or skip tokens.

Three of every four of its layers simply have no cache: they read the text the way a recurrent network does, into a state of fixed size, and only every fourth layer is ordinary attention.

Qwen3-Next is not the only one. Jamba, the Nemotron-H models, Kimi Linear and, for a while, MiniMax made the same choice: full attention in a few layers, something cheaper in the rest.

This post builds the cheaper part from scratch, from linear attention to the gated delta rule, tests what it can and cannot remember, and then looks at how real models combine the two and what that buys on a GPU.

What attention remembers

Every attention layer of a Transformer answers the same question for every token: which of the earlier tokens matter here, and what do they say. Softmax attention answers it by brute force. Each token leaves behind a key, which says what it is about, and a value, which says what it contributes.

A new token arrives with a query, compares it with every key, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and takes the weighted sum of the values:

\[o_t = \sum_{j \le t} \frac{\exp(q_t \cdot k_j / \sqrt{d})}{\sum_{i \le t} \exp(q_t \cdot k_i / \sqrt{d})}\, v_j .\]

Nothing is ever thrown away. To write token \(t\), the layer needs the keys and values of all \(t-1\) tokens before it, which is why serving engines keep them in a KV cache instead of recomputing them.

Memory therefore grows linearly with the text, and since each new token reads all of it, reading a whole text of \(n\) tokens takes time proportional to \(n^2\).

Think of a library that keeps every book it has ever received and checks the whole catalogue for every question. The answers are exact, but the building has to grow with the collection.

Attention without the softmax

The softmax is what forces the rereading: the exponential ties every query to every key. Katharopoulos and colleagues replaced it, putting a dot product of features \(\phi(q) \cdot \phi(k)\) in place of \(\exp(q \cdot k)\), with a positive map such as \(\phi(x) = \mathrm{elu}(x) + 1\), and noticed that the rest follows from associativity[1]:

\[o_t = \frac{\sum_{j \le t} \big(\phi(q_t)^\top \phi(k_j)\big) v_j}{\sum_{j \le t} \phi(q_t)^\top \phi(k_j)} = \frac{\phi(q_t)^\top S_t}{\phi(q_t)^\top z_t}, \qquad S_t = \sum_{j \le t} \phi(k_j)\, v_j^\top, \quad z_t = \sum_{j \le t} \phi(k_j).\]

The query no longer sits inside the sum. Everything the layer needs from the past now sits in \(S_t\), a \(d \times d\) matrix, and \(z_t\), a vector, and both are updated by adding one term per token:

\[S_t = S_{t-1} + \phi(k_t)\, v_t^\top .\]

This is a recurrent network. Its state has the same size after ten tokens and after ten million, writing a token costs the same at any position, and there is no cache. Done for all positions at once, the same computation is the attention formula with the brackets moved:

Both forms compute the same numbers, only in a different order. In code, the recurrent form loops over positions and the parallel one builds the masked score matrix:

def linear_recurrent(q, k, v):
    q, k = feature(q), feature(k)
    state = q.new_zeros(*q.shape[:2], q.shape[-1], v.shape[-1])  # S = sum of k v^T
    norm = q.new_zeros(*q.shape[:2], q.shape[-1])                # z = sum of k
    out = []
    for t in range(q.shape[2]):
        state = state + k[:, :, t, :, None] * v[:, :, t, None, :]
        norm = norm + k[:, :, t]
        out.append(torch.einsum("bhk,bhkv->bhv", q[:, :, t], state)
                   / torch.einsum("bhk,bhk->bh", q[:, :, t], norm)[..., None])
    return torch.stack(out, dim=2)

def linear_attention(q, k, v):
    q, k = feature(q), feature(k)
    causal = torch.ones(q.shape[2], q.shape[2], dtype=torch.bool).tril()
    scores = (q @ k.transpose(-1, -2)).masked_fill(~causal, 0)
    return (scores @ v) / scores.sum(-1, keepdim=True)

On random inputs in double precision the two functions agree to about \(10^{-15}\), which is rounding error. The recurrent form is how the layer writes text, one token at a time; the parallel form is how it trains, all positions at once.

The parallel form also shows a catch: it still builds an \(n \times n\) matrix of scores, because with a causal mask every position needs its own prefix of the sum and the brackets can’t simply move. Training a linear layer efficiently needs a third form, which comes later.

A memory of fixed size

The price of the fixed state can be read straight from the formula. The state is one matrix. Every pair \((k_j, v_j)\) is added into the same \(d^2\) numbers, and to recall the value stored under a key, the layer multiplies the state by it:

\[S^\top k_i = \sum_j (k_j \cdot k_i)\, v_j = (k_i \cdot k_i)\, v_i + \sum_{j \ne i} (k_j \cdot k_i)\, v_j .\]

The first term is the stored value. The second is interference: every other pair, weighted by how similar its key is to \(k_i\). If the keys are orthogonal, the interference is exactly zero, but a \(d\)-dimensional space has room for only \(d\) orthogonal directions.

Beyond that, each new pair blurs the ones already stored. The library has turned into one notebook page on which every note is written over the others; it stays readable while there are few notes.

Softmax attention has no such limit because it never mixes the notes: it keeps them all and lets the exponential pick out the right one. It pays for that with the growing cache. Everything below is about this trade between a fixed state and exact recall.

Arora and colleagues measured it across efficient architectures and called it “a key tradeoff between a model’s state size and recall ability”[2]: the smaller the state a model keeps while reading, the worse it recalls.

Writing with the delta rule

Plain addition has a second, quieter problem. If the same key comes back with a new value, say a variable that has been reassigned, the state holds the sum of the old and the new value, and reading it returns a mixture of both. Nothing in the notebook can be crossed out.

The remedy dates from 1960, when Widrow and Hoff trained their linear neurons with what became known as the delta rule: compare the output with the target and move the weights in proportion to the error[3].

Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber noticed that the state of linear attention is a weight matrix, written at every step, and proposed writing it the same way[4]. Before storing \(v_t\) under \(k_t\), read what is already there, and write only the difference:

\[S_t = S_{t-1} + \beta_t\, k_t \big(v_t - S_{t-1}^\top k_t\big)^\top = (I - \beta_t k_t k_t^\top)\, S_{t-1} + \beta_t\, k_t v_t^\top ,\]

with \(k_t\) of unit length and \(\beta_t \in (0, 1)\), a writing strength the layer computes for each token. This is one step of gradient descent on the memory’s error for this key, \(\tfrac12 \lVert S^\top k_t - v_t \rVert^2\), with learning rate \(\beta_t\): the gradient with respect to \(S\) is \(k_t (S^\top k_t - v_t)^\top\).

With \(\beta_t = 1\), the old value under \(k_t\) is erased and the new one is stored exactly. A layer that writes this way is called DeltaNet. In the space of values, one write looks like this:

Side by side, the three memories differ in what they keep and in how a new pair changes it:

How much of a difference does editing make? A small experiment shows both sides of it: a \(64 \times 64\) memory, random unit keys and values, written once by adding and once by the delta rule, and read back by finding the nearest stored value. Softmax attention, which keeps every pair, is the reference.

The left panel holds a surprise: from 64 pairs on, plain addition recalls more than the delta rule. With \(\beta_t = 1\), each write makes the memory return exactly \(v_t\) for \(k_t\), and since random keys are not orthogonal, it also shifts what the memory returns for every older key that overlaps with \(k_t\).

Once the memory is full, the delta rule holds the recent pairs well and the old ones poorly. Addition keeps a blur of everything, in which the nearest value is still often the right one.

The right panel shows what the delta rule is for. After 32 pairs, some of the keys get a new value. The delta rule returns the new value nearly every time.

Addition returns the sum of the old and the new value, which is nearer to the new one only about half the time, and softmax attention as written here does no better: it sees two identical keys and averages their values.

A trained Transformer can tell the later pair from the earlier one by their positions; this toy has no positions.

So the delta rule doesn’t enlarge the memory. A \(d \times d\) matrix stays a \(d \times d\) matrix, and it holds at most \(d\) pairs exactly, whichever way they are written. What the delta rule adds is the ability to correct what is stored, which plain addition doesn’t have at all.

Forgetting on purpose

Editing handles values that change. It does nothing about the opposite problem: a long text moves on, and much of what the state holds stops mattering. A memory of fixed size needs a way to let go of it.

That is what gates are for. RetNet multiplied the state by a fixed decay at every step[5], Gated Linear Attention made the decay depend on the token[6], and Mamba-2 showed that its own selective state space model is linear attention with a data-dependent scalar gate[7]. Gated DeltaNet puts the gate and the delta rule together[8]:

\[S_t = \alpha_t \,(I - \beta_t k_t k_t^\top)\, S_{t-1} + \beta_t\, k_t v_t^\top, \qquad \alpha_t \in (0, 1).\]

Both \(\alpha_t\) and \(\beta_t\) are computed from the current token, so the layer decides as it reads when to forget and how firmly to write.

The two parts split the work: in the authors’ words, the gate “can promptly clear memory by setting \(\alpha_t \to 0\)”, and with \(\alpha_t \to 1\) the layer is “effectively switching to the pure delta rule” and edits single entries without touching the rest.

This is the layer Qwen3-Next is built on, and Kimi Delta Attention is the same update with a separate gate for every channel of the state instead of one per head[9].

Training a recurrence in parallel

A recurrence over positions is awkward to train on a GPU, which is fast at large matrix products and slow at loops of ten thousand small updates. The solution is to cut the sequence into chunks.

Inside a chunk of 64 tokens, the writes depend on each other only through a small lower-triangular system that can be solved with matrix products; between chunks, only the \(d \times d\) state is passed along[10].

The chunked form is exact. My plain-PyTorch version of it agrees with the token-by-token loop to \(1.4 \times 10^{-15}\) in double precision, with the gate or without it, and it is what the experiments below train with. Production models use the Triton kernels of flash-linear-attention, which do the same thing much faster.

A test of memory: associative recall

The language modelling loss says little about memory, because much of predicting the next word needs little of it. A more direct test asks a model to remember what it was told. In multi-query associative recall, a sequence lists key-value pairs and then asks for the values of the keys in a shuffled order[11]:

k1 v1  k2 v2  ...  kN vN   |   q1 a1  q2 a2  ...  qN aN

Each \(q_i\) is one of the keys, and the model must put the right value after it. It is the skill behind answering a question about a long document, using a name defined forty pages earlier, or calling a function with the arguments described at the top of a prompt.

I trained six small models on it, each with four layers of width 64 and two heads, the same in everything except how their layers mix tokens: softmax attention in all four, linear attention, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and two hybrids with three Gated DeltaNet layers and one softmax attention layer.

In one hybrid the attention layer is second; in the other it is on top, the place it has in each block of four in Qwen3-Next.

Every layer, attention included, first passes its queries, keys and values through a short convolution over the last four positions, as Mamba and DeltaNet do, so that a value can carry its key with it.

Each model saw 64 fresh random sequences at each of 4,000 steps and was scored on held-out ones. The models with Gated DeltaNet layers trained on an Apple M2, the others on a T4 (code).

The Transformer recalls every value at every size on the chart. The three recurrent models hold up while there are few pairs and fall apart between 8 and 32: at 32 pairs DeltaNet recalls 36% of the values, linear attention 26% and Gated DeltaNet 2%, and at 64 the best of them, DeltaNet, recalls 13%.

Each head here works with keys of 32 numbers, so by the bound from earlier its state holds at most 32 pairs exactly, and at 16 pairs all three are already well short of full recall.

At 128 pairs even the Transformer didn’t learn the task in 4,000 steps, which is why the chart stops at 64.

Gated DeltaNet, the newest of the three, comes last from 16 pairs on. That is less strange than it looks, because this test gives the gate nothing to do. Every pair has to be kept until its question comes, so forgetting can only lose information.

The authors of Gated DeltaNet, who trained models of 1.3 billion parameters on 100 billion tokens of real text, found that it “consistently surpasses existing models like Mamba2 and DeltaNet”, in-context retrieval included[8]. Four layers and 4,000 steps of a synthetic task are a different regime.

The gate is also the easiest part to get wrong. In my first version it started at about one half, and weight decay kept pulling it back there, so the state lost half of what it held at every token, and Gated DeltaNet and the hybrid stayed at chance level.

Starting the gate as the Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 code does, where a typical head keeps about 94% of its state from one token to the next, and leaving it out of weight decay, fixed it.

The two hybrids differ only in the order of their layers. With attention second, the hybrid recalls every value at every size, like the Transformer, though three of its four layers are Gated DeltaNet, which on its own recalls the least.

With attention on top, the same layers recall 26% of the values at 16 pairs and 12% at 32, at the better of two learning rates: a little more than Gated DeltaNet alone and less than DeltaNet.

I can’t say for certain why. The attention layer on top has what it needs: the convolution hands each value its key, and the other hybrid shows that one attention layer among three Gated DeltaNet layers is enough. This one just doesn’t learn the lookup in 4,000 steps.

A model of four layers is far from Qwen3-Next, where twelve attention layers are spread through 48 and most of them have many recurrent layers on both sides, so this says nothing about whether its layout is a good one.

It does show that the ratio alone doesn’t describe a hybrid. With the same layers in a different order, one model recalled like a Transformer and the other like a recurrent network.

Why one layer of attention is enough

Attention solves associative recall in one layer: the query for \(k_i\) meets the stored key \(k_i\), the softmax puts nearly all the weight on it, and out comes \(v_i\), however many pairs came before.

Arora and colleagues proved that attention needs a model dimension independent of the sequence length for this, while the gated convolutions they studied need one that grows with it.

Measuring the gap in quality between the two kinds of models on real text, they found that “82% of the gap is explained by each model’s ability to recall information that is previously mentioned in-context”[11].

Copying gives the same picture. Jelassi and colleagues proved that two layers of attention can copy strings of exponential length, while models with a fixed state are “fundamentally limited by their fixed-size latent state”[12].

None of this requires attention everywhere. Much of predicting the next token is local, or a matter of keeping a running summary of what the text is about, and a gated recurrent layer does that well and cheaply.

Exact lookups into the distant past are rarer, and a layer that can make them serves the whole model: the recurrent layers around it carry the local context, the attention layer finds the match. In the library picture, most floors work from a notebook page, and every few floors someone is allowed into the archive.

The authors of Mamba-2 tried such hybrids and described the division of labour the same way: “attention layers act as a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens in the sequence instead of forcing the model to compress all the context to its memory”. They found that “around 10% of the total number of layers being attention performs best”[7].

A study at NVIDIA trained an 8-billion-parameter Transformer, pure Mamba and Mamba-2 models and a hybrid with 4 attention layers out of 56 on the same data.

The pure Mamba models began to fail at looking up a number in a phone book beyond about 500 tokens. The hybrid exceeded the Transformer on all 12 standard tasks the authors evaluated, by 2.65 points on average[13].

Hybrids in practice

The first large hybrid was Jamba from AI21, in March 2024: Mamba layers with one attention layer in every eight[14]. MiniMax, NVIDIA, Qwen and Moonshot followed, each with its own recurrent layer and its own ratio.

MiniMax-Text-01 put one softmax layer after every seven layers of lightning attention, a fast form of linear attention, after finding that lightning attention alone “demonstrates limited retrieval capabilities”[15]. NVIDIA’s Nemotron-H models keep “roughly 8% of the total number of layers” as attention, and the rest are Mamba-2 and MLP layers[16].

Qwen3-Next uses Gated DeltaNet in three layers out of four. According to the Qwen team, at this ratio “the model consistently outperforms any monolithic architecture”[17].

Kimi Linear uses Kimi Delta Attention, the variant with a gate for every channel, also at 3:1. It leaves word order entirely to the recurrent layers: its attention layers use no positional encoding at all[9].

Here is where each model keeps its full attention, read from the config files the models are published with:

Drawn to scale, the designs differ more than their headline ratios. Jamba and MiniMax-Text-01 keep one attention layer in eight, Nemotron-H-8B 4 of its 28 token-mixing layers, the Qwen and Kimi models one in four.

Kimi Linear’s released model has 27 layers, so its 3:1 turns into 20 recurrent layers and 7 attention layers, the last one attention.

Kimi K3, 93 layers deep, adds an extra attention layer at the top, “ensuring that the final layer always performs global attention”[18]. All of them spread the attention layers evenly through the depth.

The second group shrinks the cache in another way. gpt-oss and Gemma use softmax attention in every layer, but most of their layers see only a sliding window of recent tokens: 128 in gpt-oss, where windowed and full layers alternate[19], and 1,024 in Gemma 3, with five windowed layers for every full one[20].

Gemma 4 kept the ratio. A window is the opposite trade to a recurrent state: it keeps recent tokens exactly and forgets older ones completely, while a state keeps a blurred summary of everything.

The last row is MiniMax-M2, the successor of MiniMax-Text-01, with full attention in all 62 layers. The team explained why in a blog post.

Small hybrids had matched full attention on the leaderboards, but “the price paid became obvious at a larger scale: the model had clear deficits in complex, multi-hop reasoning tasks”[21].

The Qwen and Kimi hybrids keep more attention than MiniMax-Text-01 did, one layer in four rather than one in eight, and use the delta rule, which lightning attention lacks. Still, the episode is a fair warning that parity on small models and leaderboards doesn’t settle the question.

What the hybrids save is easiest to see in memory. For each model, the size of its cache follows from the config: the number of attention layers, key-value heads and head dimension.

For one sequence of 128K tokens, Qwen3-Next keeps 3 GiB of keys and values, against 32 GiB for Qwen3-32B. Not all of the factor of ten comes from the hybrid. Each attention layer of Qwen3-Next keeps two key-value heads of 256 dimensions, where Qwen3-32B keeps eight of 128, which halves the cache per layer.

The rest, a factor of 5.3, is 12 attention layers instead of 64. The recurrent layers add a state of 36 MiB that stays the same at any length.

Kimi Linear starts from multi-head latent attention, introduced in DeepSeek-V2[22], which already caches one compressed vector of 576 numbers per token and layer in place of keys and values for every head, and keeps it in 7 layers of 27.

That is 26% of the cache of an all-MLA model of the same depth, in line with the paper’s “reducing KV cache usage by up to 75%”. MiniMax-M2, at 31 GiB, keeps six times more than its predecessor.

At long context, the cache rather than the weights decides how many conversations fit on a GPU at once, and decoding speed follows from that.

The Kimi Linear authors measured decoding with a million tokens of context and put the result down to memory: the smaller cache “enables larger batches, yielding a 6.3× faster TPOT (1.84ms vs. 11.48ms) than MLA at 1M tokens”, TPOT being the time per output token.

What it costs on a GPU

The recurrent layer pays off only where the cache grows large, and a single layer on one GPU shows where that starts.

I timed one layer with 16 heads of 128 dimensions, about the size of a Gated DeltaNet layer in Qwen3-Next, in two situations: reading a prompt of \(n\) tokens at once, and writing one new token after \(n\) tokens.

Softmax attention runs through PyTorch’s fused attention kernel in half precision. Gated DeltaNet runs my plain-PyTorch chunked version in single precision, a Python loop over chunks of 64. The comparison is tilted against the recurrent layer on purpose: if it wins anyway, it wins on arithmetic, not on engineering.

Reading a prompt, softmax attention is faster up to 8K tokens, which is no surprise: its kernel is one fused program, and mine is a loop. The slopes differ, though.

From 512 to 65,536 tokens, a sequence 128 times longer, the attention layer gets 8,600 times slower and the recurrent one 124 times slower. The curves cross between 8K and 16K tokens, and at 65K the recurrent layer is 4.2 times faster.

Writing a token is where the cache costs most. Attention reads the keys and values of every earlier token, 512 MiB at 65K tokens in this one layer, and its time grows in proportion, from 0.08 ms to 3.7 ms. The recurrent layer updates a state of 1 MiB and takes 0.2 ms at any length; at that size the time is mostly the overhead of launching a few small GPU kernels.

From about 2K tokens on, the recurrent step is faster, and at 65K it is 16 times faster.

One layer and one sequence understate the difference in a real server. There, the caches of all the conversations in a batch have to fit in memory at once, so a model whose cache is a quarter or an eighth of the size can serve proportionally more conversations at the same length.

Kimi Linear’s 6.3 times, quoted above, comes from exactly that. The attention layers of a hybrid still pay the full price; three quarters of its layers stop paying it.

When a hybrid is the right choice

A hybrid pays off when contexts are long and there are many of them: agents that carry long transcripts of tool calls, reasoning models that write tens of thousands of tokens, questions over long documents, a server holding hundreds of such conversations at once.

There the cache is most of the memory and reading it is most of the decoding time, and cutting it by a factor of four to ten changes how many users one GPU can serve.

At short contexts the gain is smaller than the headlines suggest. According to Qwen, the decoding throughput of Qwen3-Next is nearly 4 times that of Qwen3-32B at 4K tokens and over 10 times beyond 32K[17].

But Qwen3-Next activates 3 billion parameters per token and Qwen3-32B all 32 billion, so the comparison mixes two savings, the mixture of experts and the hybrid, and the blog doesn’t separate them. The hybrid’s share is the part that grows with the context.

The costs are of three kinds. The first is quality on the tasks attention is best at, precise retrieval and multi-hop reasoning over long inputs: the deficits that sent MiniMax back to full attention.

The second is engineering. Recurrent layers need their own kernels, and serving tricks built around a cache of separate tokens get harder when part of the model keeps a state that has absorbed all of them.

Reusing the cache of a shared prompt needs copies of the state saved at chosen positions, and rolling back a rejected speculative token needs the state from a step earlier.

The third is that the field keeps moving. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next replaced the full attention layers of its hybrid with sparse attention[23], and DeepSeek-V4 combines two kinds of compressed attention instead of adding recurrent layers[24]. Both directions go after the same cache.

A hybrid’s way is to give most layers a memory of fixed size and to keep a few that can still read every token.

References

  1. Katharopoulos, A., Vyas, A., Pappas, N., & Fleuret, F. (2020). Transformers are RNNs: fast autoregressive Transformers with linear attention. ICML 2020. ↩
  2. Arora, S., et al. (2024). Simple linear attention language models balance the recall-throughput tradeoff. ICML 2024. ↩
  3. Widrow, B., & Hoff, M. E. (1960). Adaptive switching circuits. IRE WESCON Convention Record, 4, 96–104. ↩
  4. Schlag, I., Irie, K., & Schmidhuber, J. (2021). Linear Transformers are secretly fast weight programmers. ICML 2021. ↩
  5. Sun, Y., et al. (2023). Retentive network: a successor to Transformer for large language models. arXiv. ↩
  6. Yang, S., Wang, B., Shen, Y., Panda, R., & Kim, Y. (2024). Gated linear attention Transformers with hardware-efficient training. ICML 2024. ↩
  7. Dao, T., & Gu, A. (2024). Transformers are SSMs: generalized models and efficient algorithms through structured state space duality. ICML 2024. ↩
  8. Yang, S., Kautz, J., & Hatamizadeh, A. (2025). Gated delta networks: improving Mamba2 with delta rule. ICLR 2025. ↩
  9. Kimi Team (2025). Kimi Linear: an expressive, efficient attention architecture. arXiv. ↩
  10. Yang, S., Wang, B., Zhang, Y., Shen, Y., & Kim, Y. (2024). Parallelizing linear Transformers with the delta rule over sequence length. NeurIPS 2024. ↩
  11. Arora, S., et al. (2023). Zoology: measuring and improving recall in efficient language models. ICLR 2024. ↩
  12. Jelassi, S., Brandfonbrener, D., Kakade, S. M., & Malach, E. (2024). Repeat after me: Transformers are better than state space models at copying. ICML 2024. ↩
  13. Waleffe, R., et al. (2024). An empirical study of Mamba-based language models. arXiv. ↩
  14. Lieber, O., et al. (2024). Jamba: a hybrid Transformer-Mamba language model. arXiv. ↩
  15. MiniMax (2025). MiniMax-01: scaling foundation models with lightning attention. arXiv. ↩
  16. NVIDIA (2025). Nemotron-H: a family of accurate and efficient hybrid Mamba-Transformer models. arXiv. ↩
  17. Qwen Team (2025). Qwen3-Next: towards ultimate training & inference efficiency. Alibaba Cloud blog. ↩
  18. Kimi Team (2026). Kimi K3: open frontier intelligence. arXiv. ↩
  19. OpenAI (2025). gpt-oss-120b & gpt-oss-20b model card. arXiv. ↩
  20. Gemma Team (2025). Gemma 3 technical report. arXiv. ↩
  21. MiniMax (2025). Why did MiniMax M2 end up as a full attention model? Hugging Face blog. ↩
  22. DeepSeek-AI (2024). DeepSeek-V2: a strong, economical, and efficient mixture-of-experts language model. arXiv. ↩
  23. Qwen Team (2026). Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model card. Hugging Face. ↩
  24. DeepSeek-AI (2026). DeepSeek-V4: towards highly efficient million-token context intelligence. arXiv. ↩
entry.summary: Linear attention, the delta rule and Gated DeltaNet in PyTorch, a recall test, GPU timings, and why Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear keep few attention layers

entry.title: It works on my laptop: a reproducible Docker image of a model

link.title: It works on my laptop: a reproducible Docker image of a model

entry.content:
Transformers: from scratch to production · lesson 9 of 10 · all lessons · run on Kaggle · open in Colab · code on GitHub

On 16 June 2024 NumPy 2.0.0 came out, and code that nobody had touched started to fail. A model served with PyTorch 2.3.1 printed this on import, and stopped [1]:

A module that was compiled using NumPy 1.x cannot be run in
NumPy 2.0.0 as it may crash. To support both 1.x and 2.x
versions of NumPy, modules must be compiled with NumPy 2.0.
Some module may need to rebuild instead e.g. with 'pybind11>=2.12'.

Nothing in those projects had changed. Their requirements said numpy, or numpy>=1.24, and on that Sunday the newest NumPy that matched became a different program. NumPy had warned about it in its release notes: packages “built against a NumPy 1.xx release will not work with NumPy 2.0” [1]. PyTorch caught up five weeks later, in 2.4.0. Everyone who reinstalled in between learned what their model was really made of.

It is made of more than weights. When perevod translates a sentence, its 38 MB of weights are one part of what runs: around them are the package’s code, three dozen Python packages, Python itself, the system libraries that Python and PyTorch load, and a processor.

Change any of them, and you have a different program, which may or may not give the same translations, or start at all.

This lesson pins every layer of that stack except the last, and puts the result in one Docker image that gives the same bytes each time it’s built, so that anyone can check it was built from the code they can read.

Then it takes the image apart without Docker, runs the model from it, and finally ships the same model a second way: to the browser, where a free page translates on the visitor’s own device.

What you’ll do

  1. Watch the same requirements turn into three different programs on three different days.
  2. Freeze them in a lock file with hashes, and see pip refuse a file that doesn’t match.
  3. Take a container image apart by hand: a registry, manifests, layers and digests.
  4. Find out why two builds of one Dockerfile differ, and remove each cause.
  5. Write perevod’s Dockerfile, and a GitHub Actions job that builds the image twice and publishes it.
  6. Pull the published image without Docker, run the model from it, and check its weights.
  7. Export the model to ONNX and run it in a browser, on a free Hugging Face Space.

What you need: a CPU, as in lessons 7 and 8. Not Docker: Kaggle and Colab don’t have it, so the notebook does by hand what Docker does, which turns out to be the best way to see what an image is.

It downloads the published image (about 365 MB) and runs in a few minutes. On your own machine with Docker, the lesson also shows the commands that build and run the image.

Setup

One small helper package, tfs, draws the course’s plots and token chips and knows where the notebook runs (Kaggle, Colab or your own machine). Everything the lesson teaches is written out in the notebook itself.

import importlib.util
import subprocess
import sys

TFS = "git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@main"
if importlib.util.find_spec("tfs") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", TFS])

from tfs import env
from tfs.viz import table, token_chips, use_course_style

env.quiet()  # no progress bars or environment warnings in the outputs
SEED = 42
env.seed_everything(SEED)
COLORS = use_course_style()
WORK_DIR = env.work_dir()

import gzip
import hashlib
import io
import json
import math
import os
import py_compile
import shutil
import tarfile
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import requests
import torch
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

print("Python", sys.version.split()[0], "on", os.uname().machine)

Python 3.13.15 on x86_64

1. One requirements list, three programs

Start from perevod as lesson 8 released it, version 0.2.0: the release’s tag, and only the perevod/ folder of the course repository.

REPO = WORK_DIR / "course"
shutil.rmtree(REPO, ignore_errors=True)
URL = "https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch"
QUIET = ["-c", "advice.detachedHead=false"]
subprocess.run(["git", *QUIET, "clone", "-q", "--depth", "1", "--branch", "perevod-v0.2.0",
                "--filter=blob:none", "--sparse", URL, str(REPO)], check=True)
subprocess.run(["git", "sparse-checkout", "set", "perevod"], cwd=REPO, check=True)
os.chdir(REPO)


def write(path, text):
    Path(path).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    Path(path).write_text(text.lstrip("\n"), encoding="utf-8")


def replace(path, old, new):
    text = Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    assert text.count(old) == 1, old
    Path(path).write_text(text.replace(old, new), encoding="utf-8")


print(Path("perevod/pyproject.toml").read_text().split("[project.scripts]")[0])

[project]
name = "perevod"
dynamic = ["version"]  # read from src/perevod/__init__.py, see [tool.hatch.version]
description = "English-to-Russian translation with a small Transformer built from scratch"
readme = "README.md"
license = "MIT"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = [
    "torch>=2.1",
    "tokenizers>=0.15",
    "huggingface_hub>=0.20",
    "safetensors>=0.4",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
serve = ["fastapi>=0.110", "uvicorn>=0.29"]
demo = ["fastapi>=0.110", "uvicorn>=0.29", "gradio>=4.40"]
test = ["pytest>=8", "ruff>=0.6", "sacrebleu>=2.4", "pandas>=2.0", "pyarrow>=14",
        "fastapi>=0.110", "httpx>=0.27"]

Its dependencies are ranges: torch>=2.1 means “any PyTorch from 2.1 on”. That’s right for a package other people install. perevod has to live next to whatever else they have, and the Python Packaging User Guide calls pinning exact versions there “overly-restrictive” [2]. But a range is a question, and pip answers it on the day you install.

You can ask it on other days. uv, a fast replacement for pip written in Rust, can resolve requirements as if it were an earlier date: --exclude-newer makes it ignore every file uploaded after it.

Here is what perevod’s requirements, with the server extra, resolved to a year before this lesson, half a year before, and on the day perevod’s lock file was made:

!{sys.executable} -m pip install -q uv==0.12.24
UV = [sys.executable, "-m", "uv"]


def resolve(day):
    command = [*UV, "pip", "compile", "perevod/pyproject.toml", "--extra", "serve",
               "--python-version", "3.12", "--python-platform", "x86_64-manylinux_2_28",
               "--torch-backend", "cpu", "--exclude-newer", day,
               "--no-header", "--no-annotate", "--quiet"]
    result = subprocess.run(command, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
    versions = {}
    for line in result.stdout.splitlines():
        name, version = line.split("==")
        versions[name] = version
    return versions


DAYS = ["2025-10-27T00:00:00Z", "2026-04-27T00:00:00Z", "2026-10-27T00:00:00Z"]
resolved = {}
for day in DAYS:
    resolved[day[:10]] = resolve(day)

DIRECT = ["torch", "tokenizers", "huggingface-hub", "safetensors", "fastapi", "uvicorn"]
rows = []
for name in DIRECT:
    row = {"package": name}
    for day, versions in resolved.items():
        row[day] = versions[name]
    rows.append(row)
display(table(pd.DataFrame(rows)))

first, last = resolved["2025-10-27"], resolved["2026-10-27"]
changed = []
for name in first:
    if name in last and first[name] != last[name]:
        changed.append(name)
print(len(first), "packages a year ago,", len(last), "on the release day")
print(len(changed), "packages installed on both days, at different versions")
print("gone:", sorted(set(first) - set(last)))
print("new: ", sorted(set(last) - set(first)))
package2025-10-272026-04-272026-10-27
torch2.9.0+cpu2.10.0+cpu2.14.1+cpu
tokenizers0.22.10.22.20.23.3
huggingface-hub0.36.01.12.02.3.0
safetensors0.6.20.7.00.8.0
fastapi0.120.00.136.10.162.0
uvicorn0.38.00.46.00.54.0
34 packages a year ago, 33 on the release day
24 packages installed on both days, at different versions
gone: ['certifi', 'charset-normalizer', 'requests', 'sniffio', 'urllib3']
new:  ['httpcore2', 'httpx2', 'opentelemetry-api', 'truststore']

Same pyproject.toml, three programs. PyTorch moves by several releases, and each of them changes kernels, defaults and warnings. huggingface-hub, which downloads the model, jumps two major versions.

And these are only the packages perevod names: behind them, nearly every package it pulls in changed version too, and some were replaced outright, an HTTP library by another. None of this is a bug. It’s what a range asks for.

For a library, that’s the deal. For a service, it’s a gamble: the server you test today and the one that restarts next month install different code.

Donald Stufft, who maintained pip and PyPI for years, drew the line in 2013: “While a library tends to want to have wide open ended version specifiers an application wants very specific dependencies”[3]. perevod is both.

It keeps the ranges in pyproject.toml for people who install it as a library, and the service is deployed from a second file that pins every package: a lock file.

2. A lock file, with hashes

First, a change that the image revealed. On a laptop, some other package has always installed NumPy; in an image that holds only what perevod asks for, it’s missing, and PyTorch, which tries to import NumPy when it loads, prints Failed to initialize NumPy: No module named 'numpy'. perevod never calls NumPy, so nothing breaks, but a server that starts with a warning trains people to ignore warnings. perevod now asks for it:

replace("perevod/pyproject.toml", '    "safetensors>=0.4",\n',
        '    "safetensors>=0.4",\n'
        '    "numpy>=1.24",  # perevod doesn\'t use it, '
        'but PyTorch warns on import without it\n')

Now the lock. uv pip compile resolves the requirements once and writes the answer down, one exact version per package. Three options matter here:

  • --universal: one file for every platform. Where the answer differs, a line carries a marker, such as ; sys_platform == 'win32', and pip skips the lines that don’t apply.
  • --torch-backend cpu: PyTorch’s CPU-only build from PyTorch’s own index. The default Linux wheel on PyPI is built with CUDA and pulls in NVIDIA’s libraries: for torch 2.14.1 that’s about 3 GB of downloads, against 196 MB for the CPU build. A translation server without a GPU needs none of it.
  • --generate-hashes: next to each version, the sha256 of every file that version may be installed from.

And one more for this lesson: --exclude-newer with the day perevod 0.3’s lock was made, so that the notebook resolves the same answer even if you run it a year from now.

LOCKED_ON = "2026-10-27T12:00:00Z"  # the day perevod 0.3's lock was made
COMPILE = [*UV, "pip", "compile", "--universal", "--python-version", "3.12",
           "--generate-hashes", "--exclude-newer", LOCKED_ON, "--quiet"]
subprocess.run([*COMPILE, "pyproject.toml", "--extra", "serve", "--torch-backend", "cpu",
                "-o", "requirements.lock"], cwd="perevod", check=True)

lock = Path("perevod/requirements.lock").read_text()
pins = []
for line in lock.splitlines():
    if "==" in line and not line.startswith((" ", "#")):
        pins.append(line.rstrip(" \\"))
print(len(pins), "pinned lines,", lock.count("--hash=sha256:"), "hashes")
for pin in pins:
    if pin.startswith(("torch==", "numpy==", "huggingface-hub==")):
        print(pin)

37 pinned lines, 582 hashes
huggingface-hub==2.3.0
numpy==2.5.4
torch==2.14.1 ; sys_platform == 'darwin'
torch==2.14.1+cpu ; sys_platform != 'darwin'

PyTorch gets two lines. On macOS, PyPI’s wheel is already CPU-only and the PyTorch index has no +cpu build, so the lock takes the plain one there and the +cpu build everywhere else.

The hashes are what make the lock more than a list of versions. A version is a name: whoever controls the index, a mirror, or a proxy between you and it, decides which bytes stand behind it. A hash is the bytes themselves. With a hash on every line, pip switches to hash-checking mode, in which “Hashes are required for all requirements” and every downloaded file must match one of them [4].

Try it on one small package from the lock, h11, an HTTP/1.1 library the server uses. First as locked:

lines = lock.splitlines()
start = 0
for k, line in enumerate(lines):
    if line.startswith("h11=="):
        start = k
entry = [lines[start]]
for line in lines[start + 1:]:
    if not line.startswith("    --hash"):
        break
    entry.append(line)
good = "\n".join(entry).rstrip(" \\") + "\n"
print(good)

PIP_DOWNLOAD = [sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "download", "--no-deps", "--require-hashes",
                "--no-color", "--disable-pip-version-check"]
shutil.rmtree(WORK_DIR / "downloads", ignore_errors=True)
Path(WORK_DIR / "good.txt").write_text(good)
subprocess.run([*PIP_DOWNLOAD, "-q", "-d", str(WORK_DIR / "downloads"),
                "-r", str(WORK_DIR / "good.txt")], check=True)
for path in sorted((WORK_DIR / "downloads").glob("h11-*")):
    print(path.name, "sha256:" + hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest())

h11==0.16.0 \
    --hash=sha256:4e35b956cf45792e4caa5885e69fba00bdbc6ffafbfa020300e549b208ee5ff1 \
    --hash=sha256:63cf8bbe7522de3bf65932fda1d9c2772064ffb3dae62d55932da54b31cb6c86

h11-0.16.0-py3-none-any.whl sha256:63cf8bbe7522de3bf65932fda1d9c2772064ffb3dae62d55932da54b31cb6c86

The file pip downloaded has one of the locked hashes. Now change the last hex digit of each hash, which is what pip would see if someone swapped the file behind the version:

bad_lines = []
for line in good.splitlines():
    if "--hash=sha256:" in line:
        digest = line.split("sha256:")[1][:64]
        last = "1" if digest[-1] == "0" else "0"
        line = line.replace(digest, digest[:-1] + last)
    bad_lines.append(line)
Path(WORK_DIR / "bad.txt").write_text("\n".join(bad_lines) + "\n")
shutil.rmtree(WORK_DIR / "tampered", ignore_errors=True)
result = subprocess.run([*PIP_DOWNLOAD, "-d", str(WORK_DIR / "tampered"),
                         "-r", str(WORK_DIR / "bad.txt")], capture_output=True, text=True)
print("pip exit code:", result.returncode)
print(result.stderr.strip().replace(str(WORK_DIR) + "/", ""))
print("files downloaded:", list((WORK_DIR / "tampered").glob("*")))

pip exit code: 1
ERROR: THESE PACKAGES DO NOT MATCH THE HASHES FROM THE REQUIREMENTS FILE. If you have updated the package versions, please update the hashes. Otherwise, examine the package contents carefully; someone may have tampered with them.
    h11==0.16.0 from https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/04/4b/29cac41a4d98d144bf5f6d33995617b185d14b22401f75ca86f384e87ff1/h11-0.16.0-py3-none-any.whl (from -r bad.txt (line 1)):
        Expected sha256 4e35b956cf45792e4caa5885e69fba00bdbc6ffafbfa020300e549b208ee5ff0
        Expected     or 63cf8bbe7522de3bf65932fda1d9c2772064ffb3dae62d55932da54b31cb6c80
             Got        63cf8bbe7522de3bf65932fda1d9c2772064ffb3dae62d55932da54b31cb6c86
files downloaded: []

pip refuses, names the package, and shows the hashes the lock expects next to the one it got. Nothing is kept, let alone installed. The lock now pins the bytes of every file, not just a version number.

One more program runs during the install, and nobody asked for it by name: the build backend. To install perevod from source, pip first builds a wheel with hatchling, the backend pyproject.toml names, and by default it builds in a fresh environment with whatever hatchling is newest that day.

A newer hatchling writes slightly different metadata into the wheel, so it gets a lock of its own, and the Dockerfile will build without that fresh environment:

write("perevod/build.in", "hatchling\n")
subprocess.run([*COMPILE, "build.in", "-o", "build.lock"], cwd="perevod", check=True)
for line in Path("perevod/build.lock").read_text().splitlines():
    if "==" in line and not line.startswith((" ", "#")):
        print(line.rstrip(" \\"))

hatchling==1.32.4
packaging==26.3
pathspec==1.1.1
pluggy==1.7.0
tomlkit==0.15.2
trove-classifiers==2026.9.21.13

3. What an image is

A Docker image sounds like a disk image, one big file. It isn’t: it’s a few small JSON documents and a stack of tar archives, stored in a registry under names that are their own sha256 hashes. All of it comes over plain HTTP, and fetching it once by hand explains most of the rest of this lesson.

Registries speak one protocol, the OCI distribution spec: Docker Hub, GitHub’s registry and the others. To pull, a client asks /v2/<name>/manifests/<tag> for a manifest, then downloads what the manifest lists from /v2/<name>/blobs/<digest> (OCI distribution spec).

Public images need no account, only a short-lived anonymous token. Here are the four requests, as functions:

INDEX = "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json"
MANIFEST = "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json"
DOCKER_LIST = "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json"
DOCKER_MANIFEST = "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json"


def sha256(data):
    return "sha256:" + hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()


def pull_token(registry, repository):
    scope = f"repository:{repository}:pull"
    if registry == "registry-1.docker.io":
        params = {"service": "registry.docker.io", "scope": scope}
        response = requests.get("https://auth.docker.io/token", params=params)
    else:
        response = requests.get(f"https://{registry}/token", params={"scope": scope})
    return response.json()["token"]


def get_manifest(registry, repository, reference, token):
    accept = ", ".join([INDEX, MANIFEST, DOCKER_LIST, DOCKER_MANIFEST])
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", "Accept": accept}
    url = f"https://{registry}/v2/{repository}/manifests/{reference}"
    response = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response


def get_blob(registry, repository, digest, token):
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}
    url = f"https://{registry}/v2/{repository}/blobs/{digest}"
    response = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
    response.raise_for_status()
    assert sha256(response.content) == digest  # the name of a blob is the hash of its bytes
    return response.content

perevod’s image is built on python:3.12-slim, the official Python image on Debian. Ask Docker Hub for it:
