The digest the registry reports is the sha256 of the bytes it sent, and the OCI image spec makes that the content’s name: a digest “acts as a content identifier, enabling content addressability” (OCI image spec: descriptors). Change one byte, and it’s a different object with a different name.

What came back is an image index: one image per processor architecture, from x86-64 to IBM’s mainframes, plus as many attestations, records of how each image was built. docker pull takes the entry for your machine. Follow the one for x86-64 down to its config and its layers:

for entry in index["manifests"]:
    if entry["platform"]["architecture"] == "amd64":
        amd64 = entry
manifest = get_manifest(HUB, "library/python", amd64["digest"], hub_token).json()
config_digest = manifest["config"]["digest"]
config = json.loads(get_blob(HUB, "library/python", config_digest, hub_token))
print("built:", config["created"])
for item in config["config"]["Env"]:
    if item.startswith("PYTHON_VERSION"):
        print(item)

steps = []
for step in config["history"]:
    if not step.get("empty_layer"):
        steps.append(step["created_by"])
rows = []
for layer, step in zip(manifest["layers"], steps, strict=True):
    command = " ".join(step.split())
    rows.append({"layer": layer["digest"][:19] + "…", "MB": layer["size"] / 1e6,
                 "made by": command[:58]})
display(table(pd.DataFrame(rows), digits=1))

That’s the whole structure:

A layer is a gzipped tar archive of the files one step of a Dockerfile added or changed. The config is a JSON document with what Docker needs to start the image: environment variables, the user, the command, and the hash of each unpacked layer.

The manifest lists the config and the layers by digest, and the index lists the manifests. Every level names the next one by its hash, so the digest at the top fixes every byte below it. FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:… pins the whole base image down to the last file.

FROM python:3.12-slim pins nothing. A tag is a pointer, and Docker says so plainly: “Image tags are mutable, meaning a publisher can update a tag to point to a new image” (Docker: build best practices).

The official images are rebuilt whenever Debian or Python ships a fix; the maintainers “strive to publish updated images at least monthly for Debian”[5]. Compare today’s tag with the digest perevod’s Dockerfile pins, which was the tag’s target the day the Dockerfile was written:

PINNED = "sha256:12316debbfb86890f6b2d825820612741ba527ad5a44e3902759141d572bfe8f"
today = response.headers["Docker-Content-Digest"]
if today == PINNED:
    print("python:3.12-slim still points to the image perevod pins")
else:
    print("python:3.12-slim has moved: today it points to", today[:19] + "…")
pinned = get_manifest(HUB, "library/python", PINNED, hub_token)
print("the pinned image is still served by its digest:", sha256(pinned.content) == PINNED)

python:3.12-slim has moved: today it points to sha256:aa943ce41142…
the pinned image is still served by its digest: True

4. Why two builds of one Dockerfile differ

The definition the reproducible-builds project uses is strict: “A build is reproducible if given the same source code, build environment and build instructions, any party can recreate bit-by-bit identical copies of all specified artifacts”[6].

For an image, bit by bit means the same digest at the top. It’s worth the trouble for one reason: then anyone can check that the image was built from the source they can read, by building it and comparing one hash.

Docker doesn’t give you that by default. Build one Dockerfile twice without the cache, and you get two digests.

This lesson’s image did exactly that on its first two builds, and the differences were in places that have nothing to do with the program. Two of them you can reproduce right here.

The first is time. A layer is a tar archive, and tar stores each file’s modification time. Pack perevod’s source as a layer, then “save” the same files a minute later, as a fresh checkout in CI would:

commit_time = subprocess.run(["git", "log", "-1", "--format=%ct"], capture_output=True,
                             text=True, check=True)
EPOCH = int(commit_time.stdout)  # the time of the commit the notebook started from


def layer_digest(folder, normalize):
    buffer = io.BytesIO()
    with tarfile.open(fileobj=buffer, mode="w") as tar:
        for path in sorted(Path(folder).rglob("*")):
            info = tar.gettarinfo(str(path), arcname=str(path.relative_to(folder)))
            if normalize:
                info.mtime = min(info.mtime, EPOCH)  # no time later than the commit
                info.uid = 0
                info.gid = 0
                info.uname = ""
                info.gname = ""
            if path.is_file():
                with open(path, "rb") as file:
                    tar.addfile(info, file)
            else:
                tar.addfile(info)
    return sha256(gzip.compress(buffer.getvalue(), mtime=0))  # gzip stores a time too


def touch(path):
    stat = path.stat()
    os.utime(path, (stat.st_atime, stat.st_mtime + 60))


SOURCE = Path("perevod/src")
as_is = layer_digest(SOURCE, normalize=False)
normalized = layer_digest(SOURCE, normalize=True)
for path in SOURCE.rglob("*.py"):
    touch(path)
print("as on disk:", as_is[:23], "->", layer_digest(SOURCE, normalize=False)[:23])
print("normalized:", normalized[:23], "->", layer_digest(SOURCE, normalize=True)[:23])

as on disk: sha256:9e9b126813cbaec2 -> sha256:e673f23034cdb19a
normalized: sha256:c25edb033761b87c -> sha256:c25edb033761b87c

Same bytes in every file, a new digest. Clamping every time to the commit’s time, and dropping the owner’s name, fixes it. BuildKit, the engine behind docker build, does exactly this when asked: it takes the time from the SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH variable, a convention of the reproducible-builds project, and with the exporter option rewrite-timestamp=true it clamps the time of every file in every layer to it [7].

The second cause hides inside the files. pip compiles every .py file it installs to bytecode, a .pyc, and a .pyc starts with a 16-byte header that tells Python whether the cache is still valid. By default the header holds the source file’s modification time:

module = Path("perevod/src/perevod/config.py")
target = WORK_DIR / "config.pyc"


def compiled():
    py_compile.compile(str(module), cfile=str(target))
    return target.read_bytes()


def header(pyc):
    flags = int.from_bytes(pyc[4:8], "little")
    if flags == 0:
        mtime = int.from_bytes(pyc[8:12], "little")
        size = int.from_bytes(pyc[12:16], "little")
        return f"flags {flags}, source modified at {mtime}, source size {size}"
    return f"flags {flags}, source hash {pyc[8:16].hex()}"


first = compiled()
touch(module)
second = compiled()
print(header(first))
print(header(second))
print("same bytes:", first == second)

flags 0, source modified at 1793220667, source size 1856
flags 0, source modified at 1793220727, source size 1856
same bytes: False

Even if the archive’s times are clamped, the time inside the file survives, and pip installs thousands of .pyc files. PEP 552 added a second kind of header, with a hash of the source instead of its time, and py_compile, which pip uses through compileall, switches to it by itself when SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is set [8]:

os.environ["SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH"] = str(EPOCH)
first = compiled()
touch(module)
second = compiled()
del os.environ["SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH"]
print(header(first))
print(header(second))
print("same bytes:", first == second)

flags 3, source hash 6e4327a19146f24e
flags 3, source hash 6e4327a19146f24e
same bytes: True

Flags 3 mean “checked hash”: Python compares the stored hash with the source’s when it imports the module. The bytes no longer depend on when the file was saved.

There’s a catch in the Dockerfile, though: BuildKit hands SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH to the build, but a RUN step only sees a build argument that the Dockerfile declares with ARG. Without that one line, pip in the image never sees the variable.

The rest of the list, from the first naive builds to two identical ones:

What differed Why The fix
file times in every layer each file gets the time it was written SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH and rewrite-timestamp=true
the dates in the image’s config the clock at build time SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH
every .pyc that pip wrote the header holds the source’s time ARG SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, so pip sees it
a log file in the model’s layer hf-xet names its log by the time delete it in the same RUN
the base image, next month the tag moves FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:…
the packages, next month new releases the lock file, with hashes
the wheel’s metadata pip fetches the newest hatchling build.lock and --no-build-isolation
the archives, and the parser each BuildKit version writes and parses its own way BuildKit’s version pinned in CI
attestations they record when and where a build ran --provenance=false --sbom=false

The order of the entries in a tar archive can differ too, in general; here BuildKit’s builds agreed on it. And one cause this table missed: perevod 0.3.0 shipped with it, and section 7 shows it.

5. perevod’s Dockerfile

Before the image, two small changes in the package. An image runs somewhere you can’t see, so it should be able to say what it is: /health now reports the model’s commit along with the package’s version. The translator remembers where its weights came from; a snapshot downloaded from the Hub lives in a folder named by its commit:

TRANSLATOR = "perevod/src/perevod/translator.py"
replace(TRANSLATOR, "        self.generation = generation\n",
        "        self.generation = generation\n"
        "        self.source = None  "
        "# where the weights came from; from_pretrained fills it in\n")
replace(TRANSLATOR,
        "        if not path.is_dir():\n"
        "            path = Path(snapshot_download(model, revision=revision, "
        "allow_patterns=FILES))\n",
        "        if path.is_dir():\n"
        "            source = str(path)\n"
        "        else:\n"
        "            path = Path(snapshot_download(model, revision=revision, "
        "allow_patterns=FILES))\n"
        '            source = f"{model}@{path.name}"  '
        "# a snapshot's folder is named by its commit\n")
replace(TRANSLATOR,
        "        return cls(network.to(device), tokenizer, "
        "GenerationConfig.from_dict(settings))\n",
        "        generation = GenerationConfig.from_dict(settings)\n"
        "        translator = cls(network.to(device), tokenizer, generation)\n"
        "        translator.source = source\n"
        "        return translator\n")

The server returns it, and its test checks it:

replace("perevod/src/perevod/server.py",
        "    async def health():\n"
        '        return {"status": "ok", "version": __version__}\n',
        "    async def health():  "
        "# what is running: the package's version and the model's commit\n"
        "        model = app.state.batcher.translator.source\n"
        '        return {"status": "ok", "version": __version__, "model": model}\n')

        "def test_the_health_check(client):\n"
        '    assert client.get("/health").json()["status"] == "ok"\n',
        "def test_the_health_check_names_the_model(client, tiny_dir):\n"
        '    health = client.get("/health").json()\n'
        '    assert health["status"] == "ok"\n'
        '    assert health["model"] == str(tiny_dir)\n')
replace("perevod/src/perevod/__init__.py", '__version__ = "0.2.0"', '__version__ = "0.3.1"')

Now the Dockerfile, top to bottom.

FROM takes the Python image by digest, as section 3 showed. The Dockerfile’s parser is part of BuildKit, so pinning BuildKit’s version in CI pins it too. (A # syntax= line on top can name a newer parser, as an image of its own; then pin that by digest as well.)

ARG SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is the line from section 4 that lets pip see the build’s time. A user with uid 1000 instead of root: a process that has no reason to write to the system shouldn’t be able to.

The dependencies are installed before the code, and exactly as locked: --require-hashes turns on the checks, --no-deps makes pip install only what the lock lists, and the lock already lists everything. The order matters for speed, too.

Docker caches each step and reruns a step only when something it depends on changes, so the slow step that installs PyTorch, which changes least often, comes first, and editing perevod’s code rebuilds only the cheap steps after it.

The package is installed with --no-build-isolation, so that pip builds it with the locked hatchling from the previous step. Then the model, in a folder of its own, at the commit perevod pins.

The download leaves more than the model behind in ~/.cache, and all of that goes in the same step, because a file deleted in a later step stays in the earlier layer forever.

Finally HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1: in the running container, “no HTTP calls will be made to the Hugging Face Hub” (huggingface_hub: environment variables), so the image runs where there is no network, and never quietly downloads anything else. The labels say where the image came from; GitHub uses org.opencontainers.image.source to link the image to its repository.

write("perevod/Dockerfile", """
# perevod's server with its model inside: one commit builds one image, bit for bit.
# The base image by digest; the Dockerfile's parser comes with BuildKit, pinned in CI.
FROM \\
    python:3.12-slim@sha256:12316debbfb86890f6b2d825820612741ba527ad5a44e3902759141d572bfe8f

# a fixed time instead of the clock: with it pip writes .pyc files that don't record when
ARG SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH
ENV PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
RUN useradd --uid 1000 --create-home perevod
WORKDIR /home/perevod

# dependencies first, exactly as locked: they change least often, so this layer is cached
COPY requirements.lock build.lock ./
RUN pip install --require-hashes --no-deps -r requirements.lock -r build.lock \\
        --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

# the package itself, built with the locked build backend
COPY pyproject.toml README.md ./src/
COPY src ./src/src
RUN pip install --no-deps --no-build-isolation ./src && rm -rf ./src

# the model, at the commit this version of perevod was tested with, in a folder of its own;
# the rest of what the download leaves in ~/.cache goes: hf-xet's log is named by the time,
# and huggingface_hub caches a list of AI agents that the Hub can change at any moment
ENV HF_HUB_CACHE=/home/perevod/models
USER perevod
RUN python -c "from perevod import Translator; Translator.from_pretrained()" \\
    && rm -rf /home/perevod/.cache
ENV HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1

ARG VERSION=dev REVISION=unknown
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch \\
      org.opencontainers.image.version=$VERSION \\
      org.opencontainers.image.revision=$REVISION
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["perevod-server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
""")
assert PINNED in Path("perevod/Dockerfile").read_text()

The build context, the folder Docker sends to the builder, is perevod/. A .dockerignore keeps out what the image doesn’t need, and what would change its bytes without changing the program, like Python’s caches:

write("perevod/.dockerignore", """
# only what the image needs: the code, its metadata and the lock files
tests
**/__pycache__
.pytest_cache
.ruff_cache
dist
build
*.egg-info
""")

On a machine with Docker, this builds the image and runs it, with the same options CI uses below (Docker Desktop and OrbStack ship with BuildKit):

cd perevod
export SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$(git log -1 --format=%ct)
docker buildx build . --build-arg SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH --provenance=false --sbom=false \
    --output type=docker,name=perevod:dev,rewrite-timestamp=true
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 perevod:dev

And without a network at all, from the command line of lesson 7:

docker run --rm --network none perevod:dev perevod "Tom is afraid of the dark."

One trap when you limit the container’s CPUs. docker run --cpus 2 is a quota on CPU time, not a set of processors, and PyTorch doesn’t read quotas: it starts as many threads as the host has physical cores, and they fight over the two CPUs’ worth of time. Tell it explicitly, with -e OMP_NUM_THREADS=2.

6. Build twice, publish once

Reproducibility that nobody checks decays: one day a step starts writing a timestamp, and nobody notices until the day it matters. So the CI job that publishes the image also checks it.

On every pull request that touches the package it builds the image twice, the second time without any cache, and compares the two digests. On a release tag it does the same and pushes the first build to the GitHub Container Registry, ghcr.io, as ghcr.io/xmarva/perevod:<version>.

Some details of the workflow below. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is the time of the commit, so a rebuild of the same commit next year uses the same time. QEMU, an emulator, lets the x86 runner build the ARM image too, for people on Apple silicon and ARM servers. The builder is pinned, moby/buildkit:v0.34.1, because another version of BuildKit may pack the same files into different bytes. Attestations are switched off: they record when and where a build ran, so no two builds have the same ones. The job logs in to the registry with the token GitHub gives every workflow run, and needs the packages: write permission for it [9].

write(".github/workflows/image.yml", """
name: image

# perevod's Docker image. On pull requests that touch the package: build it twice and check
# that the two builds are the same, bit for bit. On a release tag: the same, and publish it.
on:
  push:
    tags: ["perevod-v*"]
  pull_request:
    paths: ["perevod/**", ".github/workflows/image.yml"]

env:
  IMAGE: ghcr.io/xmarva/perevod
  PLATFORMS: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
  # OCI media types in both builds, and no attestations: those record when and where a build
  # ran, so no two builds have the same ones
  OUTPUT: oci-mediatypes=true,rewrite-timestamp=true
  PUSH: ${{ github.ref_type == 'tag' }}  # only a release tag publishes

jobs:
  image:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v4  # runs the arm64 build on an x86 machine
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
        with:
          driver-opts: image=moby/buildkit:v0.34.1  # a pinned builder writes the same bytes
      - name: Settings from the commit
        run: |
          echo "SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$(git log -1 --format=%ct)" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          init=perevod/src/perevod/__init__.py
          version=$(sed -n 's/^__version__ = "\\(.*\\)"$/\\1/p' "$init")
          echo "VERSION=$version" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          echo "REVISION=$GITHUB_SHA" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - name: The tag matches the package's version
        if: github.ref_type == 'tag'
        run: test "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" = "perevod-v$VERSION"
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        if: github.ref_type == 'tag'
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - name: Build, and push on a release tag
        run: |
          docker buildx build perevod --platform "$PLATFORMS" \\
            --provenance=false --sbom=false \\
            --build-arg SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH --build-arg VERSION --build-arg REVISION \\
            --output "type=image,name=$IMAGE:$VERSION,push=$PUSH,$OUTPUT" \\
            --metadata-file first.json
      - name: Build again from scratch, and compare
        run: |
          docker buildx build perevod --platform "$PLATFORMS" \\
            --provenance=false --sbom=false --no-cache \\
            --build-arg SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH --build-arg VERSION --build-arg REVISION \\
            --output "type=oci,dest=second.tar,$OUTPUT" --metadata-file second.json
          first=$(jq -r '."containerimage.digest"' first.json)
          second=$(jq -r '."containerimage.digest"' second.json)
          echo "first build:  $first"
          echo "second build: $second"
          test "$first" = "$second"
""")

manifests = {}

Most layers differ, and should: Debian, Python and PyTorch are compiled for each processor. The interesting rows are the others. The copied files are the same bytes on both, and so is the model’s layer, which was made by running Python on each architecture, the ARM one inside an emulator, and keeping what the download wrote.

Two different processors, one emulated, produced the same bytes, because nothing in that layer depends on when or where it was made.

Two small layers of ours differ for a reason that took some digging: both carry times inherited from the base image, which was built separately, minutes apart, for each architecture.

useradd copies the new user’s start-up files from /etc/skel with their original times. And running pip makes Python import a few modules of its own standard library that the base image hadn’t cached yet, so Python writes their .pyc files into the layer that installs perevod.

Python’s import system writes timestamp headers no matter what SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH says, which only changes the default of py_compile and compileall, and the timestamps are those of the standard library’s files.

rewrite-timestamp only rewrites times later than SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, and these are earlier. Inside one architecture they’re pinned along with the base, so two builds still agree.

There’s a stronger test than CI’s. CI builds twice on the same machine, minutes apart. The real promise of a reproducible build is that anyone, anywhere, later, gets the same bytes.

A day after the release, a rebuild of the same commit on a laptop, an ARM Mac, with the same command and the same pinned BuildKit, gave the published digest, on a fresh builder.

On a builder that had built earlier versions, one directory in one layer came out with the time of an old build, and the digest differed: rebuild on a fresh builder, as CI always does.

7. The image, without Docker

The notebook can’t run Docker, but it can do what Docker does when it pulls an image: download the layers, check each against its digest, and unpack them on top of each other into one folder. That folder is the image’s filesystem. One detail matters while unpacking. A layer can’t change an earlier layer, so when a step deletes a file, its layer carries an empty marker named .wh.<name>, a whiteout, and the file must be removed from what’s been unpacked so far. And a tar archive from the internet deserves suspicion: Python’s data filter refuses entries that would land outside the folder, including links to absolute paths, which would point into this machine’s own system instead of the image’s [10].

MACHINES = {"x86_64": ("amd64", "x86_64-linux-gnu", "ld-linux-x86-64.so.2"),
            "aarch64": ("arm64", "aarch64-linux-gnu", "ld-linux-aarch64.so.1")}
ARCH, TRIPLET, LOADER = MACHINES[os.uname().machine]
ROOT = WORK_DIR / "rootfs"
shutil.rmtree(ROOT, ignore_errors=True)
ROOT.mkdir()
refused = []


def unpack(member, path):
    name = Path(member.name)
    if name.name.startswith(".wh."):  # a whiteout: a later layer deleted this file
        gone = Path(path) / name.parent / name.name.removeprefix(".wh.")
        if gone.is_dir() and not gone.is_symlink():
            shutil.rmtree(gone)
        elif gone.exists() or gone.is_symlink():
            gone.unlink()
        return None
    try:
        return tarfile.data_filter(member, path)
    except tarfile.FilterError:
        refused.append(member.name)
        return None

    with tarfile.open(fileobj=io.BytesIO(data), mode="r:gz") as tar:
        tar.extractall(ROOT, filter=unpack)

25 AI coding agents, starting with ['antigravity', 'augment-cli', 'cline', 'cowork']

Next to the model sat a list of AI coding agents. huggingface_hub 2.x labels its requests with the agent that made them, if any, and to recognise agents it downloads the list from the Hub, “at most once a day”, and caches it in ~/.cache/huggingface.

The list lives on the Hub’s server and changes when the Hub adds an agent. So the two builds of the release agreed, but a rebuild of the same commit after the next change to that list would not: the model layer would hold a different file and get a different digest.

Nothing pins a file the build downloads from a server, except the build itself. perevod 0.3.1 keeps the model in a folder of its own and deletes everything else under ~/.cache in the same step, which is the line you saw in the Dockerfile.

The lesson in it is general: a step that runs a program records everything that program writes, not only what you asked for. Look inside a layer at least once.

Now run the image. A container is, at heart, a process that sees the image’s folder as its whole filesystem.

Docker arranges that with the kernel’s namespaces, which a notebook can’t use, but there’s a simpler trick that’s enough here: run the image’s own Python through the image’s own dynamic loader, the program that starts every Linux binary and loads its libraries.

Pointed at the image’s libraries, it runs the image’s Python with the image’s C library and the image’s packages, whatever this machine has installed. The environment comes from the image’s config, with its paths moved into the folder:

A different Python and a different PyTorch, and here every translation came out the same. That isn’t guaranteed.

PyTorch’s kernels change between versions, and so does the order of their arithmetic; when two hypotheses in a beam are nearly tied, a difference in the last digit of a score picks a different one. The image is how you stop wondering whether that will happen to you.

8. The same model in a browser

An image needs a machine to run on, and someone to pay for the machine. For a demo there’s a cheaper place to run a model this small: the visitor’s own device.

The obvious host for a free demo used to be a Hugging Face Space with Gradio on a free CPU. That changed in July 2026: now “Gradio and Docker Spaces run on compute and require a paid plan to create”, while “Static Spaces are free for everyone”[11].

A static Space serves files, HTML and JavaScript, and nothing stops one of those files from being a model. ONNX Runtime Web runs ONNX models in the browser with WebAssembly, and perevod’s weights take 38 MB. So the page downloads the model once, and every translation runs on the visitor’s processor: no server, and nothing typed leaves the device.

ONNX is a file format for a computation graph: the operations of a network and its weights, readable by many runtimes. The model goes in as two graphs. The encoder runs once per sentence.

The decoder step takes the hypotheses so far and returns the log-probabilities of the next token for each, so the beam search of lesson 3 stays outside the graph, written in JavaScript, where it’s a loop of forty lines.

The step has no KV cache, so each step recomputes the whole prefix; for short sentences that costs less than it sounds, and keeps the graph simple.

The export is a script in the course repository, next to the page’s files:

write("space/export_onnx.py", '''
# Export perevod's model to the two ONNX graphs of the in-browser demo:
#   encoder.onnx: source ids -> memory
#   decoder.onnx: hypotheses, memory, source ids -> log-probabilities of the next token
# and the tokenizer, which the page loads as it is.
# Usage: python export_onnx.py --out model
import argparse
import logging
from pathlib import Path

import torch
from torch.export import Dim

from perevod import Translator, decoding


class Encoder(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, model):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = model

    def forward(self, src):
        return self.model.encode(src)


class DecoderStep(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, model):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = model

    def forward(self, tgt, memory, src):
        return self.model.decode(tgt, memory, src)[:, -1].log_softmax(-1)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Export perevod's model to ONNX")
    parser.add_argument("--out", default="model")
    out = Path(parser.parse_args().out)
    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    logging.getLogger("torch.onnx").setLevel(logging.ERROR)  # the exporter is chatty
    translator = Translator.from_pretrained(device="cpu")
    model = translator.model
    _, bos, _ = decoding.special_ids(translator.tokenizer)
    ids = decoding.source_ids(translator.tokenizer, "Tom is afraid of the dark.", 256)
    src = torch.tensor([ids, ids])  # two rows, three target tokens: any sizes above one do
    tgt = torch.tensor([[bos, bos, bos], [bos, bos, bos]])
    batch = Dim("batch")
    source = Dim("source", max=256)  # the model's positions
    target = Dim("target", max=256)
    # export leaves a module in the mode it found it in, and a new module starts in training
    # mode: without eval() the wrappers would switch the model's dropout back on afterwards
    encoder = Encoder(model).eval()
    step = DecoderStep(model).eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        memory = model.encode(src)
        torch.onnx.export(encoder, (src,), out / "encoder.onnx", input_names=["src"],
                          output_names=["memory"], external_data=False, verbose=False,
                          dynamic_shapes={"src": {0: batch, 1: source}})
        torch.onnx.export(step, (tgt, memory, src), out / "decoder.onnx",
                          input_names=["tgt", "memory", "src"], output_names=["logp"],
                          external_data=False, verbose=False,
                          dynamic_shapes={"tgt": {0: batch, 1: target},
                                          "memory": {0: batch, 1: source},
                                          "src": {0: batch, 1: source}})
    translator.tokenizer.save(str(out / "tokenizer.json"))  # the page needs it too
    for path in sorted(out.glob("*.onnx")):
        print(f"{path.name}: {path.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
''')

The two graphs share the embeddings in PyTorch, so together they’re larger than the weights: each file carries its own copy. Dim tells the exporter which sizes may change between calls: the number of hypotheses, and the lengths of the source and of the translation so far.

Before anything goes near a browser, check that the graphs compute what PyTorch computes. ONNX Runtime has a Python package with the same engine:

import onnxruntime as ort

encoder = ort.InferenceSession("space/model/encoder.onnx")
decoder = ort.InferenceSession("space/model/decoder.onnx")
pad_id, bos_id, eos_id = decoding.special_ids(translator.tokenizer)

src = torch.tensor([decoding.source_ids(translator.tokenizer, sentences[0], 256)])
tgt = torch.tensor([[bos_id]])
with torch.no_grad():
    memory = translator.model.encode(src)
    expected = translator.model.decode(tgt, memory, src)[:, -1].log_softmax(-1).numpy()
onnx_memory = encoder.run(None, {"src": src.numpy()})[0]
got = decoder.run(None, {"tgt": tgt.numpy(), "memory": onnx_memory, "src": src.numpy()})[0]
print("largest difference in log-probabilities:", float(np.abs(got - expected).max()))
print("the same first token:", int(got.argmax()) == int(expected.argmax()))

largest difference in log-probabilities: 7.62939453125e-06
the same first token: True

The differences are in the fifth or sixth decimal place: the same arithmetic, done in a different order. What matters is the translations. Here is lesson 3’s beam search once more, written against the two graphs the way the page’s JavaScript does it, step for step: every hypothesis is fed again whole, and the four best continuations survive.

def length_penalty(length, alpha=0.6):
    return ((5 + length) / 6) ** alpha


def onnx_translate(sentence, beam_size=4, max_tokens=128):
    ids = decoding.source_ids(translator.tokenizer, sentence, 256)
    src = np.array([ids], dtype=np.int64)
    memory = encoder.run(None, {"src": src})[0]
    beams = [([bos_id], 0.0)]
    finished = []
    for _ in range(max_tokens):
        n = len(beams)
        tgt = np.array([tokens for tokens, score in beams], dtype=np.int64)
        feeds = {"tgt": tgt, "memory": np.repeat(memory, n, axis=0),
                 "src": np.repeat(src, n, axis=0)}
        logp = decoder.run(None, feeds)[0]
        candidates = []
        for (tokens, score), row in zip(beams, logp):
            for token in np.argsort(-row, kind="stable")[:beam_size]:
                candidates.append((tokens + [int(token)], score + float(row[token])))
        candidates.sort(key=lambda candidate: candidate[1], reverse=True)
        beams = []
        for tokens, score in candidates:
            if tokens[-1] == eos_id:
                finished.append((tokens, score))
            else:
                beams.append((tokens, score))
            if len(beams) == beam_size:
                break
        if len(finished) >= beam_size or not beams:
            break
    pool = finished or beams
    best, best_score = pool[0][0], -math.inf
    for tokens, score in pool:
        normalized = score / length_penalty(len(tokens) - 1)
        if normalized > best_score:
            best, best_score = tokens, normalized
    return translator.tokenizer.decode([token for token in best[1:] if token != eos_id])


start = time.time()
through_onnx = []
for sentence in sentences:
    through_onnx.append(onnx_translate(sentence))
same = 0
for a, b in zip(here, through_onnx, strict=True):
    if a == b:
        same += 1
seconds = time.time() - start
print(f"identical to the package: {same} of {len(sentences)}, in {seconds:.0f} s")
for sentence, translation in list(zip(sentences, through_onnx))[:3]:
    print(sentence, "->", translation)

Word for word. The page itself is three small files in the course repository’s space/ folder, and only one of them is about the page.

translate.js is the function above in JavaScript. tokenizer.js rewrites the tokenizer of lesson 1, whose tokenizer.json the page loads as it is, and it had one trap worth knowing.

The tokenizer splits text into words with the regular expression \w+, and in the Rust library behind Hugging Face’s tokenizers, \w matches letters of every alphabet. In JavaScript it matches only [A-Za-z0-9_], even with the Unicode flag, so a word like “naïve” or “Москва” would come apart.

The JavaScript version spells the classes out, [\p{Alphabetic}\p{M}\p{Nd}\p{Pc}\p{Join_Control}], and a script in the same folder checks it against the original on every English sentence of the test set, id for id.

The rest is a static Space: a README.md whose header says sdk: static, uploaded with the two graphs:

python space/export_onnx.py --out space/model
hf upload xmarva/perevod space . --repo-type space

Here it is, xmarva/perevod:

The first visit downloads the two graphs once, and the browser keeps them. After that the page works without a network, and the translation takes about as long as in this notebook, on whatever device it opened on. The model can’t do more there than here, of course; it’s the same model, with the same limits its card lists.

Two ways to ship one model, then, for two jobs. The image is for running it as a service: the same bytes on every server, checkable by anyone, with nothing left to chance at startup.

The page is for showing it to people: free, private, and limited by the visitor’s device. Both are built from the same weights at the same commit, and both were checked against the package, translation for translation.

9. Release 0.3.1

Before a release, the fast tests, which now include the health check that names the model:

!cd perevod && {sys.executable} -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider -m "not slow" --color=no

........................                                                 [100%]
24 passed, 2 deselected in 6.97s

The release is a commit and a tag, perevod-v0.3.1, and the image is whatever CI builds from them. That gives the notebook one last check: are the files it wrote and edited the same as the release’s?

Only the files that go into the image count, the build context and the workflow. The lock files are compared without their first lines, where uv records the command, which here includes --exclude-newer:

RELEASE = "perevod-v0.3.1"
subprocess.run(["git", "fetch", "-q", "--depth", "1", "origin", "tag", RELEASE], check=True)
listed = subprocess.run(["git", "ls-tree", "-r", "--name-only", RELEASE, "perevod"],
                        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.split()
IMAGE_FILES = {"Dockerfile", ".dockerignore", "requirements.lock", "build.lock",
               "pyproject.toml", "README.md"}
context = [".github/workflows/image.yml"]
for name in listed:
    if name.startswith("perevod/src/") or name.removeprefix("perevod/") in IMAGE_FILES:
        context.append(name)


def without_command(text):
    lines = []
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if not line.startswith("#    uv pip compile"):
            lines.append(line)
    return lines


different = []
for name in context:
    released = subprocess.run(["git", "show", f"{RELEASE}:{name}"], capture_output=True,
                              text=True, check=True).stdout
    if without_command(Path(name).read_text()) != without_command(released):
        different.append(name)
print(len(context), "files compared, different:", different or "none")

15 files compared, different: none

The notebook rebuilt the release’s inputs file for file, and CI turned them into ghcr.io/xmarva/perevod:0.3.1, the image section 7 took apart. On your machine:

docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/xmarva/perevod:0.3.1
curl localhost:8000/health

0.3.1 is a patch release in lesson 7’s terms: the package’s code is the same as in 0.3.0, and only the way the image is built changed. Pinned by its digest, the image will translate the same way in a year, on any machine that runs Docker, with or without a network. That was the point of the lesson.

References

  1. NumPy 2.0.0 release notes, and the error in practice: PyTorch issue #129310. ↩
  2. Python Packaging User Guide: install_requires vs requirements files. ↩
  3. Stufft, D. (2013). setup.py vs requirements.txt. Abstract and concrete dependencies. ↩
  4. pip: secure installs and hash-checking mode; uv: uv pip compile and using uv with PyTorch. ↩
  5. docker-library FAQ and Docker’s build best practices, on tags and digests. ↩
  6. reproducible-builds.org: the definition, and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH. ↩
  7. BuildKit: reproducible builds; Docker: image exporter options. ↩
  8. PEP 552: Deterministic pycs; py_compile. ↩
  9. GitHub: publishing Docker images and the Container registry. ↩
  10. Python: tarfile extraction filters; the dynamic loader: ld.so(8). ↩
  11. Hugging Face: Spaces overview and static Spaces. ↩
  12. Open Container Initiative: image specification (index, manifest, config, layers, descriptors) and distribution specification.
  13. huggingface_hub environment variables (HF_HUB_CACHE, HF_HUB_OFFLINE).
  14. PyTorch: exporting to ONNX; ONNX Runtime Web.
entry.summary: Ship a model so that it runs the same next year: a lock file with hashes, an image pinned by digest, builds that give the same bytes twice, GitHub Actions publishing to GHCR, the image pulled and run without Docker, and the model exported to ONNX for a free in-browser demo.

entry.title: Is it rational to be good? Game theory and the ethics of cooperation

link.title: Is it rational to be good? Game theory and the ethics of cooperation

entry.content:
In the second book of Plato’s Republic, Glaucon offers Socrates a challenge that moral philosophy has been answering ever since. People, he says, praise justice not for itself but for its consequences.

Left to ourselves we would all prefer to wrong others and get away with it; we settle for justice because we fear being wronged more than we enjoy wronging.

Justice, on this account, is “a mean or compromise, between the best of all, which is to do injustice and not be punished, and the worst of all, which is to suffer injustice without the power of retaliation” (Republic 359a)[1].

To make the point he tells the story of Gyges, a shepherd who finds a ring that makes him invisible, and uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king and take the throne.

Give such a ring to a just man and to an unjust one, Glaucon says, and they will end up doing the same things, since “no man can be imagined to be of such an iron nature that he would stand fast in justice”, and “wherever any one thinks that he can safely be unjust, there he is unjust” (360b–c).

Glaucon’s argument has a structure, and the structure has a name. Twenty-three centuries after the Republic, the mathematicians of game theory found it in a two-by-two table and called it the prisoner’s dilemma.

The table turned the old question into a precise one: under which conditions is it rational to be just, and which kind of justice is rational?

This essay follows the answers that game theory gives, from Hobbes to evolutionary simulations, and marks the point where they stop. The models are small enough to compute exactly, and every picture below is computed from them.

1. The prisoner’s dilemma

Two people can each do something for the other at a cost to themselves: keep a promise, share credit, return a favour. If both do, both are better off.

If one does and the other doesn’t, the one who didn’t is best off of all and the one who did is worst off. If neither does, both lose what they could have had together.

Game theory calls this structure the prisoner’s dilemma, after a story Albert Tucker told in 1950 to illustrate a game that Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher had invented a few months earlier at the RAND Corporation[2].

Only the order of the four outcomes matters. The temptation to exploit beats the reward for mutual cooperation, which beats the punishment for mutual defection, which beats the sucker’s payoff:

\[T > R > P > S, \qquad 2R > T + S.\]

The second condition says that taking turns at exploiting each other is worse than cooperating, so that cooperation, not alternation, is what the two players lose. The numbers in the table, \(T = 5\), \(R = 3\), \(P = 1\), \(S = 0\), are the ones Robert Axelrod used, and the rest of this essay uses them too.

The reasoning that follows is short and, within its assumptions, impeccable. Whatever the other player does, you do better by defecting: \(5 > 3\) if they cooperate, \(1 > 0\) if they don’t. Defection is a dominant strategy, and two players who see this end up with 1 point each, while 3 each was on the table.

The outcome is a Nash equilibrium, since neither can gain by changing alone, and it is worse for both than another outcome they could have reached. Individual rationality, applied correctly by both, produces a result that both regard as a failure.

This is Glaucon’s compromise in miniature. Each would most like to wrong the other with impunity; each fears most to be wronged; and justice, mutual cooperation, is an agreement they would both welcome and neither has a reason to keep.

2. Hobbes: changing the game

Thomas Hobbes described the same structure as the condition of humanity without government.

In the state of nature, where nobody can trust anybody to hold back, everyone has reason to strike first, and the result is a war of all against all, in which there is “no place for Industry; because the fruit thereof is uncertain”, and the life of man is “solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short” (Leviathan, ch. 13)[3].

Hobbes also gave Glaucon’s position its sharpest voice. “The Foole hath sayd in his heart, there is no such thing as Justice”, and he argues that “to make, or not make; keep, or not keep Covenants, was not against Reason, when it conduced to ones benefit” (ch. 15). The Foole is the player who has noticed that defection dominates.

Hobbes’s reply is not that the Foole makes a logical error in the single case. It is that the Foole is not in a single case.

A man who breaks his covenant, and declares that he may with reason do so, “cannot be received into any Society, that unite themselves for Peace and defence, but by the errour of them that receive him”, and “if he be left, or cast out of Society, he perisheth” (ch. 15).

The Foole’s defection is a single move, but it tells everyone what kind of player he is, and the rest of the game is played against that knowledge.

Hobbes’s remedy for the war of all against all, though, is not an argument but an institution: “Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words, and of no strength to secure a man at all” (ch. 17).

The sovereign does not persuade the players to cooperate; he changes their payoffs, so that defection no longer pays. In the language of game theory, Hobbes’s solution is to make the game stop being a prisoner’s dilemma.

That works, and modern states, courts and contracts are its descendants. But it leaves Glaucon’s question untouched, because it explains why people keep promises when someone watches them, which Glaucon never doubted. His question was about the ring.

3. Can cooperation in a single encounter be rational?

Some philosophers have argued that the dominance reasoning itself is wrong, or at least incomplete, even when the two players meet once and no sovereign watches.

The first argument is Kantian. Kant’s categorical imperative reads, in Thomas Kingsmill Abbott’s translation, “Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law” (Groundwork, Ak 4:421)[4].

One of Kant’s own examples is close to the dilemma: a man borrows money with a promise he knows he will not keep.

If everyone acted on that maxim, “the promise itself would become impossible, as well as the end that one might have in view in it, since no one would consider that anything was promised to him” (Ak 4:422).

The defector’s maxim, accept the cooperation of others and give none back, has the same shape. It works only as an exception, and made universal it destroys the cooperation it lives on.

In 1983 the cognitive scientist Douglas Hofstadter turned a related thought into an argument about the game itself. His superrational thinkers, “by recursive definition, include in their calculations the fact that they are in a group of superrational thinkers”[5].

Two such players know that they will reach the same conclusion, so the only outcomes really open to them are the two on the diagonal, and of those mutual cooperation is better.

David Lewis showed that this is a special case of a deeper split in decision theory: “Prisoners’ Dilemma is a Newcomb Problem—or rather, two Newcomb Problems side by side, one per prisoner”[6].

In Newcomb’s problem, a very reliable predictor has put a million dollars into an opaque box if it predicted that you would take only that box, and nothing if it predicted that you would also take a transparent box with a thousand dollars in it.

Against a player who reasons as you do, the other player’s choice is like the predictor’s: your choice does not cause it, but it is very good evidence about it.

Evidential decision theory, which chooses the act that is the best news about the outcome, recommends taking one box, and cooperating. Causal decision theory, which chooses the act with the best causal consequences, recommends taking both boxes, and defecting, because nothing you do now changes what is in the box or what the other player does.

Philosophers have not agreed which theory is right, and the disagreement is now half a century old.

David Gauthier took a different route[7]. Rather than ask which act is rational, he asked which disposition it is rational to have. A straightforward maximizer always chooses the act with the best expected outcome; a constrained maximizer cooperates with others who are disposed to cooperate, and defects otherwise.

If dispositions are translucent, if others can tell, at least sometimes, what kind of person you are, constrained maximizers are offered cooperation and straightforward maximizers are not, and the constrained ones do better. The rational choice of a disposition can then require acts that, taken one at a time, are not rational.

Critics have pointed out that the argument works only to the extent that dispositions really are visible, which brings Gauthier close to the next idea: that what makes cooperation rational is that the encounter is not, in fact, single.

4. The shadow of the future

David Hume saw the problem in an agricultural setting (Treatise 3.2.5.8)[8]:

Your corn is ripe to-day; mine will be so to-morrow. ‘Tis profitable for us both, that I shou’d labour with you to-day, and that you shou’d aid me to-morrow. I have no kindness for you, and know you have as little for me. I will not, therefore, take any pains upon your account; and should I labour with you upon my own account, in expectation of a return, I know I shou’d be disappointed, and that I shou’d in vain depend upon your gratitude. Here then I leave you to labour alone: You treat me in the same manner. The seasons change; and both of us lose our harvests for want of mutual confidence and security.

The farmers in Hume’s example are not wicked; they are prudent, and prudence ruins them both. What saves them is not a sovereign but the expectation of further dealings.

“Hence I learn to do a service to another, without bearing him any real kindness; because I forsee, that he will return my service, in expectation of another of the same kind” (3.2.5.9).

The promise, on Hume’s account, is a convention that makes this expectation public: whoever promises “subjects himself to the penalty of never being trusted again in case of failure” (3.2.5.10).

Game theory makes this precise. Suppose that after each round there is another with probability \(w\), so that a relationship lasts \(1/(1 - w)\) rounds on average. Now a strategy can depend on what the other player did.

The simplest such strategy, tit for tat, cooperates first and then copies the other player’s previous move. Against it, a defection buys \(T\) today and costs a punishment tomorrow, and it pays to cooperate if and only if

\[w \;\ge\; \max\!\left(\frac{T - R}{T - P},\; \frac{T - R}{R - S}\right) = \frac{2}{3}.\]

The first term guards against always defecting, the second against defecting and making up in turns[9]. Axelrod called \(w\) the shadow of the future[10].

The most striking illustration comes from the First World War. On quiet stretches of the Western Front, British and German battalions faced each other for weeks at a time and, without negotiating anything, stopped trying to kill each other.

A British staff officer was “astonished to observe German soldiers walking about within rifle range behind their own line. Our men appeared to take no notice … These people evidently did not know there was a war on. Both sides apparently believed in the policy of ‘live and let live’“[11, 10].

When a salvo landed by mistake, a German climbed onto his parapet and shouted: “We are very sorry about that; we hope no one was hurt. It is not our fault, it is that damned Prussian artillery.”

The truce ended when headquarters ordered raids, whose results it could check: “There was no effective way to pretend that a raid had been undertaken when it had not.”

Two philosophical lessons follow, and the second is less comfortable than the first. The first is that the rationality of cooperation is a fact about the structure of a relationship as much as about the people in it. The same person has more reason to keep a promise to a neighbour than to a stranger at an airport.

The second is that the repeated game does not select cooperation; it only permits it. The theorems that show cooperation can be an equilibrium of a repeated game, known collectively as the folk theorem, also show that almost any pattern of behaviour can be one, including mutual defection forever and many unequal arrangements in between.

Rationality alone underdetermines what rational people will do together. Something else, a convention, a norm, a shared history, has to pick one equilibrium among many, and that something is where much of morality lives.

5. Which character is rational?

If many strategies can sustain cooperation, which ones do well? Axelrod asked game theorists, economists, psychologists and mathematicians to submit programs and played them against each other in a round robin[12].

The winner was “the simplest of all strategies submitted”, tit for tat, sent by the psychologist Anatol Rapoport[9]. In a second round, 62 entrants who knew this tried to beat it, and it won again[13].

A rerun of that second tournament from Axelrod’s original code with 25,000 random seeds has since found that tit for tat wins about 63% of them[14], so the result is a tendency, not a law. Here is a small tournament of the same kind, with twelve classic strategies:

The six strategies that never defect first take the top six places, and between them they win almost no individual matches. Always defect wins nine of its eleven matches and finishes ninth.

The Extortioner, one of the zero-determinant strategies that William Press and Freeman Dyson found in 2012, is built never to earn less than its partner[15]. It loses no match and finishes eleventh. Its generous twin, built never to earn more than its partner, wins no match and finishes first[16].

Axelrod’s explanation is that a nice strategy can never get more than its partner in a single game, since it only defects in answer to a defection; it wins the tournament by doing reasonably well with everyone.

His advice “Don’t be envious” is a point about which comparison is rational: your score is measured against others in your position, not against the person across the table.

Axelrod summed up the winning character in four words, “nice, retaliatory, forgiving, and clear”[10]. Each word names something a moral philosopher would recognise: benevolence, a readiness to resent injury, a willingness to let it go, and the transparency that makes a person predictable.

What game theory adds is that the four belong together. Niceness without retaliation is exploited, retaliation without forgiveness turns every accident into a feud, and both without clarity are wasted, because the other side cannot learn from them.

The feud is easy to see once mistakes are allowed, as they always are in life:

Between two tit for tat players, one misread gesture starts an exchange of punishments that never ends, each side certain that it is only responding. A generous version of tit for tat, which forgives a defection with some probability \(q\), stops the echo after a few rounds[17].

How large should \(q\) be? Forgive too rarely, and mistakes turn into feuds; forgive too often, and a player who alternates defection and apology earns more than honest cooperators. The largest forgiveness that no exploiter can profit from is

\[q^* = \min\!\left(1 - \frac{T - R}{R - S},\; \frac{R - P}{T - P}\right) = \frac{1}{3}\]

with these payoffs[18, 17]:

It is hard not to read this as a formal version of Aristotle’s doctrine of the mean.

“Virtue, then, is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean, i.e. the mean relative to us”; to feel anger “at the right times, with reference to the right objects, towards the right people, with the right motive, and in the right way, is what is both intermediate and best” (Nicomachean Ethics II.6)[19].

Forgiveness here has an excess and a deficiency, and its mean is not a midpoint but depends on the situation, as Aristotle said it should: as the temptation \(T\) grows relative to the reward \(R\), the right amount of forgiveness falls.

6. Evolution and the origin of morality

If cooperative dispositions pay, natural selection and cultural imitation will spread them, and biologists have taken this as an explanation of where morality comes from.

Robert Trivers opened the paper that introduced reciprocal altruism with an admission: “Models that attempt to explain altruistic behavior in terms of natural selection are models designed to take the altruism out of altruism”[20].

Here is what imitation does to a population of a hundred players who copy strategies that earn more, with relationships of twenty rounds on average and one move in fifty going wrong:

With only always defect, tit for tat and unconditional cooperation available, the population never settles. Tit for tat drives out defectors; unconditional cooperators then drift in, since among reciprocators they do just as well; once there are enough of them, defectors return.

Lorens Imhof, Drew Fudenberg and Martin Nowak described this cycle in finite populations[21]. Over twenty runs of the simulation, defectors held the majority 49% of the time.

When generous tit for tat is available, it takes over and holds the population: defectors held the majority 18% of the time, and the average payoff rose from 1.94 to 2.58 points per round.

Unconditional kindness, on this picture, is not a stable state of a society but a phase of it, and what protects a cooperative society is a willingness to punish that erodes exactly when it seems least necessary.

The evolutionary story raises an old worry in a new form. If our moral dispositions exist because they paid, are they really moral?

One answer is that the explanation of a disposition’s origin is not an account of its content: a person who keeps a promise because they value honesty is honest, whatever selection did to their ancestors.

Another answer comes from the way cooperation among strangers actually works. Richard Alexander argued that “moral systems are systems of indirect reciprocity” (p. 77)[22]: I help you, and someone else helps me, because they saw what I did.

Reputation then does the work that repetition does between two people, and it requires judging others, which brings normative questions back in. Martin Nowak and Karl Sigmund showed that cooperation can be sustained by a public “image score” that rises when you help and falls when you refuse[23].

But a player who refuses to help a known cheat then loses reputation for enforcing the norm, so a rule called standing, which looks at whom you refused, works much better[24]:

When Hisashi Ohtsuki and Yoh Iwasa checked all 4096 rules of this kind, only eight kept cooperation stable, and all eight share two features: helping a good person is good and refusing one is bad; refusing a bad person is good, “because it works as sanction”[25].

The evolution of cooperation selects not only for helping but for a particular moral judgement: that punishing the guilty is just and punishing the punisher is not.

Indirect reciprocity also gives an answer to Hume’s sensible knave, who reasons: “That honesty is the best policy, may be a good general rule; but is liable to many exceptions: And he, it may, perhaps, be thought, conducts himself with most wisdom, who observes the general rule, and takes advantage of all the exceptions” (Enquiry 9.22)[26].

Hume admitted that if a man thinks this reasoning requires an answer, “it will be a little difficult to find any, which will to him appear satisfactory and convincing” (9.23).

The answer he did give was about the knave’s inner life: knaves “are, in the end, the greatest dupes, and have sacrificed the invaluable enjoyment of a character, with themselves at least, for the acquisition of worthless toys and gewgaws” (9.25).

The game-theoretic answer is about his outer life. In a world of indirect reciprocity, the knave’s exceptions are exactly what others observe and remember, and only a knave who could be sure of never being seen would profit from them. That knave is Gyges again, and rings like his are rare.

7. The stag hunt and the social contract

Not every problem of cooperation is a prisoner’s dilemma. Rousseau told a story in which nobody gains by betraying anyone: “Was a deer to be taken? Every one saw that to succeed he must faithfully stand to his post; but suppose a hare to have slipped by within reach of any one of them, it is not to be doubted but he pursued it without scruple”[27].

Brian Skyrms argued that this game deserves at least as much attention as the prisoner’s dilemma: “The Stag Hunt is a story that became a game. The game is a prototype of the social contract”[28].

In the stag hunt, mutual cooperation is an equilibrium: nobody wants to leave a successful hunt. But mutual distrust is an equilibrium too, and it is the safer one, what John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten called risk-dominant[29].

With a stag worth 4 to each hunter, a hare worth 3 and nothing for hunting the stag alone, hunting the stag pays only if more than three quarters of the others will hunt it too.

The problem is not temptation but trust, and trust here is self-fulfilling: the same people, with the same values, end up in either equilibrium depending on what they expect of each other.

This is the structure of what Hume called convention, and his example is the cleanest: “Two men, who pull the oars of a boat, do it by an agreement or convention, tho’ they have never given promises to each other” (Treatise 3.2.2.10)[8].

David Lewis built his analysis of convention on such cases, Hume’s rowers among them: a regularity is a convention if everyone conforms to it, everyone expects everyone else to conform, and everyone prefers to conform on condition that the others do (p. 42)[30].

On this view, a good deal of what we call morality, the rules of fair division, of turn-taking, of truthfulness in ordinary talk, is less a constraint on self-interest than a way of coordinating on one of many equilibria.

Skyrms noted the link with the shadow of the future: “If the probability of repetition is high enough, the stag hunting equilibrium becomes risk dominant.”

8. What game theory cannot settle

Every model in this essay takes the payoffs as given and asks only how to play. Amartya Sen argued that this is where the theory is weakest: a person who acts only on their own preferences, with no room for commitment to others or to principles, is not a model of rationality but of a kind of impoverishment.

In his words, “The purely economic man is indeed close to being a social moron” (p. 336)[31]. Experiments agree that real players are not like this.

In the ultimatum game, where one player proposes how to split a sum and the other can accept or let both get nothing, the narrowly rational offer is the smallest possible one, and typical offers are 40 to 50 percent[32].

Across fifteen small-scale societies, mean offers ranged from 26 to 58 percent, and “the higher the degree of market integration and the higher the payoffs to cooperation, the greater the level of cooperation in experimental games”[33].

Even the trench truce has been questioned as an example: Andrew Gelman argued that not shooting simply lowered each side’s own risk, so the soldiers may not have faced a prisoner’s dilemma at all[34].

This sets the limit of the whole approach. Game theory can show that, given what people want, certain dispositions are rational: niceness, retaliation, a measured forgiveness, attention to reputation, a readiness to trust when trust is likely to be returned. It cannot show what people should want.

The payoffs are inputs, and the question of what is worth wanting, which is most of ethics, comes before the first row of the table.

What, then, of Glaucon? Game theory answers him in part. For people who expect to meet again, who are watched by others, and who cannot be sure that their rings will keep working, justice is very often the rational choice, and the models even say which kind of justice: nice, firm, forgiving within limits, and clear.

They do not answer the question Glaucon actually asked, which was whether justice is good in itself, for someone whose ring never fails. That question the models leave where Plato found it.

References

  5. Hofstadter, D. R. (1983). Dilemmas for superrational thinkers, leading up to a luring lottery. Scientific American, 248(6), 14–28. Reprinted in Metamagical Themas (1985), ch. 30. ↩
  6. Lewis, D. (1979). Prisoners’ dilemma is a Newcomb problem. Philosophy & Public Affairs, 8(3), 235–240. ↩

  9. Axelrod, R., & Hamilton, W. D. (1981). The evolution of cooperation. Science, 211(4489), 1390–1396. ↩
  10. Axelrod, R. (1984). The Evolution of Cooperation. Basic Books. Chapter 4, The live-and-let-live system in trench warfare in World War I, pp. 73–87. ↩
  11. Ashworth, T. (1980). Trench Warfare 1914–1918: The Live and Let Live System. Macmillan. ↩
  12. Axelrod, R. (1980a). Effective choice in the prisoner’s dilemma. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 24(1), 3–25. ↩

  14. Knight, V., Campbell, O., Harper, M., Gaffney, T. J., & Glynatsi, N. E. (2025). Reviving, reproducing, and revisiting Axelrod’s second tournament. arXiv:2510.15438. ↩

  19. Aristotle. Nicomachean Ethics, book II. Translated by W. D. Ross. ↩
  20. Trivers, R. L. (1971). The evolution of reciprocal altruism. Quarterly Review of Biology, 46(1), 35–57. ↩
  21. Imhof, L. A., Fudenberg, D., & Nowak, M. A. (2005). Evolutionary cycles of cooperation and defection. PNAS, 102(31), 10797–10800. ↩
  22. Alexander, R. D. (1987). The Biology of Moral Systems. Aldine de Gruyter; reissued by Routledge, 2017. ↩
  23. Nowak, M. A., & Sigmund, K. (1998). Evolution of indirect reciprocity by image scoring. Nature, 393, 573–577. ↩
  24. Leimar, O., & Hammerstein, P. (2001). Evolution of cooperation through indirect reciprocity. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 268, 745–753. ↩
  25. Ohtsuki, H., & Iwasa, Y. (2004). How should we define goodness? Reputation dynamics in indirect reciprocity. Journal of Theoretical Biology, 231(1), 107–120. ↩

  32. Güth, W., & Kocher, M. G. (2014). More than thirty years of ultimatum bargaining experiments. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 108, 396–409. ↩
