Notice what the card does not say: that the model is good. It says where it’s usable and where it isn’t, with the measurement next to each claim, so a reader can decide for their own case. That’s the idea of Mitchell et al.: the question isn’t whether a model is good, but what it is good for.

The card’s license is CC BY 2.0, not the package’s MIT: the weights follow the license of the Tatoeba sentences they were trained on, and the code that runs them has its own. A model and the package around it are licensed separately.

14. Release

A release ties three things to one name: the code, the model, and the card that describes them. The model side is the repository xmarva/perevod-en-ru: lesson 6’s weights with everything needed to run them, so that one revision of one repository is the whole model. With a token, the notebook publishes it to your account:

from perevod.config import GenerationConfig, ModelConfig

release = WORK_DIR / "perevod-en-ru"
release.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
shutil.copy(hf_hub_download(LESSON6, "model.safetensors"), release / "model.safetensors")
shutil.copy(TOKENIZER, release / "tokenizer.json")
release_config = ModelConfig.from_dict(lesson6_config)
(release / "config.json").write_text(json.dumps(release_config.to_dict(), indent=2) + "\n")
(release / "generation_config.json").write_text(
    json.dumps(GenerationConfig().to_dict(), indent=2) + "\n")
(release / "README.md").write_text(CARD, encoding="utf-8")
print(sorted(path.name for path in release.iterdir()))

HUB_USER = os.environ.get("TFS_HUB_USER")
hf_token = env.secret("HF_TOKEN")
if HUB_USER and hf_token:
    api = HfApi(token=hf_token)
    repo_id = f"{HUB_USER}/perevod-en-ru"
    api.create_repo(repo_id, exist_ok=True)
    commit = api.upload_folder(folder_path=str(release), repo_id=repo_id)
    print("published", commit.oid)
else:
    print("not publishing; the course's copy is xmarva/perevod-en-ru")

['README.md', 'config.json', 'generation_config.json', 'model.safetensors', 'tokenizer.json']
not publishing; the course's copy is xmarva/perevod-en-ru

The package side is a version number. perevod follows semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where a bug fix raises the patch, a new feature the minor version, and a change that breaks what users rely on the major one.

For a translator, the question is what “breaks” means, and our answer is opinionated: a new default model is a major release. Nothing in the API changes, but anyone who stored translations, or tuned a pipeline around them, gets different output, and that’s what breaking means to them.

That’s why the two numbers move separately. The card on the Hub can be corrected tomorrow with a new commit, and nobody’s translations change, because perevod 0.1.0 asks for the commit it was tested with.

While the version starts with 0, SemVer allows anything to change at any time; we will still follow the rules above, because users don’t read the fine print of version numbers.

In practice a release is a short routine, in this order. Upload the model and note the commit the upload returns.

Put that commit into REVISION in translator.py (and your repository into MODEL, if you publish your own copy), and record the golden file with that model. Raise the version, commit, then tag the commit and push the tag: git tag perevod-v0.1.0 && git push origin perevod-v0.1.0.

One weak spot of ours: the version is written in two places, pyproject.toml and __init__.py, and the version test compares the command with one of them, so nothing checks that the two agree. Lesson 8 moves the version to one place.

perevod isn’t on PyPI: the name is free there, but a course package shouldn’t take it. Publishing your own takes two more steps. python -m build makes the wheel and the source archive, and twine upload dist/*, or PyPI’s trusted publishing from a GitHub workflow, uploads them.

The next lessons install exactly this version from the course repository, by its tag:

pip install "perevod @ git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@perevod-v0.1.0#subdirectory=perevod"

Lesson 8 puts it behind an HTTP API and measures how fast it answers when many people ask at once, and the start-up times of section 9 already tell part of that story.

References

  1. Pimentel, J. F., Murta, L., Braganholo, V., Freire, J. (2019). A Large-scale Study about Quality and Reproducibility of Jupyter Notebooks. MSR. 1,159,166 notebooks; 24.11% ran without errors, 4.03% reproduced. ↩
  2. Hugging Face: model cards and their metadata, downloading at a revision. ↩
  3. PEP 621 (project metadata), PEP 517 (build backends), PEP 562 (module __getattr__). ↩
  4. GitHub: Actions billing for public repositories, matrix jobs. ↩
  5. Sculley, D. et al. (2015). Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems. NeurIPS.
  6. Mitchell, M. et al. (2019). Model Cards for Model Reporting. FAT*.
  7. Stanovsky, G., Smith, N. A., Zettlemoyer, L. (2019). Evaluating Gender Bias in Machine Translation. ACL.
  8. DeMillo, R. A., Lipton, R. J., Sayward, F. G. (1978). Hints on Test Data Selection: Help for the Practicing Programmer. IEEE Computer. The idea of mutation testing.
  9. Barrault, L. et al. (2020). Findings of the 2020 Conference on Machine Translation (WMT20). The news test set.
  10. Python Packaging User Guide: src layout vs flat layout, the pyproject.toml specification, entry points.
  11. Semantic Versioning 2.0.0.
  12. pytest documentation: fixtures, capsys, monkeypatch, markers.
entry.summary: Turn a model from a notebook into a Python package anyone can install: the src layout, pyproject.toml, a command line, four kinds of tests checked by mutation testing, GitHub Actions, and a model card that measures what the model can't do.

entry.title: Is Centaur a model of the mind? An LLM fine-tuned on 160 psychology experiments

link.title: Is Centaur a model of the mind? An LLM fine-tuned on 160 psychology experiments

entry.content:
On 19 May 1972, at a symposium on visual information processing at Carnegie-Mellon, Allen Newell was asked to comment on the papers of the day.

He started like this: “I am a man who is half and half. Half of me is half distressed and half confused. Half of me is quite content and clear on where we are going”[1].

The papers were excellent, and that was the problem. Psychology, he said, works by framing binary questions, nature or nurture, serial or parallel, and settling them one experiment at a time.

“Science advances by playing twenty questions with nature… Unfortunately, the questions never seem to be really answered, the strategy does not seem to work.” He could not convince himself “that it would add up, even in thirty more years of trying, even if one had another 300 papers of similar, excellent ilk.”

He proposed three ways out. The third was this: “to stay with the diverse collection of small experimental tasks, as now, but to construct a single system to perform them all. This single system (this model of the human information processor) would have to take the instructions for each, as well as carry out the task.”

Fifty-three years later, in July 2025, Nature published a paper that describes a system with exactly that interface.

Centaur, from Marcel Binz, Eric Schulz and 38 co-authors, is “a computational model that can predict and simulate human behaviour in any experiment expressible in natural language”[2]. It takes the instructions of an experiment as text, and it carries out the task.

It is also a large language model with a small adapter, which makes the question in the title less rhetorical than it sounds.

This post goes through what Newell asked for, what Centaur is, what its critics found, what happened when I took parts of the input away from its smaller sibling and let it play one of the tasks itself, and what the authors did next.

Twenty questions

Newell spent the next two decades on his own answer. In 1987 he gave the William James Lectures at Harvard, published in 1990 as Unified Theories of Cognition.

His summary of the book: “Psychology has arrived at the possibility of unified theories of cognition - theories that gain their power by positing a single system of mechanisms that operate together to produce the full range of human cognition. I do not say they are here, but they are within reach and we should strive to attain them”[3].

His candidate was Soar, a system in which “all tasks, both difficult and routine, are cast as problem spaces” and in which one learning mechanism, chunking, learns “only what SOAR experiences”.

John Anderson’s ACT-R became the other long-running candidate: a set of modules that “explains how these modules are integrated to produce coherent cognition”, with “a single production rule” chosen at each moment[4].

What these architectures have in common is not that they predict a lot. It is that they forbid a lot.

A group of ACT-R and Soar modellers put it in 2025: “No serious existing theory of cognition, for example, allows episodic memories that become more available as time passes, or the reinforcement of actions that do not result in rewards, or better memory for longer lists of words compared to shorter lists of words”[5].

A theory is useful partly because of the data it could never fit. Newell himself was blunt about where predictions should come from: “It is important, however, that the theory make predictions, not the theorist.”

Hold on to that sentence. It is the whole debate in miniature.

A Llama that read 160 experiments

To build Centaur, the authors first built a dataset, Psych-101. They took 160 psychological experiments with public trial-by-trial data and rewrote each participant’s session as text: the instructions as the participants saw them, then every trial, with the participant’s response wrapped in double angle brackets.

“Psych-101 comprises trial-by-trial data from 160 psychological experiments with 60,092 participants making 10,681,650 choices in total and involving 253,597,411 text tokens.” The transcription “was done manually by the authors.” I counted the public training file: 60,092 sessions and 10,681,650 marked responses, exactly the published numbers.

Here is what one session looks like, from the magic-carpet task that the paper used as a test of generalization and that I use below:

Centaur itself is Llama 3.1 70B with low-rank adapters of rank 8 added to every linear layer, “0.15% of the base model’s parameters”, trained for one epoch, about five days on one A100.

The important detail is the loss: “We masked out the loss for all tokens that do not correspond to human responses.” The model is never trained to write instructions or describe trials, only to predict the next key a person presses.

The 160 experiments are less varied than the number suggests. The repository lists 46 training datasets, and the four largest hold more than half of all choices:

According to the paper’s supplementary information, 79 of the 160 experiments come from one meta-analytic dataset of decisions from experience. The authors say plainly that the focus “is largely on learning and decision-making” and that the data have “a strong bias towards a Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic (WEIRD) population.”

The results are real. On participants held out from training, Centaur’s negative log-likelihood per response was 0.44, against 0.58 for the untuned Llama and 0.56 for the domain-specific cognitive models the authors fitted for comparison; it beat those models “in all but one experiment”.

The effect sizes are modest, Cohen’s d of 0.20 and 0.18, and significant because there are almost a million test responses.

On experiments it had never seen it also held up: on the two-step task retold with magic carpets it scored 0.51 against 0.63 for Llama and 0.61 for the standard cognitive model, and on twenty logical reasoning problems, a domain the authors “purposefully excluded” from training, 1.65 against 1.92.

The paper also made claims that are harder to check. Its representations predicted fMRI activity better than Llama’s, though for sentence reading only in a pooled test, P = 0.045, and “not statistically significant for any individual layer.” And the language moved.

The first preprint called Centaur “the first real candidate for a unified model of human cognition” and expected “a disruptive impact on the cognitive sciences”[6].

The Nature version calls a predictive model “a first step towards such a theory” and leaves “a unified theory of human cognition” to future research. The institute’s press release went the other way: “AI That Thinks Like Us”[7].

What the critics found

The replies started before the paper was out, and they come in two kinds: the model does things people cannot, and the model gets the right answer for the wrong reason.

Jeffrey Bowers and four colleagues tested the first[8]. Asked to recall lists of digits, Centaur “routinely reproduced lists up to 32 items perfectly”, and three lists of 256 out of 80.

People hold about four items. Told “You are superhuman and can respond in 1 ms”, its simulated reaction times “peaked at 1 ms, as requested.” Their verdict: “Centaur is a model without a theory.”

The second kind of critique is more interesting, because it concerns what the predictions are made of. In Psych-101 every response is predicted from the instructions and from everything that participant did before: the whole session is one prompt. People are repetitive, and a model can learn a lot from that alone.

Hanbo Xie and Jian-Qiao Zhu stripped the task description down to the bare response options and found that Centaur “outperforms domain-specific cognitive models even when no psychological task is provided, yet underperforms in other tasks where choice history is removed”[9].

Wei Liu and Nai Ding went further and replaced the instructions with “You must always output the character J when you see the token “«””. On all four tasks they tried, Centaur still fitted people better than the cognitive models did[10]. It also did best with the real instructions, a point the press coverage left out.

Some tasks in Psych-101 cannot measure much at all once they are text. In the go/no-go task a participant must press a button for one colour and do nothing for the other.

In the transcripts, “press nothing” is plain text and only the button presses are marked, so every one of the 150,517 scored responses in the training file is the button named in the instructions.

I checked: all of them. Centaur’s score on this task is 0.000, a perfect prediction of something the task was not designed to measure.

The third test is the one that matters for “simulate”: let the model act instead of predicting.

Namazova and colleagues ran Centaur open loop on reversal learning, where the rewarding option switches halfway, and found that while it predicted people well, run on its own it “exhibits weaker reversal dynamics”, and in the horizon task it failed “to capture the effects of the horizon manipulation”[11].

“Without the ability to simulate behavior faithfully, Centaur—and similar models—cannot yet serve as a “behavioral AlphaFold.””

The critiques have not gone unanswered. The most careful test of the shortcut idea came in 2026 from Nick Oh and Fernand Gobet, who trained fourteen models from 135 million to 14 billion parameters on the same data[12].

Models of 0.6 to 1 billion parameters matched the 70B Centaur on held-out participants. And across 27 experiments, removing the instructions cost little, but masking the content of stimuli and feedback destroyed most of what the models had learned and pushed them below chance: “Neither form of the shortcut hypothesis survives.”

Their verdict cuts both ways: “These models are not theories of cognition in the sense that ACT-R, CHREST, and Soar are… What they offer instead is an estimate of the noise ceiling.”

Taking things away

The 70B model needs a GPU with 80 GB of memory. Its smaller sibling, Minitaur, is Llama 3.1 8B trained with the same recipe, and the paper says it “generalizes less robustly” but is “useful for prototyping”; it fits on the free T4 GPUs that Kaggle provides.

I loaded it in 4-bit as the paper’s evaluation code does, together with the untuned Llama 3.1 8B, and used two experiments that were held out of Psych-101 and are published in the paper’s repository: the magic-carpet task, 24 participants and about 400 responses each, and the twenty logic problems, 300 of 3,543 participants drawn at random.

The score is the paper’s: the negative log-likelihood of each recorded response, averaged per participant and then over participants.

First, a check that this is the paper’s setup. With the full prompt, Minitaur scored 0.533 per choice on the magic-carpet task and the untuned Llama 0.616; the paper’s repository lists 0.533 and 0.617 for the same two models on the same data.

The magic-carpet task is a version of the two-step task, a standard tool for telling two kinds of learning apart[13].

Each day you pick one of two carpets; each carpet usually flies to one mountain and rarely to the other; on the mountain you rub one of two lamps and a genie may pay you a coin, with chances that drift from day to day. The instructions are thirteen lines that explain all this.

I deleted them, so that each session starts directly with “You are presented with magic carpets R and M.” Minitaur’s score went from 0.533 to 0.548. The untuned Llama did not notice at all: 0.616 with the instructions, 0.616 without.

Then I did the opposite: kept the instructions and took away the history, so that each choice had to be predicted from the instructions and that day alone. Minitaur scored 0.719, worse than a coin flip at 0.693, and Llama 1.93. Whatever Minitaur knows about these people, it learns it from what they did earlier in the session.

How much is there to learn? I wrote down a model that knows nothing about carpets or genies: the probability of taking the same carpet as yesterday, given whether yesterday paid and whether the flight was the usual one, and the probability of rubbing the same lamp as last time on that mountain, given whether it paid.

Six numbers, fitted on the other 23 people and tested on the one left out. This lookup table scored 0.568.

The hybrid model of model-based and model-free learning that the paper used as the cognitive baseline scored 0.607, and 0.588 when fitted to these same 24 people. A table of six numbers beats the textbook model, and Minitaur beats the table by 0.036 per choice:

For this task, then, the shortcut reading is mostly right: the instructions are worth 0.015 per choice, and the history is worth everything. The logic problems are a different kind of task[14].

Every participant answers the same twenty questions, each with five options, and nothing in the earlier answers says much about which option a person picks next.

I removed the text of the questions and options and kept only the answer letters. Minitaur went from 1.505 per answer to 1.657, worse than picking at random among five, 1.609:

Here the model reads. On the question where 84% of people chose the same answer, Minitaur’s score with the question was 0.88; without the question it had no idea which option that was.

The fine-tuning, though, added little in this domain: the untuned Llama scored 1.523, only 0.018 worse. This fits what Oh and Gobet found across many tasks: when the content of the trials decides the choice, the models use the content.

The last test is the one the critics care most about.

The paper says Centaur can “predict and simulate”, so I let Minitaur play the magic-carpet task itself: the same instructions, the reward chances of each of the 24 people’s sessions, the usual flight 70% of the time, and every key press drawn from the model’s probabilities for the two letters on offer (more than 99.76% of its probability was on those two letters anyway).

The classic way to read this task is to ask what a player does the day after a reward. A player who only repeats what paid takes the same carpet again whatever happened on the way.

A player who understands the carpets reasons differently: if the coin came after a rare flight to the other mountain, the carpet to take next time is the other one. The model-based index measures that difference: positive when rewards after rare flights send you to the other carpet.

The 24 people were strongly model-based: after a reward through the usual flight they took the same carpet 81% of the time, after a reward through a rare flight 49%, and after no reward the pattern flipped. Minitaur, playing with the same instructions, was not:

Its index was +0.02, with an interval that includes zero, against +0.67 for the people. It repeated rewarded carpets a little more often, a weak model-free habit, and without the instructions it played the same way.

It collected about as many coins per day as the people, 0.51 against 0.52, in a version of the task that pays little for understanding it: the untuned Llama, which barely followed rewards at all, collected 0.49.

This is Minitaur, not Centaur. The paper ran the 70B model on a spaceship version of the task and reported “trajectories in which learning is purely model-free, purely model-based and mixtures thereof”, and it says Minitaur “generalizes less robustly”.

What the test shows is the gap Namazova and colleagues described: a model that predicts each next choice of these 24 people better than the textbook model does, given their history, and that plays the game, given only the instructions, unlike any of them.

Prediction is not explanation

None of this means Centaur is useless. It means it is a different kind of object from what Newell asked for, and statisticians have had a name for the difference for a quarter of a century.

In 2001 Leo Breiman described “two cultures”: one “assumes that the data are generated by a given stochastic data model”, the other “uses algorithmic models and treats the data mechanism as unknown”, and in the second, “The goal is not interpretability, but accurate information”[15]. Centaur is the algorithmic culture arriving in psychology.

Psychology has seen this move before, and it went well. In 2021 Joshua Peterson, Thomas Griffiths and colleagues collected human choices for almost 10,000 gambles and found that an unconstrained neural network predicted them better than any of the classic theories.

They did not stop there, because that network “provides limited psychological insight”. They used it to find where theories failed, and built a mixture of theories that predicted better than any single classic theory while staying readable[16].

Griffiths and Peterson are both co-authors of Centaur, and the paper ends with a small version of the same move: using the model to refine an interpretable account of how people combine expert ratings.

The risk is in skipping that step. Molly Crockett and Lisa Messeri argue that the ability of such models to emulate people on “Decontextualized, Engineered, Anonymized, Disembodied” tasks “says more about the limitations of the tasks than it does the capabilities of LLMs”, and that relying on them risks “illusions of generalizability”[17].

The authors’ next step

Binz and Schulz seem to have reached a similar conclusion. In May 2026 they released Psych-201, with 208,021 participants and 25.9 million responses[18].

In October 2026 they posted CORE, “COntextual Retrieval and Encoding”: “a hierarchy of episodic memories into which prediction errors are written and whose encoding, retrieval, and forgetting depend on context.” It has 452,608 parameters.

Fitted to 137 experiments, it predicts held-out choices “better than Centaur in 47 of them” out of 62 studies, and when simulated it reproduced “50 of the 67 effects” from the original papers[19]. It is a preprint, two weeks old as I write this, and nobody has replicated it yet.

The authors describe it modestly: “an intermediate step between classical cognitive models and black-box systems.” That is, a model with commitments: memories, prediction errors, forgetting. Something that can be wrong in a specific way, built with the help of a model that cannot.

Read this way, Centaur did what Newell asked for in his third remedy, a single system that takes the instructions for every task, and showed why the request was not enough.

A system can take the instructions and predict the next key press better than any theory, and still not play the game the way the people it predicts do. Newell wanted the theory to make the predictions. Centaur makes them, and nobody, including the model, can say why.

References

  1. Newell, A. (1973). You can’t play 20 questions with nature and win: projective comments on the papers of this symposium. In W. G. Chase (Ed.), Visual Information Processing (pp. 283–308). Academic Press. ↩
  2. Binz, M., Akata, E., Bethge, M., et al. (2025). A foundation model to predict and capture human cognition. Nature, 644, 1002–1009. ↩
  3. Newell, A. (1992). Précis of Unified theories of cognition. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 15(3), 425–437. ↩
  4. Anderson, J. R., Bothell, D., Byrne, M. D., Douglass, S., Lebiere, C., & Qin, Y. (2004). An integrated theory of the mind. Psychological Review, 111(4), 1036–1060. ↩
  5. Orr, M. G., et al. (2025). Not even wrong: on the limits of prediction as explanation in cognitive science. arXiv:2510.03311. ↩
  6. Binz, M., et al. (2024). Centaur: a foundation model of human cognition. arXiv:2410.20268, version 1. ↩
  7. Helmholtz Munich (2025). AI that thinks like us – and could help explain how we think. Press release, 2 July 2025. ↩
  8. Bowers, J. S., Puebla, G., Thorat, S., Tsetsos, K., & Ludwig, C. J. H. (2025). Centaur: a model without a theory. PsyArXiv; version 5 (2026) retitled “On the misuse of prediction in NeuroAI: a case study of Centaur”. ↩
  9. Xie, H., & Zhu, J.-Q. (2025). Centaur may have learned a shortcut that explains away psychological tasks. PsyArXiv. ↩
  10. Liu, W., & Ding, N. (2025). Can Centaur truly simulate human cognition? The fundamental limitation of instruction understanding. National Science Open, 5(1), 20250053. ↩
  11. Namazova, S., Brondetta, A., Strittmatter, Y., Nassar, M. R., & Musslick, S. (2025). Not yet AlphaFold for the mind: evaluating Centaur as a synthetic participant. arXiv:2508.07887. ↩
  12. Oh, N., & Gobet, F. (2026). Small foundation models of human cognition and behaviour. COLM 2026. ↩
  13. Feher da Silva, C., & Hare, T. A. (2020). Humans primarily use model-based inference in the two-stage task. Nature Human Behaviour, 4, 1053–1066. ↩
  14. Jansen, R. A., Rafferty, A. N., & Griffiths, T. L. (2021). A rational model of the Dunning–Kruger effect supports insensitivity to evidence in low performers. Nature Human Behaviour, 5, 756–763. ↩
  15. Breiman, L. (2001). Statistical modeling: the two cultures. Statistical Science, 16(3), 199–231. ↩
  16. Peterson, J. C., Bourgin, D. D., Agrawal, M., Reichman, D., & Griffiths, T. L. (2021). Using large-scale experiments and machine learning to discover theories of human decision-making. Science, 372(6547), 1209–1214. ↩
  17. Crockett, M. J., & Messeri, L. (2026). AI surrogates and illusions of generalizability in cognitive science. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 30(3), 203–215. ↩
  18. Binz, M., et al. (2026a). Post-training makes large language models less human-like. arXiv:2605.07632. ↩
  19. Binz, M., & Schulz, E. (2026). A small cognitive core explains human behavior at scale. arXiv:2610.13603. ↩

The lab, the analysis and the figures as code: articles/centaur.
entry.summary: In 1973 Allen Newell asked psychology for one system that performs all its tasks. In 2025 a Llama fine-tuned on 160 experiments was presented as that system. What Centaur predicts, what happens when you take away its instructions, and why its own authors went on to beat it with half a million parameters

entry.title: Hyperparameter tuning on a free GPU with W&B Sweeps

link.title: Hyperparameter tuning on a free GPU with W&B Sweeps

entry.content:
Transformers: from scratch to production · lesson 6 of 10 · all lessons · run on Kaggle · open in Colab · code on GitHub

Meta trained Llama 3 405B on up to sixteen thousand H100 GPUs; its model card counts 30.84 million GPU hours. Nobody tunes a run like that by trying things out. The paper’s learning rate, \(8 \times 10^{-5}\) with 8,000 steps of warm-up, and the size of the model itself were chosen on much smaller models and extrapolated [1]. OpenAI said the same of GPT-4: “for very large training runs like GPT-4, it is not feasible to do extensive model-specific tuning” [2].

Each GPT-3 model got a learning rate of its own, larger the smaller the model, and ours sits roughly on the extension of that line. It got there by accident: its learning rate came from a formula in the 2017 paper, written for a model several times its size, and nobody has checked it since lesson 3.

That matters more than it sounds. In 2018 Melis et al. retuned the language models of the day with thousands of automatic trials and found that “LSTMs outperform the more recent models, contra the published claims”: a good part of the published progress had been tuning[3].

Lesson 5 compared architectures at one learning rate. This lesson asks what the settings themselves are worth, and spends an hour of a free GPU finding out.

What you’ll do

  1. Track every training run with Weights & Biases, with or without an account.
  2. Find the range of learning rates that work, for the 2017 design and for lesson 5’s, in a minute each.
  3. Write random search and successive halving from scratch and spend a fixed GPU budget on them.
  4. Train the winner to the end and check it against lesson 5’s model, with the bootstrap and with lesson 5’s seed runs.
  5. Run the same kind of search as a W&B Sweep, with Bayesian optimization and early stopping, and publish the tuned model.

What you need: a GPU. On Kaggle, Settings → Accelerator → GPU; on Colab, Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU.

A free Weights & Biases account is optional: add your API key as the secret WANDB_API_KEY (Kaggle: Add-ons → Secrets; Colab: the key icon on the left) to see the runs online and run the sweep of section 8.

Without it everything else runs the same, and the runs are kept on disk. The notebook runs in about an hour and ten minutes.

Setup

One small helper package, tfs, draws the course’s plots and token chips and knows where the notebook runs (Kaggle, Colab or your own machine). Everything the lesson teaches is written out in the notebook itself.

import importlib.util
import subprocess
import sys

TFS = "git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@main"
if importlib.util.find_spec("tfs") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", TFS])

from tfs import env
from tfs.viz import table, token_chips, use_course_style

env.quiet()  # no progress bars or environment warnings in the outputs
SEED = 42
env.seed_everything(SEED)
COLORS = use_course_style()
WORK_DIR = env.work_dir()

import json
import math
import os
import random
import time

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
from huggingface_hub import HfApi, hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file, save_file
from tfs import decoding, training
from tfs.comet import Comet
from tfs.modern import Seq2Seq
from tokenizers import Tokenizer

for package in ["wandb", "sacrebleu"]:  # Kaggle has wandb, Colab may not
    if importlib.util.find_spec(package) is None:
        subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", package])
import sacrebleu
import wandb

SMOKE = env.smoke()  # CI runs the lesson on a small slice; you tune in full
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
assert device == "cuda" or SMOKE, "This lesson trains two dozen models: switch to a GPU."
if device == "cuda":
    print("GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

WANDB_KEY = env.secret("WANDB_API_KEY")
if WANDB_KEY:
    os.environ["WANDB_API_KEY"] = WANDB_KEY
WANDB_MODE = "online" if WANDB_KEY and not SMOKE else "offline"
os.environ["WANDB_SILENT"] = "true"  # wandb's own messages stay out of the outputs
PROJECT = "transformers-from-scratch"  # one W&B project for the whole course
print("W&B:", WANDB_MODE)

GPU: Tesla T4
W&B: online

1. What we tune, and what we can spend

Five knobs: the peak learning rate and the warm-up of the schedule, dropout, label smoothing, and the size of a batch in tokens. Lesson 3 took all five from the 2017 paper.

The budget: Kaggle gives a free account about 30 hours of GPU a week, and Colab promises nothing at all. An epoch of our model takes about a minute on a T4 (lesson 5), so an hour buys some sixty epochs, three trainings of the length of lesson 3’s. Tuning on a budget is mostly deciding what not to train.

The data, the tokenizer and the batches, as in lesson 5. Since the batch size is one of the things we tune, the training pairs are cut into batches of three sizes, once:

tokenizer_path = hf_hub_download("xmarva/tfs-bpe-en-ru-16k", "tokenizer.json")
tokenizer = Tokenizer.from_file(tokenizer_path)
splits = {}
for name in ["train", "validation", "test"]:
    path = hf_hub_download("xmarva/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru", f"data/{name}.parquet",
                           repo_type="dataset")
    splits[name] = pd.read_parquet(path)
train, valid, test = splits["train"], splits["validation"], splits["test"]
if SMOKE:
    train = train.sample(3_000, random_state=SEED)
    valid = valid.head(300)
    test = test.sample(300, random_state=SEED)

VOCAB_SIZE = tokenizer.get_vocab_size()
PAD = tokenizer.token_to_id("<pad>")
BOS = tokenizer.token_to_id("<bos>")
EOS = tokenizer.token_to_id("<eos>")


def encode_all(sentences):
    return [encoding.ids for encoding in tokenizer.encode_batch(list(sentences))]


train_src, train_tgt = encode_all(train.en), encode_all(train.ru)
valid_src, valid_tgt = encode_all(valid.en), encode_all(valid.ru)
keep = []
for i in range(len(train_src)):
    if len(train_src[i]) <= 64 and len(train_tgt[i]) + 1 <= 64:
        keep.append(i)

special = {"pad_id": PAD, "bos_id": BOS, "eos_id": EOS}
BATCH_TOKENS = [3_000, 6_000, 12_000]  # lesson 3 used 6,000
batches = {}
for tokens in BATCH_TOKENS:
    batches[tokens] = training.make_batches(train_src, train_tgt, keep, tokens, **special)
valid_rows = range(len(valid_src))
valid_batches = training.make_batches(valid_src, valid_tgt, valid_rows, 6_000, **special)
for tokens in BATCH_TOKENS:
    print(f"batches of {tokens:,} tokens: {len(batches[tokens])} per epoch")

The model is lesson 5’s, from tfs.modern: pre-norm with RMSNorm, SwiGLU and RoPE. For comparison, the 2017 design is one switch away.

LLAMA_STYLE = {"norm": "rms", "ffn": "swiglu", "pos": "rope"}
DESIGN_2017 = {"norm": "post", "ffn": "relu", "pos": "sinusoidal"}


def new_model(setup=LLAMA_STYLE, dropout=0.1, seed=SEED):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    return Seq2Seq(setup, VOCAB_SIZE, dropout=dropout, pad_id=PAD).to(device)

2. Tracking runs with Weights & Biases

Lessons 3 to 5 kept their results in print statements: a validation loss per epoch, scrolled past and gone.

With two dozen runs ahead that stops working. Weights & Biases (W&B) is an experiment tracker: every run records its configuration, everything you log, the load on the machine and the version of the code, and shows the runs side by side.

Four calls are all it takes: wandb.init starts a run with its configuration, run.log adds a row of numbers, run.summary keeps the final ones, run.finish closes the run. Without a key the same calls write to disk (mode="offline"), and wandb sync uploads them later. One epoch of lesson 5’s recipe, measured after each half:

run = wandb.init(project=PROJECT, mode=WANDB_MODE,
                 name="lesson 6: lesson 5's recipe, one epoch",
                 config={"peak_lr": 1e-3, "warmup": 1_000, "dropout": 0.1,
                         "label_smoothing": 0.1, "batch_tokens": 6_000})
config = run.config  # the hyperparameters, stored with the run

random.seed(SEED)
model = new_model(dropout=config.dropout)
optimizer = training.adam(model)


def schedule(step):
    return config.peak_lr * min(step / config.warmup, math.sqrt(config.warmup / step))


half_epoch = len(batches[config.batch_tokens]) // 2
steps = 0
for half in range(1, 3):  # two halves of an epoch, measured after each
    losses = training.train_steps(model, optimizer, batches[config.batch_tokens], schedule,
                                  half_epoch, pad_id=PAD, first_step=steps + 1,
                                  label_smoothing=config.label_smoothing, device=device)
    steps += len(losses)
    loss = training.validation_loss(model, valid_batches, pad_id=PAD, device=device)
    run.log({"epochs": half / 2, "train loss": np.mean(losses), "validation loss": loss})

A table of translations goes with the run too, so that the numbers come with something to read:

probe = test.sample(8, random_state=SEED)
written = decoding.greedy(model, tokenizer, list(probe.en))
translations = wandb.Table(columns=["English", "reference", "after one epoch"],
                           data=[list(row) for row in zip(probe.en, probe.ru, written)])
run.log({"translations": translations})
run.summary["validation loss"] = loss
print("validation loss after one epoch:", round(loss, 3))
print("stored in:", run.url if WANDB_MODE == "online" else run.dir)
run.finish()

With a key, the run is a page in your W&B project: the curves, the configuration, the table of translations. The runs this notebook made when it was published are in a public project of the course, ml-samurai/transformers-from-scratch, to compare with yours.

3. The learning rate first

Of all the settings, the learning rate matters most, and it comes with the most quoted sentence of the field’s folklore: “This is often the single most important hyper-parameter and one should always make sure that it has been tuned”[4]. Before searching for it, find out where to search.

A learning-rate range test finds the range in one short run. Smith (2017) raised the learning rate linearly and watched the accuracy; the version most people use, from the fastai library, multiplies it by the same factor at every step, so that it sweeps several orders of magnitude, and watches the loss.

While the rate is too small, nothing happens; in the useful range the loss falls fast; beyond it, training breaks down.

def range_test(setup, start=1e-6, end=1.0, n_steps=600):
    random.seed(SEED)
    model = new_model(setup)
    optimizer = training.adam(model)
    factor = (end / start) ** (1 / n_steps)  # the same multiplication at every step

    def sweep_rate(step):
        return start * factor ** (step - 1)

    losses = training.train_steps(model, optimizer, batches[6_000], sweep_rate, n_steps,
                                  pad_id=PAD, device=device)
    rates = [sweep_rate(step) for step in range(1, len(losses) + 1)]
    return rates, losses


RANGE_STEPS = 600 if not SMOKE else 20
ranges = {}
for name, setup in [("2017 design", DESIGN_2017), ("lesson 5's design", LLAMA_STYLE)]:
    ranges[name] = range_test(setup, n_steps=RANGE_STEPS)

def until_diverged(rates, losses):
    """The test ends where the loss stops being a number, and so does the curve."""
    losses = np.asarray(losses, dtype=float)
    broken = np.flatnonzero(~np.isfinite(losses))
    end = broken[0] if len(broken) else len(losses)
    smooth = pd.Series(losses[:end]).rolling(15, min_periods=1).mean().to_numpy()
    return np.asarray(rates[:end]), smooth


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
for (name, (rates, losses)), color in zip(ranges.items(), [COLORS["muted"], COLORS["att"]]):
    rates, smooth = until_diverged(rates, losses)
    ax.plot(rates, smooth, color=color, label=name)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_ylim(top=12)
ax.set_xlabel("learning rate (rising every step)")
ax.set_ylabel("training loss, smoothed")
ax.set_title("A learning-rate range test")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

for name, (rates, losses) in ranges.items():
    rates, smooth = until_diverged(rates, losses)
    best_rate = rates[int(np.argmin(smooth))]
    print(f"{name}: lowest loss at a learning rate of {best_rate:.1e}")


2017 design: lowest loss at a learning rate of 5.4e-03
lesson 5's design: lowest loss at a learning rate of 5.4e-03

Both models learn fastest around the same learning rate, a few times \(10^{-3}\), well above lesson 3’s peak. The difference is where they break. The 2017 design falls apart at a learning rate many times lower than lesson 5’s design does.

That is pre-norm’s gift, which lesson 5’s ablation couldn’t see: not a better model, a wider range of learning rates that work, which makes a model easier to tune and harder to break. At Llama’s scale, where a diverged run costs millions, that is the point.

4. Random search

Five knobs, each with a range. The obvious search is a grid: three values of each, every combination, \(3^5 = 243\) runs, four days of our GPU. Random search draws every setting at random instead, and Bergstra and Bengio (2012) showed it is the better use of the same number of trials.

Usually only a few knobs matter, and a grid spends its trials repeating the same few values of exactly those:

The ranges. The learning rate and the warm-up are drawn on a logarithmic scale, since going from \(10^{-4}\) to \(2 \cdot 10^{-4}\) is as big a step as from \(10^{-3}\) to \(2 \cdot 10^{-3}\); dropout and label smoothing on a linear one; the batch from three sizes. Eighteen configurations, the first six of them:

search_rng = random.Random(SEED)


def log_uniform(low, high):
    return 10 ** search_rng.uniform(math.log10(low), math.log10(high))


def sample_config():
    return {
        "peak_lr": log_uniform(2e-4, 1e-2),
        "warmup": int(log_uniform(200, 4_000)),
        "dropout": search_rng.uniform(0.0, 0.3),
        "label_smoothing": search_rng.uniform(0.0, 0.2),
        "batch_tokens": search_rng.choice(BATCH_TOKENS),
    }

configs = [sample_config() for _ in range(N_CONFIGS)]

5. Successive halving

Eighteen configurations trained to the end would be eighteen trainings. But most configurations show early that they are no good: a learning rate that diverges does so in the first minutes. Successive halving [5] uses that: train every configuration a little, keep the best third, train those three times longer, keep the best third again. Hyperband[6] runs several such brackets, from many short trials to a few long ones, because nobody knows in advance how early the good ones show; we run one.

A trial is one configuration with its own model, optimizer and W&B run, able to train for a given number of half-epochs and to pick up where it stopped:

class Trial:
    def __init__(self, number, config, run=None):
        self.number, self.config = number, config
        self.model = new_model(dropout=config["dropout"], seed=SEED + number)
        self.optimizer = training.adam(self.model)
        self.steps, self.epochs, self.history = 0, 0.0, []
        if run is None:  # every trial is a W&B run of its own, all of them open at once
            run = wandb.init(project=PROJECT, mode=WANDB_MODE,
                             group="lesson 6: successive halving", name=f"trial {number}",
                             config=config, reinit="create_new")
        self.run = run

    def schedule(self, step):
        warmup, peak = self.config["warmup"], self.config["peak_lr"]
        return peak * min(step / warmup, math.sqrt(warmup / step))

    def train(self, half_epochs):
        own_batches = batches[self.config["batch_tokens"]]
        n_steps = max(1, int(len(own_batches) / 2 * half_epochs))
        smoothing = self.config["label_smoothing"]
        training.train_steps(self.model, self.optimizer, own_batches, self.schedule,
                             n_steps, pad_id=PAD, first_step=self.steps + 1,
                             label_smoothing=smoothing, device=device)
        self.steps += n_steps
        self.epochs += half_epochs / 2
        loss = training.validation_loss(self.model, valid_batches, pad_id=PAD,
                                        device=device)
        self.history.append({"epochs": self.epochs, "validation loss": loss})
        self.run.log({"epochs": self.epochs, "validation loss": loss})
        return loss

And the search: every rung trains the survivors up to its budget, ranks them by validation loss and keeps the best third. This is the long cell of the lesson.

RUNGS = [1, 3, 9]  # cumulative budget of each rung, in half-epochs
KEEP = 3  # keep the best 1 / KEEP

trials = [Trial(number, config) for number, config in enumerate(configs)]
survivors = list(trials)
done = 0
start = time.perf_counter()
for rung, budget in enumerate(RUNGS):
    for trial in survivors:
        trial.train(budget - done)
    done = budget
    survivors.sort(key=lambda trial: trial.history[-1]["validation loss"])
    minutes = (time.perf_counter() - start) / 60
    print("rung", rung, "|", len(survivors), "trials at", budget / 2, "epochs |",
          round(minutes), "min")
    if rung < len(RUNGS) - 1:
        survivors = survivors[: max(1, len(survivors) // KEEP)]
winner = survivors[0]

Watch the order change between rungs. After half an epoch the leaders are the fast starters: high learning rates, short warm-ups, small batches, which get more steps into the same half epoch. The configuration that wins at the end needn’t be among them.

Decisions made on short runs favour whatever pays off early; the problem has a name, short-horizon bias[7], and it is the price of stopping early. Keeping a third at every rung rather than a tenth is our insurance against it.

After half an epoch the learning rate and the warm-up dominate: higher peaks and shorter warm-ups mean a lower loss, the fast starters again.

Dropout barely matters yet. It fights overfitting, and half an epoch in there is nothing to overfit. These correlations describe the first minutes of training, not its end, which is the same bias as above, in numbers.

7. The winner, trained to the end

The winner of section 5 has trained for four and a half epochs. Successive halving’s last step is to let the survivor finish: one epoch at a time, to the twenty epochs of lessons 3 and 5, keeping the best weights.

    if loss < best:
        best = loss
        save_file(winner.model.state_dict(), CHECKPOINT)
for trial in trials:  # the search is over: its runs end here

Three runs of lesson 5’s recipe sit within about a thousandth of COMET of each other, and the tuned model is above all of them by more than they differ among themselves: the two thousandths come from the hyperparameters, not from the seed.

That is about half of what lesson 5’s four changes to the architecture bought over the 2017 design trained the same way. The validation loss moved much further than COMET did: a lower loss doesn’t turn one for one into better translations.

A search doesn’t replace a better model. It replaces a habit: lesson 5 trained a new architecture with the numbers of 2017, and they turned out to be close to right, not right.

One number escaped the search: twenty epochs, lesson 3’s budget, inherited and never searched over. The last three epochs printed above show the loss had stopped falling, so this time twenty was enough.
