Every layer keeps the shape it receives: one vector of 256 numbers per token. The encoder never sees the Russian side, and the decoder sees the English side only through the memory. Only the last step leaves the width of the model, and there every Russian position gets one score for each of the sixteen thousand tokens.

Where do the parameters live? Group them by the part of the model they belong to:

parts = collections.Counter()
for name, parameter in model.named_parameters():
    if name.startswith("embedding"):
        part = "embedding E, shared"
    elif "norm" in name:
        part = "layer norms"
    else:
        stack = name.split(".")[0]  # "encoder" or "decoder"
        sub_layer = name.split(".")[2]  # self_attention, cross_attention or feed_forward
        part = stack + ": " + sub_layer.replace("_", "-")
    parts[part] += parameter.numel()

colors = []  # the course's concept colors: amber embedding, teal encoder, rose decoder
for part in parts:
    if part.startswith("embedding"):
        colors.append(COLORS["data"])
    elif part.startswith("encoder"):
        colors.append(COLORS["enc"])
    elif part.startswith("decoder"):
        colors.append(COLORS["dec"])
    else:
        colors.append(COLORS["muted"])

bars(dict(parts), colors=colors, title="Where the parameters live")
plt.show()

The shared embedding is the largest single part, which is why lesson 1 weighed every extra token against its row. Every count follows from the shapes, so the total is a formula, with \(d = d_{\text{model}}\):

\[\underbrace{\lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert\, d}_{\text{embedding}} + N\big(\underbrace{4(d^2 + d)}_{\text{attention}} + \underbrace{2 d d_{\text{ff}} + d_{\text{ff}} + d}_{\text{ feed-forward}} + \underbrace{2 \cdot 2d}_{\text{norms}}\big) + N\big(2 \cdot 4(d^2 + d) + 2 d d_{\text{ff}} + d_{\text{ff}} + d + 3 \cdot 2d\big):\]

the embedding, \(N\) encoder layers, and \(N\) decoder layers with their two attentions and three norms. An attention has four \(d \times d\) matrices with biases; a feed-forward network two matrices of \(d \times d_{\text{ff}}\) with biases; a norm has \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\).

def count_parameters(vocab_size, d, d_ff, n_layers):
    attention_params = 4 * (d * d + d)
    feed_forward_params = 2 * d * d_ff + d_ff + d
    encoder_layer = attention_params + feed_forward_params + 2 * 2 * d
    decoder_layer = 2 * attention_params + feed_forward_params + 3 * 2 * d
    return vocab_size * d + n_layers * encoder_layer + n_layers * decoder_layer


by_formula = count_parameters(VOCAB_SIZE, D_MODEL, D_FF, N_LAYERS)
assert by_formula == sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print("the formula matches the model:", by_formula)

the formula matches the model: 9625600

11. A first run, and a parrot

Make a batch of real sentence pairs and run the model. The source is the English ids; the decoder reads <bos> and the Russian ids, and the target is the Russian ids followed by <eos>, “end of sentence”.

def make_batch(pairs):
    src = pad_batch([tokenizer.encode(en).ids for en, _ in pairs])
    tgt_in = pad_batch([[BOS] + tokenizer.encode(ru).ids for _, ru in pairs])
    tgt_out = pad_batch([tokenizer.encode(ru).ids + [EOS] for _, ru in pairs])
    return src.to(device), tgt_in.to(device), tgt_out.to(device)


pairs = list(zip(valid.en[:64], valid.ru[:64]))
src, tgt_in, tgt_out = make_batch(pairs)

model.eval()  # no dropout while we measure
with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(src, tgt_in)
print("source:", tuple(src.shape))
print("decoder input:", tuple(tgt_in.shape))
print("scores:", tuple(logits.shape))

source: (64, 38)
decoder input: (64, 42)
scores: (64, 42, 16000)

The model will be trained to make the correct next token likely. Its loss is the course’s cross-entropy, the average of \(-\log\) of the probability it gives the right token:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{t=1}^{m} \log p_\theta(y_t \mid y_{<t}, \mathbf{x}),\]

where the probabilities come from the scores by softmax. In terms of the scores \(z_j\) at one position, the loss there is \(\log \sum_j e^{z_j} - z_{\text{target}}\).

Before training, we can predict its value. Section 3 set the scores up to be roughly independent, with mean 0 and a variance \(\sigma^2\) of about 1.

The target’s score is then 0 on average, and a sum over sixteen thousand tokens is close to its expected value, \(\lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert\,\mathbb{E}[e^{z}] = \lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert\, e^{\sigma^2/2}\) (the mean of \(e^z\) when \(z\) is normal). So

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{init}} \approx \log\lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}.\]

The \(\log\lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert\) part is the loss of a model that gives every token the same probability, the most honest thing a model can do before it has learned anything. Measure it:

real = tgt_out != PAD  # positions that hold real target tokens
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits[real], tgt_out[real]).item()
sigma2 = logits[real].var().item()

print("measured loss:     ", round(loss, 3))
print("log|V| + sigma²/2: ", round(math.log(VOCAB_SIZE) + sigma2 / 2, 3))

measured loss:      11.603
log|V| + sigma²/2:  10.186

More than a whole unit too high. A gap like this usually means a bug, so look at what the model predicts: its top token at every position, under the token it has just read.

predicted = logits.argmax(dim=-1)
same_as_input = (predicted[real] == tgt_in[real]).float().mean().item()
print(f"top prediction = the token the decoder just read: {same_as_input:.1%} of positions")

n = int(real[0].sum())  # the first sentence of the batch
read = [tokenizer.id_to_token(i) for i in tgt_in[0, :n].tolist()]
guessed = [tokenizer.id_to_token(i) for i in predicted[0, :n].tolist()]
token_chips([read, guessed], labels=["reads", "predicts"])
plt.show()

top prediction = the token the decoder just read: 100.0% of positions

The untrained model is a parrot: at every position it predicts the token it has just read. That’s not a bug, and the explanation joins two sections of this lesson. The residual stream carries the input embedding \(\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}\,\mathbf{e}_t\) up through every layer, so the final vector still points partly along \(\mathbf{e}_t\). And the output layer is the same matrix \(E\), so the score of token \(t\) is the dot product of that vector with \(\mathbf{e}_t\) itself. Here are all sixteen thousand scores at one position:

position = 3  # the fourth position of the first sentence
scores_here = logits[0, position].cpu()
just_read = tgt_in[0, position].item()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.8))
ax.hist(scores_here, bins=80, color=COLORS["muted"])
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.axvline(scores_here[just_read], color=COLORS["data"], linewidth=2)
label_height = ax.get_ylim()[1] / 4
ax.text(scores_here[just_read], label_height, " " + tokenizer.id_to_token(just_read))
ax.set_xlabel("score")
ax.set_ylabel("tokens")
ax.set_title("One score far from all the others: the token just read")
plt.show()

The bulk of the scores sits around 0, as section 3 planned, and one token, the one just read, stands far to the right. Measured over the whole batch:

is_just_read = F.one_hot(tgt_in, VOCAB_SIZE).bool()  # (B, T, |V|): True at the token read
own_scores = logits[is_just_read & real.unsqueeze(-1)]
print("score of the token just read, on average:", round(own_scores.mean().item(), 2))
print("spread of all scores, std:", round(logits[real].std().item(), 2))

score of the token just read, on average: 10.98
spread of all scores, std: 1.01

One score in sixteen thousand, far above all the others, is exactly what pushes \(\log\sum_j e^{z_j}\) up.

Take it out at every position, as if that token weren’t in the vocabulary, and check the two parts of the loss separately: the log of the sum, which the formula now predicts as \(\log(\lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert - 1) + \sigma^2/2\), and the score of the right token, which it assumes to be 0 on average.

# drop the score of the token just read; skip the rare positions whose answer is that token
without_own = logits.masked_fill(is_just_read, float("-inf"))
keep = real & (tgt_in != tgt_out)

others = without_own[keep]  # (positions, |V|)
log_sum = torch.logsumexp(others, dim=-1).mean().item()
rows_index = torch.arange(len(others))
right_score = others[rows_index, tgt_out[keep]].mean().item()  # each row's right token
sigma2_others = others[torch.isfinite(others)].var().item()
expected = math.log(VOCAB_SIZE - 1) + sigma2_others / 2

print("log of the sum, measured:   ", round(log_sum, 4))
print("log(|V| - 1) + sigma²/2:    ", round(expected, 4))
print("score of the right token:   ", round(right_score, 3))
assert abs(log_sum - expected) < 0.02

log of the sum, measured:    10.1796
log(|V| - 1) + sigma²/2:     10.1818
score of the right token:    -0.204

Now the formula holds to the second decimal. The score of the right token is near 0 but not exactly: a different random initialization moves it a little above or below, and the loss with it.

The parrot is the big effect, and the first steps of training break the habit, because it is wrong almost everywhere: a translation rarely repeats a token twice in a row.

12. Can it learn?

Before spending an hour of GPU time on training (lesson 3), make sure the model can learn at all. The cheapest test is to teach it a handful of sentence pairs by heart: a model that can’t memorize sixteen pairs has a bug somewhere. Karpathy (2019) calls this step “overfit one batch”.

One detail: lesson 1 kept groups of linked pairs together, so the validation set holds several translations of some English sentences. Nobody can memorize two answers to one question, so we take one pair per English sentence, plus our own sentence.

The training loop is the simplest possible; lesson 3 explains each of its parts and adds the ones a real run needs.

distinct = valid.drop_duplicates("en")
lesson_pairs = [(EN_EXAMPLE, RU_EXAMPLE)] + list(zip(distinct.en[:15], distinct.ru[:15]))
src, tgt_in, tgt_out = make_batch(lesson_pairs)

model.train()  # dropout on, as in real training
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

losses = []
start = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(200):
    logits = model(src, tgt_in)
    flat_logits = logits.reshape(-1, VOCAB_SIZE)  # every position of every sentence
    loss = F.cross_entropy(flat_logits, tgt_out.reshape(-1), ignore_index=PAD)
    optimizer.zero_grad()  # forget the previous step's gradients
    loss.backward()  # compute new ones, through every layer
    optimizer.step()  # move every parameter a little against its gradient
    losses.append(loss.item())

seconds = round(time.perf_counter() - start, 1)
print(len(losses), "steps in", seconds, "s")
print("loss:", round(losses[0], 2), "->", round(losses[-1], 4))

200 steps in 12.9 s
loss: 11.05 -> 0.0017
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(losses, color=COLORS["enc"])
ax.axhline(math.log(VOCAB_SIZE), color=COLORS["muted"], linestyle=(0, (3, 3)), linewidth=1)
ax.text(len(losses) - 1, math.log(VOCAB_SIZE) + 0.3, "log|V|", ha="right")
ax.set_xlabel("step")
ax.set_ylabel("loss")
ax.set_title("Sixteen pairs, learned by heart")
plt.show()

To translate, the model writes one token at a time: encode the English sentence once, then repeatedly feed the decoder everything written so far and append its top prediction, until it predicts <eos>. This is greedy decoding; lesson 3 shows why it isn’t the best way to decode, and does better.

def translate_greedy(model, sentence, max_tokens=60):
    model.eval()
    src = torch.tensor([tokenizer.encode(sentence).ids], device=device)
    written = [BOS]
    with torch.no_grad():
        memory = model.encode(src)  # the English side, once
        for _ in range(max_tokens):
            tgt = torch.tensor([written], device=device)
            scores = model.decode(tgt, memory, src)[0, -1]  # scores for the next token
            next_id = scores.argmax().item()
            if next_id == EOS:
                break
            written.append(next_id)
    return tokenizer.decode(written[1:])


rows = []
for en, ru in lesson_pairs:
    output = translate_greedy(model, en)
    rows.append({"English": en, "model's Russian": output, "exact": output == ru})
memorized = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(memorized.exact.sum(), "of", len(memorized), "translations reproduced exactly")
assert memorized.exact.all()
table(memorized.head(6))

16 of 16 translations reproduced exactly
Englishmodel's Russianexact
The researcher said she was exhausted.Исследовательница сказала, что вымоталась.True
You are not old enough to go swimming by yourself.Ты недостаточно большая, чтобы идти плавать одной.True
You are made to be a poet.Ты прирождённый поэт.True
You are the next in line for promotion.Вы — следующий в очереди на повышение.True
You are the master of your own destiny.Ты хозяин своей собственной судьбы.True
You are wearing your socks inside out.У тебя носки наизнанку.True

Every pair comes back exactly, our sentence with its three feminine forms included. The model memorized, though; it hasn’t learned to translate anything it hasn’t seen. Its attention shows it.

Here is the cross-attention of the last decoder layer while it writes our sentence, averaged over the four heads: every row is a Russian token, and its cells show how much it took from each English token.

src = torch.tensor([tokenizer.encode(EN_EXAMPLE).ids], device=device)
tgt = torch.tensor([[BOS] + tokenizer.encode(RU_EXAMPLE).ids], device=device)
with torch.no_grad():
    model(src, tgt)  # the attention modules keep their last weights

cross = model.decoder[-1].cross_attention.weights[0].mean(dim=0).cpu()  # (T_ru, T_en)
en_tokens = tokenizer.encode(EN_EXAMPLE).tokens
ru_read = ["<bos>"] + tokenizer.encode(RU_EXAMPLE).tokens

heatmap(
    cross,
    rows=ru_read,
    cols=en_tokens,
    vmax=1,
    title="Cross-attention after memorizing: nearly flat",
    xlabel="English (keys)",
    ylabel="Russian (queries)",
)
plt.show()

print("uniform weight over the English tokens:", round(1 / len(en_tokens), 3))
print("largest weight in the map:", round(cross.max().item(), 3))


uniform weight over the English tokens: 0.111
largest weight in the map: 0.259

Nearly flat: almost every Russian token spreads its attention evenly across the English sentence. Memorizing sixteen pairs doesn’t require knowing which English word a Russian word translates; the model can get by on what each sentence looks like as a whole.

Lesson 3 trains on half a million pairs, where that shortcut no longer works, and we will come back to this picture to see whether сказала has learned to look at she.

13. Our code, at the size of a real model

Back to the table of section 1. opus-mt-en-ru has the shape of the 2017 base model, and our class implements that architecture. Build it with opus-mt-en-ru’s numbers instead of ours, and count:

opus = configs["opus-mt-en-ru (2020)"]
opus_sized = Transformer(
    vocab_size=opus["vocab_size"],
    d_model=opus["d_model"],
    n_heads=opus["encoder_attention_heads"],
    d_ff=opus["encoder_ffn_dim"],
    n_layers=opus["encoder_layers"],
    dropout=0.1,
    pad_id=opus["pad_token_id"],
)
opus_sized_params = sum(p.numel() for p in opus_sized.parameters())
print("our class at opus-mt-en-ru's size:", opus_sized_params, "parameters")
print(round(opus_sized_params / by_formula, 1), "times the size of our model")

our class at opus-mt-en-ru's size: 76147712 parameters
7.9 times the size of our model

The real model’s weights are a file of about 300 MB. Without downloading it, the Hub tells us its size, and at four bytes per number we can account for nearly every byte.

Two differences from our model are known in advance: Marian stores its sinusoidal position tables in the file (one for the encoder and one for the decoder) instead of computing them, and it adds a bias to the output scores.

info = HfApi().model_info("Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-ru", files_metadata=True)
file_size = [f.size for f in info.siblings if f.rfilename == "pytorch_model.bin"][0]

position_tables = 2 * opus["max_position_embeddings"] * opus["d_model"]
output_bias = opus["vocab_size"]
accounted = 4 * (opus_sized_params + position_tables + output_bias)

print("the real file:             ", file_size, "bytes")
print("our parameters and extras: ", accounted, "bytes")
left_over = file_size - accounted
print(f"left over: {left_over} bytes, {left_over / file_size:.3%} of the file")

the real file:              306991893 bytes
our parameters and extras:  306938072 bytes
left over: 53821 bytes, 0.018% of the file

What is left over is the file format itself: the tensors’ names and headers. The translator we will compete with is, number for number, the model you just wrote, at several times our size.

The model’s code is also in the course package, tfs.model, so that later lessons can import it instead of repeating it. Check that it is the same model, weight for weight:

from tfs.model import Transformer as PackagedTransformer

packaged = PackagedTransformer(VOCAB_SIZE, D_MODEL, N_HEADS, D_FF, N_LAYERS, DROPOUT, PAD)
packaged = packaged.to(device)
packaged.load_state_dict(model.state_dict())

src, tgt_in, _ = make_batch(lesson_pairs[:4])
model.eval()
packaged.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    assert torch.allclose(packaged(src, tgt_in), model(src, tgt_in), atol=1e-5)
print("tfs.model.Transformer is the model of this lesson")

tfs.model.Transformer is the model of this lesson

References

  1. Geva, M., Schuster, R., Berant, J., Levy, O. (2021). Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories. EMNLP. ↩
  2. He, K., Zhang, X., Ren, S., Sun, J. (2016). Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition. CVPR. ↩
  3. Elhage, N. et al. (2021). A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits. Where the “residual stream” comes from. ↩
  4. Ba, J. L., Kiros, J. R., Hinton, G. E. (2016). Layer Normalization. ↩
  5. Press, O., Wolf, L. (2017). Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models. EACL. ↩
  6. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention Is All You Need. NeurIPS.
  7. Bahdanau, D., Cho, K., Bengio, Y. (2015). Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate. ICLR. Attention itself was invented for translation, three years before the Transformer.
  8. Rush, A. (2018). The Annotated Transformer. The paper, line by line, in PyTorch.
  9. Junczys-Dowmunt, M. et al. (2018). Marian: Fast Neural Machine Translation in C++. ACL.
  10. Tiedemann, J., Thottingal, S. (2020). OPUS-MT: Building open translation services for the World. EAMT.
  11. Karpathy, A. (2019). A Recipe for Training Neural Networks.
  12. Model configurations: GPT-2, opus-mt-en-ru, Llama 3.1 8B, DeepSeek-V3.
entry.summary: Attention, masks, heads, positions and the full encoder-decoder of the 2017 paper, written line by line in PyTorch and checked against real models.

entry.title: How language models read: tokenization and BPE from scratch

link.title: How language models read: tokenization and BPE from scratch

entry.content:
Transformers: from scratch to production · lesson 1 of 10 · all lessons · run on Kaggle · open in Colab · code on GitHub

Chatbots used to be famously bad at one question: how many r’s are in “strawberry”? It looks like a test of attention to detail. Mostly it tests something the model cannot see. Here is what GPT-4o actually receives when you ask it:

Eight integers. The word  strawberry, together with the space in front of it, arrives as one of them, and its letters are not in the input at all.

Whatever the model knows about how that integer is spelled, it had to pick up indirectly, from the rare places in its training text where someone spelled the word out.

The program that turns text into integers is the tokenizer. It is built before the model, from a large pile of text, and then frozen: every model you have heard of reads the world through a fixed list of pieces chosen that way.

The choice of pieces decides what a request costs, which languages a model handles well, and, as you just saw, what it can count.

This course builds a Transformer that translates English into Russian, and in this lesson you build the tokenizer it will read and write with. Russian is a good language to learn this on: as you are about to see, tokenizers trained mostly on English handle it badly, and the reasons are instructive.

What you’ll do

  1. Take apart the tokenizers of GPT-2, GPT-4, Llama 3, DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-4o.
  2. Prepare an English–Russian corpus with training, validation and test splits that don’t leak into each other.
  3. Write byte-pair encoding (BPE), the algorithm behind all of those tokenizers, from scratch.
  4. Train the course’s tokenizer with Hugging Face tokenizers and put it next to GPT-4o’s.

What you need: Python and some pandas. No previous lessons. A free CPU runtime is enough; the notebook runs in about ten minutes.

Setup

One small helper package, tfs, draws the course’s plots and token chips and knows where the notebook runs (Kaggle, Colab or your own machine). Everything the lesson teaches is written out in the notebook itself.

import importlib.util
import subprocess
import sys

TFS = "git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@main"
if importlib.util.find_spec("tfs") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", TFS])

from tfs import env
from tfs.viz import table, token_chips, use_course_style

env.quiet()  # no progress bars or environment warnings in the outputs
SEED = 42
env.seed_everything(SEED)
COLORS = use_course_style()
WORK_DIR = env.work_dir()

import collections
import csv
import json
import os
import re
import time
import unicodedata

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from datasets import load_dataset
from tokenizers import Regex, Tokenizer, decoders, models, normalizers
from tokenizers import pre_tokenizers, trainers

1. Inside the tokenizers of real models

OpenAI publishes its tokenizers in the tiktoken library. Xenova/gpt-4o on the Hugging Face Hub is a port of GPT-4o’s tokenizer to the tokenizers library, which this course uses throughout; it produces the same tokens. Loading it downloads one JSON file of about 10 MB: the whole tokenizer, rules and vocabulary.

gpt4o = Tokenizer.from_pretrained("Xenova/gpt-4o")

question = "How many r's are in strawberry?"
print(gpt4o.encode(question).ids)

[5299, 1991, 428, 885, 553, 306, 101830, 30]

The same eight numbers as in the picture above. Each one is a position in GPT-4o’s vocabulary, and decode turns positions back into text.

Decoding the ids one at a time shows the piece behind each of them. The function below does that for a few texts and draws the pieces as chips, with the id under each chip:

def show_tokens(tokenizer, texts):
    rows, row_ids = [], []
    for text in texts:
        # add_special_tokens=False: some tokenizers (Llama's) add a "start of text" token
        ids = tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False).ids
        rows.append([tokenizer.decode([token_id]) for token_id in ids])
        row_ids.append(ids)
    token_chips(rows, ids=row_ids, labels=[repr(text) for text in texts])
    plt.show()


spellings = ["strawberry", " strawberry", " Strawberry", " STRAWBERRY", " strawberries"]
show_tokens(gpt4o, spellings)

Five spellings of one word, five unrelated sequences of numbers (␣ marks a space inside a token). In the middle of a sentence the word comes with a space in front of it and is a single token.

At the very start of a message there is no space, and the same word becomes three tokens, st, raw and berry. The capitalized word has a token of its own, the word in capitals falls apart into four pieces, and the plural is yet another token.

Nothing in these numbers says that they are the same word. The model works it out from how the tokens are used, and it learns how each of them is spelled the same indirect way.

Tokenizers keep the space attached to the word that follows it because that saves a token per word; the price is that a word has a different token at the start of a text than in the middle.

The same sentence in two languages

API prices, context windows and the speed of generation are all measured in tokens. So, does a sentence cost the same in every language? Take one sentence and its Russian translation:

The researcher said she was exhausted.

Исследовательница сказала, что вымоталась.

and count their tokens with the tokenizers of five models released between 2019 and 2024. All of them are on the Hugging Face Hub. Meta’s own Llama repositories require signing in, so Llama 3’s tokenizer comes from a public copy of Llama 3.2, which uses the same tokenizer.

LLM_TOKENIZERS = {
    "GPT-2 (2019)": "openai-community/gpt2",
    "GPT-4 (2023)": "Xenova/gpt-4",
    "Llama 3 (2024)": "unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B",
    "DeepSeek-V3 (2024)": "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3",
    "GPT-4o (2024)": "Xenova/gpt-4o",
}

llm_tokenizers = {}
for name, repo in LLM_TOKENIZERS.items():
    llm_tokenizers[name] = Tokenizer.from_pretrained(repo)

EN_EXAMPLE = "The researcher said she was exhausted."
RU_EXAMPLE = "Исследовательница сказала, что вымоталась."


def count_tokens(tokenizer, text):
    return len(tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False).ids)


rows = []
for name, tokenizer in llm_tokenizers.items():
    rows.append(
        {
            "model": name,
            "vocabulary": tokenizer.get_vocab_size(),
            "English": count_tokens(tokenizer, EN_EXAMPLE),
            "Russian": count_tokens(tokenizer, RU_EXAMPLE),
        }
    )
example_counts = pd.DataFrame(rows)
table(example_counts)
modelvocabularyEnglishRussian
GPT-2 (2019)50,257746
GPT-4 (2023)100,263719
Llama 3 (2024)128,256714
DeepSeek-V3 (2024)128,815714
GPT-4o (2024)200,000711

The same numbers as a chart. We will draw this chart again at the end of the lesson, with one more tokenizer in it, so it gets a function.

English is teal and Russian is rose here and in every plot of the course: they are the colors of the encoder, which reads English, and of the decoder, which writes Russian.

def plot_token_counts(counts, title):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 0.9 + 0.6 * len(counts)))
    rows = np.arange(len(counts))
    bar = 0.38
    english = ax.barh(rows - 0.2, counts.English, bar, color=COLORS["enc"], label="English")
    russian = ax.barh(rows + 0.2, counts.Russian, bar, color=COLORS["dec"], label="Russian")
    ax.bar_label(english, fmt="{:.3g}", padding=4, fontsize=9, color=COLORS["muted"])
    ax.bar_label(russian, fmt="{:.3g}", padding=4, fontsize=9, color=COLORS["muted"])

    labels = []
    for model, vocabulary in zip(counts.model, counts.vocabulary):
        labels.append(f"{model} · {vocabulary // 1000}k")
    ax.set_yticks(rows, labels)
    ax.invert_yaxis()  # the first model on top

    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=True)
    ax.set_xlabel("tokens")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(loc="lower right")
    plt.show()


plot_token_counts(example_counts, "One sentence, two languages, five tokenizers")

Every tokenizer spends about the same on the English sentence. The Russian one costs several times more in GPT-2, and the newer tokenizers narrow the gap.

Note the vocabulary sizes next to the names: the gap closed as the vocabularies grew from about fifty thousand pieces to two hundred thousand, enough room for frequent pieces of many languages. Even in GPT-4o, though, the Russian sentence is more expensive than the English one.

The extra cost has a name, the token tax: Petrov et al. (2023) measured it across hundreds of languages and found that the same text can take up to 15 times as many tokens as in English.

Where does GPT-2’s bill come from? Look at the pieces it cuts the first Russian word into:

show_tokens(llm_tokenizers["GPT-2 (2019)"], ["Исследовательница"])

Most letters are tokens of their own, and some, like the first one, are cut in half: each � is a fragment of a letter that is not valid text on its own. That is not a display bug.

GPT-2 tokenizes bytes. It writes text in UTF-8, where every Cyrillic letter takes two bytes, and starts from the 256 possible bytes as its alphabet.

GPT-2 was trained on WebText, a crawl from which, as the GPT-2 paper notes, OpenAI deliberately removed non-English pages, and its merges rarely glue Russian bytes into anything longer than a letter.

GPT-4o works on bytes too, but among its 200 000 pieces there are plenty of Russian letters, syllables and words. Here is a word from the Russian sentence and one more:

show_tokens(gpt4o, [" вымоталась", " недопонимание"])

Fewer tokens, but look at where the cuts fall in the second word, недопонимание, “misunderstanding”. It is built as недо (under-) + понима (the stem of понимать, to understand) + ние (which turns a verb into a noun), and GPT-4o’s pieces cut across all three.

That isn’t a mistake: a tokenizer learns statistics, not grammar, and it learns the statistics of the text it was built from.

By the end of this lesson you will have a tokenizer of your own, trained in a couple of minutes on English–Russian sentences, with sixteen thousand pieces instead of two hundred thousand. On the Russian sentences of our data it will need fewer tokens than GPT-4o.

Every tokenizer you’ve seen so far, and ours too, turns text into numbers in the same four stages:

We build them in this order. First, though, the tokenizer needs text to learn from.

2. The data

Tatoeba (“for example” in Japanese) is a collection of example sentences and their translations, started by Trang Ho in 2006 and written by volunteers ever since. The sentences are short and everyday, which is what a small translator can learn from, and they are licensed under CC BY 2.0 FR. We use two pieces of it:

  • training data: the English–Russian pairs prepared by the sentence-transformers project;
  • test data: the English–Russian test set of the Tatoeba Translation Challenge (Tiedemann, 2020), a public benchmark. In lesson 4 we compare our model with published systems on it.

Both downloads are pinned to an exact revision, so the numbers in this notebook don’t change when the sources do.

Before cleaning anything, read some data; every corpus has habits. Tatoeba’s most famous one is a man called Tom.

Prolific contributors use him (and Mary) as the default name in example sentences, so often that in 2019 the project discussed banning them and decided not to. He is everywhere:

This matters more than it seems. Russian declines names: Tom is Том, Тома, Тому, Томом, о Томе depending on his role in the sentence, so our translator will get plenty of practice with Russian cases on one name.

It will also be much better at sentences about Tom than about anyone else. A model learns the distribution of its data, quirks included.

Some variants are a matter of style («ёлочки» versus "straight quotes"). Others are invisible: the letter й can be stored as one code point, or as и followed by a combining breve, a mark that the font draws on top of the previous letter.

Every reader sees the same letter. Python sees two different strings:

one_code_point = "\u0439"
two_code_points = "\u0438\u0306"

print(one_code_point, two_code_points)

False

A tokenizer that doesn’t know this would learn two tokens for one letter, and the model would have to learn twice that they mean the same. Unicode defines normal forms for exactly this. Normal form NFKC composes letters with their accents, and also maps “compatibility” characters to plain ones: subscript digits, non-breaking spaces, the one-character ellipsis ….

print(unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", two_code_points) == one_code_point)
print(unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", "H₂O"))
nbsp = "\u00a0"  # a non-breaking space
print(repr(unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", "two" + nbsp + "words")))

True
H2O
'two words'

On top of NFKC we make four choices of our own. They are written down because the model will inherit them: whatever we erase here, it will never be able to read or write.

  1. Drop the combining marks that survive NFKC. Tatoeba marks stress in some Russian sentences (То́му), which is a pronunciation hint, not spelling.
  2. Use straight quotes and apostrophes, and one kind of dash, —.
  3. Read a hyphen surrounded by spaces as a dash.
  4. Collapse runs of whitespace into one space.
QUOTES = {"«": '"', "»": '"', "„": '"', "“": '"', "”": '"', "‘": "'", "’": "'", "–": "—"}


def normalize(text):
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text)

    # Unicode category "Mn" is a combining mark, such as a stress accent
    kept = [char for char in text if unicodedata.category(char) != "Mn"]
    text = "".join(kept)

    for fancy, plain in QUOTES.items():
        text = text.replace(fancy, plain)

    text = re.sub(r"\s+-\s+", " — ", text)  # " - " is a dash
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)  # one space between words
    return text.strip()

A cleaning step is a hypothesis about your data. Test it by reading what it removes.

The test set must stay unseen

The Tatoeba test set was cut from the same pool of sentences as our training data. If a test sentence also appears in training, the model can recite the answer and the test score stops measuring translation.

This problem, contamination, is one that large-model papers take seriously: the GPT-4 technical report has a whole appendix of contamination checks for its benchmarks.

Comparing exact strings is not enough: Хватит! and хватит. are the same sentence for our purposes. We compare fingerprints instead: lowercase, without punctuation and spaces, and with ё read as е (Russian texts use the two letters interchangeably).

def fingerprint(text):
    text = text.casefold()  # lowercase that also handles special cases like ß
    text = text.replace("ё", "е")
    return re.sub(r"[\W_]+", "", text)  # drop everything that is not a letter or a digit


print(fingerprint("Хватит!"), fingerprint("хватит."), fingerprint("Ты безнадёжна!"))

хватит хватит тыбезнадежна

A training pair leaks when its English or its Russian sentence has the fingerprint of a test sentence. Compare the two ways of checking:

test_ru_prints = set(test.ru.map(fingerprint))

exact_ru = train.ru.isin(set(test.ru))
print("pairs that share a sentence with the test set")

printed_en = train.en.map(fingerprint).isin(test_en_prints)
printed_ru = train.ru.map(fingerprint).isin(test_ru_prints)

A validation split that doesn’t leak

We also need a validation set: data the model never trains on, used to choose settings and to stop training at the right moment. The usual move is to hold out a random 2% of the pairs. Here that would be a mistake, and the picture shows why.

These are real pairs from our data. Think of every sentence as a node and every translation pair as an edge.

A random split cuts edges independently, so a validation pair like Cut it out! → Прекрати! still has both of its sentences in training pairs. The model has seen the source and has learned to produce the target, and validation would reward memory.

The fix is to split whole connected components: groups of sentences linked by translation, directly or through each other. A classic data structure finds them, union–find. Every sentence starts as a group of its own.

Every pair says “these two sentences belong together”, and we merge their groups. To tell whether two sentences are already in one group, each group has a representative, its root: every sentence keeps a link to a “parent” sentence, and following the parents leads to the root.

class UnionFind:
    def __init__(self):
        self.parent = {}  # sentence -> its parent; a root is its own parent

    def find(self, x):
        if x not in self.parent:
            self.parent[x] = x  # a sentence seen for the first time is a group of one

        root = x
        while self.parent[root] != root:
            root = self.parent[root]

        # path compression: point everything on the way straight at the root
        while self.parent[x] != root:
            next_x = self.parent[x]
            self.parent[x] = root
            x = next_x
        return root

    def union(self, a, b):
        root_a = self.find(a)
        root_b = self.find(b)
        if root_a != root_b:
            self.parent[root_a] = root_b  # the two groups become one

The second loop in find is what keeps it fast. Without it, a chain of parents can grow long, and every lookup walks the whole chain. With it, a lookup shortens the chain for everyone after it:

That is the actual state of the structure halfway through the example below. A sentence is stored together with its language, ("en", "Stop it."), because the same string can occur on both sides (names, numbers). Run it on the pairs from the pictures, plus one unrelated pair:

All eight pairs from the picture end up in one group, and the unrelated pair forms its own.

With path compression alone, \(m\) operations on \(n\) sentences cost \(O(m \log n)\) in the worst case. Also attaching the smaller group under the larger one (union by rank) gives the famous near-linear bound \(O(m\,\alpha(n))\), where \(\alpha\) is the inverse Ackermann function, which stays below 5 for any \(n\) that fits in our universe[1]. For our data compression alone is plenty. Now the real thing: every training pair, and a group label for each.

    root = groups.find(("en", en))
    labels.append(str(root))  # a pair is labeled with the root of its group
train = train.assign(group=labels)

Now compare the two ways of splitting. leak_rate measures the share of validation pairs whose English or Russian sentence also occurs somewhere in training:

def leak_rate(train_part, valid_part):
    seen_english = set(train_part.en)
    seen_russian = set(train_part.ru)
    leaked = valid_part.en.isin(seen_english) | valid_part.ru.isin(seen_russian)
    return leaked.mean()

First the random split: every pair goes to validation with probability 2%.

train = train[~in_valid].drop(columns="group")

Split by whatever must not be shared. Here that’s sentences, so we split by groups of linked sentences; for medical images it would be patients, for code it would be repositories.

3. Why not words, and why not characters

Two designs come to mind before BPE does: one token per word, or one token per character. Both have been used, and both fail in instructive ways.

A word tokenizer gives each distinct word an id. Its problem is that the number of distinct words never stops growing. Watch it grow as we read through the training data, recording the number of distinct words after every thousand words read:

WORD = re.compile(r"\w+")  # a run of letters or digits


def vocabulary_growth(sentences, every=1_000):
    seen = set()
    words_read = 0
    n_points, v_points = [], []
    for sentence in sentences:
        for word in WORD.findall(sentence.lower()):
            seen.add(word)
            words_read += 1
            if words_read % every == 0:
                n_points.append(words_read)
                v_points.append(len(seen))
    return np.array(n_points), np.array(v_points)


shuffled = train.sample(frac=1, random_state=SEED)
growth = {"en": vocabulary_growth(shuffled.en), "ru": vocabulary_growth(shuffled.ru)}

Empirically, vocabulary growth follows Heaps’ law:

\[V(N) = K N^{\beta}, \qquad 0 < \beta < 1,\]

where \(N\) is the number of words read, \(V(N)\) the number of distinct words among them, and \(K\), \(\beta\) constants of the language and the text. \(\beta\) is the interesting one: it says how fast new word forms keep appearing. With \(\beta = 0.5\), reading four times more text doubles the vocabulary.

Taking logarithms turns the law into a straight line, \(\log V = \log K + \beta \log N\), so we can estimate \(\beta\) as the slope of a least-squares line through the points in log–log coordinates; np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns the slope and the intercept.

fig, ax = plt.subplots()

for lang, color in [("en", COLORS["enc"]), ("ru", COLORS["dec"])]:
    n, v = growth[lang]
    beta, log_k = np.polyfit(np.log(n), np.log(v), 1)
    label = f"{lang}: β = {beta:.2f}, {v[-1]:,} distinct words"
    ax.loglog(n, v, color=color, label=label)
    fitted = np.exp(log_k) * n**beta  # the fitted law, dashed
    ax.loglog(n, fitted, color=color, linestyle=(0, (2, 3)), linewidth=1.2)

ax.set_xlabel("words read, N")
ax.set_ylabel("distinct words, V(N)")
ax.set_title("Russian keeps producing new word forms")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()

Russian grows faster and ends with several times more distinct words, although the Russian side has fewer words in total. The reason is morphology: понимать, понимаю, понимаешь, понимание, недопонимание, понимания, … are all different strings to a word tokenizer, while English mostly reuses understand.

The other side of the same coin is the long tail. Count how many distinct words occur exactly once in all of the training data (linguists call them hapax legomena, “said once”):

word_freqs = {}
for lang in ["en", "ru"]:
    counts = collections.Counter()
    for sentence in train[lang]:
        counts.update(WORD.findall(sentence.lower()))
    word_freqs[lang] = counts

    seen_once = 0
    for count in counts.values():
        if count == 1:
            seen_once += 1
    print(f"{lang}: {seen_once / len(counts):.0%} of distinct words occur once")

en: 33% of distinct words occur once
ru: 42% of distinct words occur once

A large share of the vocabulary is words the model would see once in all of training, too rarely to learn anything about them. A real vocabulary has to stop somewhere anyway. Keep the 30 000 most frequent training words and count how many validation words fall outside, the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rate:

def oov_rate(counts, valid_sentences, size=30_000):
    vocabulary = set()
    for word, _ in counts.most_common(size):
        vocabulary.add(word)

    total, unknown = 0, 0
    for sentence in valid_sentences:
        for word in WORD.findall(sentence.lower()):
            total += 1
            if word not in vocabulary:
                unknown += 1
    return unknown / total


for lang in ["en", "ru"]:
    rate = oov_rate(word_freqs[lang], valid[lang])
    print(f"{lang}: {rate:.2%} of validation words are unknown")

en: 0.35% of validation words are unknown
ru: 3.33% of validation words are unknown

Every unknown word becomes the same placeholder, and the model can neither read nor write it. For Russian that happens an order of magnitude more often than for English, and those are exactly the rare inflected forms a translator must produce.

The opposite extreme, one token per character, has no unknown words at all, but the sequences get long:

for lang in ["en", "ru"]:
    chars = valid[lang].str.len().mean()
    words = word_count(valid[lang]).mean()
    print(f"{lang}: {chars:.1f} characters, {words:.1f} words per sentence;")
    print(f"    {chars / words:.1f} times longer in characters")

en: 31.0 characters, 6.2 words per sentence;
    5.0 times longer in characters
ru: 31.0 characters, 5.4 words per sentence;
    5.7 times longer in characters

Length is expensive. In lesson 2 you will see that self-attention compares every position with every other, so its cost grows with the square of the sequence length \(T\):

\[\text{cost} \propto T^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\text{cost}_{\text{chars}}}{\text{cost}_{\text{words}}} = \left(\frac{T_{\text{chars}}}{T_{\text{words}}}\right)^2.\]

Sequences \(k\) times longer make attention \(k^2\) times more expensive: with the ratios above, a character model pays for attention dozens of times more than a word model, and it has to learn spelling before it can learn meaning.

Subword tokenization is the compromise: frequent words stay whole, rare words are split into frequent pieces, and every string can still be written with the basic alphabet. Byte-pair encoding is the most widely used way to find those pieces.

4. BPE from scratch

BPE was invented in 1994 by Philip Gage as a way to compress files: find the most common pair of adjacent bytes, replace it everywhere with a byte value the file doesn’t use, repeat.

In 2016 Sennrich, Haddow and Birch noticed that the same procedure, run on the letters of words, finds good subword units for translation. Today it builds the tokenizers of GPT-2, GPT-4o, Llama 3 and DeepSeek-V3, all of which you took apart in section 1.

The idea fits in one picture:

Start with every word spelled out as single characters. Then repeat: find the pair of adjacent symbols that occurs most often in the corpus, merge it into one new symbol everywhere, and add that symbol to the vocabulary.

Frequent words end up as one symbol, because merging their pieces paid off again and again; rare words stay split into pieces that other words share.

Formally, let \(f(w)\) be the frequency of word \(w\) in the corpus and \(n_{ab}(w)\) the number of times symbol \(a\) is immediately followed by symbol \(b\) in the current spelling of \(w\). The frequency of the pair is

\[c(a, b) = \sum_{w} f(w)\, n_{ab}(w),\]

and each step merges

\[(a^*, b^*) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{(a, b)} c(a, b).\]

If two pairs are equally frequent we take the one that compares greater as a pair of Python strings, that is, by Unicode code points.

Any fixed rule works; what matters is that it is deterministic, so the same corpus always yields the same tokenizer. After \(M\) merges the vocabulary holds the initial alphabet \(\Sigma\) plus one symbol per merge: \(\lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert = \lvert\Sigma\rvert + M\).

Pre-tokenization

Merges never cross word boundaries, so we first split text into words and punctuation. A word keeps the space in front of it, written as ▁ (the convention of SentencePiece, Kudo and Richardson, 2018).

It’s the same trick you saw in GPT-4o’s ␣strawberry: with the spaces inside the tokens, decoding is plain concatenation, and the model can tell the beginning of a word from the middle of one.

The regular expression has two alternatives:  ?\w+ is an optional space followed by letters or digits, and  ?[^\w\s]+ is an optional space followed by punctuation (anything that is neither a word character nor whitespace).

PRE_TOKEN = re.compile(r" ?\w+| ?[^\w\s]+")


def pretokenize(text):
    pieces = PRE_TOKEN.findall(" " + text)  # the leading space marks the first word too
    return [piece.replace(" ", "▁") for piece in pieces]


print(pretokenize(RU_EXAMPLE))
print(pretokenize("Let's go — now!"))

['▁Исследовательница', '▁сказала', ',', '▁что', '▁вымоталась', '.']
['▁Let', "'", 's', '▁go', '▁—', '▁now', '!']

Counting pairs on a toy corpus

Before touching half a million sentences, run every step on three Russian words whose counts you can check by hand. A word is stored as a tuple of its symbols, with its frequency:

toy = {
    tuple("▁понимание"): 5,
    tuple("▁недопонимание"): 3,
    tuple("▁понимать"): 4,
}


def pair_counts(words):
    counts = collections.Counter()
    for word, freq in words.items():
        for left, right in zip(word, word[1:]):  # every adjacent pair in the word
            counts[left, right] += freq
    return counts


pair_counts(toy).most_common(5)

[(('н', 'и'), 20),
 (('п', 'о'), 12),
 (('о', 'н'), 12),
 (('и', 'м'), 12),
 (('м', 'а'), 12)]

н + и wins: it occurs twice in понимание (five times), twice in недопонимание (three times) and once in понимать (four times), which gives \(2 \cdot 5 + 2 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 4 = 20\), the formula for \(c(a, b)\) above.

Picking the winner, with our rule for ties:

def most_frequent_pair(counts):
    best_pair, best_count = None, 0
    for pair, count in counts.items():
        if count > best_count or (count == best_count and pair > best_pair):
            best_pair, best_count = pair, count
    return best_pair


most_frequent_pair(pair_counts(toy))

('н', 'и')

Merging a pair rewrites a word, scanning it from left to right:

def merge_word(word, pair):
    merged = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(word):
        if i + 1 < len(word) and (word[i], word[i + 1]) == pair:
            merged.append(word[i] + word[i + 1])  # two symbols become one
            i += 2
        else:
            merged.append(word[i])
            i += 1
    return tuple(merged)


before = tuple("▁недопонимание")
after = merge_word(before, ("н", "и"))
token_chips([before, after], labels=["before", "after"])
plt.show()

The straightforward trainer

Training is these three steps in a loop:

def train_bpe_simple(words, n_merges):
    merges = []
    for _ in range(n_merges):
        counts = pair_counts(words)
        if not counts:  # every word is a single symbol, nothing left to merge
            break
        pair = most_frequent_pair(counts)
        merges.append(pair)

        merged_words = {}
        for word, freq in words.items():
            merged_words[merge_word(word, pair)] = freq
        words = merged_words
    return merges


train_bpe_simple(toy, 6)

[('н', 'и'),
 ('п', 'о'),
 ('по', 'ни'),
 ('пони', 'м'),
 ('поним', 'а'),
 ('▁', 'понима')]

Six merges on the toy corpus, each one built on the previous ones: ни, then по, then по + ни = пони, and so on until the whole stem ▁понима. Now a real sample: we count the words of 40 000 sentences, English and Russian together, and run 300 merges.

def word_counts(sentences):
    counts = collections.Counter()
    for sentence in sentences:
        counts.update(pretokenize(sentence))

    words = {}
    for word, freq in counts.items():
        words[tuple(word)] = freq
    return words


SAMPLE_SENTENCES = 40_000
SAMPLE_MERGES = 300

sample = pd.concat([train.en, train.ru]).sample(SAMPLE_SENTENCES, random_state=SEED)
sample_words = word_counts(sample)
print("distinct words in the sample:", len(sample_words))

start = time.perf_counter()
simple_merges = train_bpe_simple(sample_words, SAMPLE_MERGES)
simple_seconds = time.perf_counter() - start
print(len(simple_merges), "merges in", round(simple_seconds, 1), "s")

distinct words in the sample: 23926
300 merges in 12.0 s

The first merges are the most frequent pieces of both languages, interleaved:

first_30 = ["".join(pair) for pair in simple_merges[:30]]
token_chips(
    [first_30[0:10], first_30[10:20], first_30[20:30]],
    labels=["merges 1–10", "11–20", "21–30"],
)
plt.show()

Word starts like ▁t, ▁н, ▁п come first, then frequent syllables and whole short words. ▁T seems to appear twice in the second row: one is the Latin T, the other the Cyrillic Т that starts Том. They look identical and are different characters, which is why we never compare text by how it looks.

The trainer is correct but slow. Every merge recounts all pairs in all words, so the cost is \(O(M \cdot L)\), where \(L\) is the total number of symbols in all distinct words. Both factors grow for the real run: the full training set has several times more distinct words than this sample, and we want thousands of merges, not hundreds.

The incremental trainer

Most of that recounting is wasted, because a merge changes very little. Take one word of the toy corpus and compare its pairs before and after merging н + и:

Only the pairs that touch the merge change, and only in words that contain the pair. So instead of recounting, we keep two tables between steps:

  • pair_freq: how often each pair occurs in the corpus, \(c(a, b)\);
  • words_with_pair: for each pair, which words contain it.

After a merge we visit only the affected words. For each of them, remove_pairs takes all its pairs out of the tables, the word is rewritten, and add_pairs puts its new pairs back.

Removing and re-adding the whole word is simpler than computing the exact difference, and the result is the same: the pairs that didn’t change go out and come back with the same count.

def train_bpe(word_freqs, n_merges):
    words = [list(word) for word in word_freqs]  # current spelling of every word
    freqs = list(word_freqs.values())
    pair_freq = collections.Counter()
    words_with_pair = collections.defaultdict(set)  # pair -> indices of words with it

    def add_pairs(i):
        for pair in zip(words[i], words[i][1:]):
            pair_freq[pair] += freqs[i]
            words_with_pair[pair].add(i)

    def remove_pairs(i):
        for pair in zip(words[i], words[i][1:]):
            pair_freq[pair] -= freqs[i]
            if pair_freq[pair] == 0:
                del pair_freq[pair]
            words_with_pair[pair].discard(i)

    for i in range(len(words)):
        add_pairs(i)

    merges = []
    for _ in range(n_merges):
        if not pair_freq:
            break
        pair = most_frequent_pair(pair_freq)
        merges.append(pair)
        for i in list(words_with_pair[pair]):  # only the words that contain the pair change
            remove_pairs(i)
            words[i] = list(merge_word(words[i], pair))
            add_pairs(i)

    final_spelling = {}
    for word, spelling in zip(word_freqs, words):
        final_spelling[word] = tuple(spelling)
    return merges, final_spelling

A faster algorithm is only useful if it computes the same thing. Same input, same number of merges:

start = time.perf_counter()
fast_merges, _ = train_bpe(sample_words, SAMPLE_MERGES)
fast_seconds = time.perf_counter() - start

assert fast_merges == simple_merges
print("identical merges")
print("simple:", round(simple_seconds, 1), "s, incremental:", round(fast_seconds, 2), "s")
print(round(simple_seconds / fast_seconds), "times faster")

identical merges
simple: 12.0 s, incremental: 0.46 s
26 times faster

Now the full training set, both languages together, and 8 000 merges. One shared vocabulary for English and Russian lets the model share one embedding table between encoder and decoder later on, and the two languages have more in common than their alphabets suggest: digits, punctuation, names, borrowed words.

N_MERGES = 8_000
all_words = word_counts(pd.concat([train.en, train.ru]))

start = time.perf_counter()
merges, segmentation = train_bpe(all_words, N_MERGES)
seconds = round(time.perf_counter() - start)
print(len(merges), "merges over", len(all_words), "distinct words in", seconds, "s")

alphabet = set()
for word in all_words:
    alphabet.update(word)
vocabulary_size = len(alphabet) + len(merges)
print("vocabulary:", len(alphabet), "characters +", len(merges), "merges")
print("          =", vocabulary_size, "symbols")

8000 merges over 119567 distinct words in 15 s
vocabulary: 242 characters + 8000 merges
          = 8242 symbols

Encoding: replay the merges in order

To tokenize new text we don’t count anything. We apply the learned merges in the order they were learned: in each word, find the adjacent pair that was merged earliest during training, its rank, merge it, and repeat until no adjacent pair is in the merge table.

Ranks matter because merges build on each other: ▁недо exists only because ▁н, ▁не and до were merged first.

ranks = {}
for rank, pair in enumerate(merges):
    ranks[pair] = rank  # pair -> when it was merged: 0, 1, 2, ...


def encode_word(word, ranks, steps=None):
    symbols = list(word)
    while True:
        # find the adjacent pair with the lowest rank
        best_i, best_rank = None, None
        for i in range(len(symbols) - 1):
            rank = ranks.get((symbols[i], symbols[i + 1]))
            if rank is not None and (best_rank is None or rank < best_rank):
                best_i, best_rank = i, rank

        if best_i is None:  # no pair left that training ever merged
            return symbols

        symbols[best_i : best_i + 2] = [symbols[best_i] + symbols[best_i + 1]]
        if steps is not None:
            steps.append((list(symbols), best_i))  # remember every step, to draw it below


steps = []
encode_word("▁недопонимание", ranks, steps)
rows = [symbols for symbols, _ in steps]
token_chips(rows, strong=lambda row, col, _: col == steps[row][1], size=11)
plt.show()

Each row is one merge; the highlighted symbol is the one just created. Replaying merges by rank should reproduce exactly the segmentation that training arrived at. Rather than believe it, check it for every word in the training data:

mismatches = []
for word, trained in segmentation.items():
    if encode_word("".join(word), ranks) != list(trained):
        mismatches.append(word)

assert not mismatches, mismatches[:5]
print("encoding reproduces the training segmentation for all", len(segmentation), "words")

encoding reproduces the training segmentation for all 119567 words

Encoding a sentence is pre-tokenization plus encode_word, and decoding is concatenation with ▁ turned back into spaces. Nothing is lost on the way; the round trip over the whole validation set confirms it:

def encode(text):
    tokens = []
    for word in pretokenize(text):
        tokens.extend(encode_word(word, ranks))
    return tokens


def decode(tokens):
    text = "".join(tokens).replace("▁", " ")
    return text[1:]  # drop the space we added in front of the first word


for sentence in pd.concat([valid.en, valid.ru]):
    assert decode(encode(sentence)) == sentence

print(encode(RU_EXAMPLE))

['▁И', 'сс', 'ледо', 'ва', 'тель', 'ница', '▁сказала', ',', '▁что', '▁вы', 'мо', 'т', 'алась', '.']

What the merges learned

Nobody told BPE about prefixes or suffixes, yet some appear on their own, because a frequent morpheme is a frequent string:

words = [
    "▁misunderstanding",
    "▁недопонимание",
    "▁исследовательница",
    "▁вымоталась",
    "▁researcher",
    "▁untranslatable",
]
segmented = [encode_word(word, ranks) for word in words]
token_chips(segmented, labels=[word[1:] for word in words], size=11)
plt.show()

Some splits look like a linguist’s: недо, or the feminine suffix ница, the piece that turns исследователь (a researcher) into a woman researcher. Others don’t (st + and).

BPE optimizes frequency, not meaning. The model will learn what the pieces mean from context; what the tokenizer controls is that frequent things are short and every rare thing can still be spelled.

5. The production tokenizer

Our implementation is readable and correct. It would also be slow at serving time and easy to break: the normalization lives in one function, the pre-tokenization in another, and nothing forces a server to call them the same way as training did.

Hugging Face tokenizers, written in Rust, packs the whole pipeline into one object that is saved as one file:

The tokenizers of section 1 are such files; you downloaded five of them. The rule we follow:

The tokenizer owns its normalization. Then training, evaluation and the deployed service can’t normalize differently, because there is no separate step to forget.

First the normalizer, rebuilt from the same choices as normalize, step for step:

hf_normalizer = normalizers.Sequence(
    [
        normalizers.NFKC(),
        normalizers.Replace(Regex(r"\p{Mn}"), ""),  # combining marks
        *[normalizers.Replace(fancy, plain) for fancy, plain in QUOTES.items()],
        normalizers.Replace(Regex(r"\s+-\s+"), " — "),
        normalizers.Replace(Regex(r"\s+"), " "),
        normalizers.Strip(),
    ]
)

print(hf_normalizer.normalize_str("Он сказал:   «Я не знаю» - и ушёл…"))

Он сказал: "Я не знаю" — и ушёл...

“Rebuilt from the same choices” is a claim, so check it on every raw sentence we have:

raw_sentences = pd.concat([train_raw.en, train_raw.ru, test_raw.en, test_raw.ru])

different = []
for sentence in raw_sentences:
    if hf_normalizer.normalize_str(sentence) != normalize(sentence):
        different.append(sentence)

assert not different, different[:5]
print("identical normalization on all", len(raw_sentences), "raw sentences")

identical normalization on all 1156102 raw sentences

Then the pre-tokenizer: the same regular expression splits words and punctuation, and Metaspace turns the spaces into ▁. Regular-expression engines don’t always agree on what a “word character” is (Python’s and the Rust library’s disagree on combining marks and subscript digits), which is one more reason the normalizer removed those first. Check this one too:

hf_pre_tokenizer = pre_tokenizers.Sequence(
    [
        pre_tokenizers.Split(Regex(r" ?\w+| ?[^\w\s]+"), behavior="isolated"),
        pre_tokenizers.Metaspace(replacement="▁", prepend_scheme="never", split=False),
    ]
)


def hf_pretokenize(text):
    pieces = hf_pre_tokenizer.pre_tokenize_str(" " + text)  # (piece, position) pairs
    return [piece for piece, _ in pieces]


normalized_sentences = pd.concat([train.en, train.ru, valid.en, valid.ru, test.en, test.ru])
for sentence in normalized_sentences:
    assert hf_pretokenize(sentence) == pretokenize(sentence), sentence
print("identical pre-tokenization on all", len(normalized_sentences), "sentences")

identical pre-tokenization on all 1109696 sentences

The tokenizer needs four special tokens, which the model will use from lesson 2 on: <pad> fills shorter sentences in a batch, <unk> stands for a character never seen in training, <bos> and <eos> mark the beginning and end of a sentence. They take ids 0 to 3.

<unk> is the price of starting from characters rather than bytes, as GPT-2 does: a character that never occurred in training (an emoji, a Chinese name) has no symbol. For a translator between two languages that is a fair trade; the tokens stay readable, and no letter gets cut in half.

SPECIAL_TOKENS = ["<pad>", "<unk>", "<bos>", "<eos>"]


def build_tokenizer(vocab_size):
    tokenizer = Tokenizer(models.BPE(unk_token="<unk>"))
    tokenizer.normalizer = normalizers.Sequence([hf_normalizer, normalizers.Prepend(" ")])
    tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = hf_pre_tokenizer
    tokenizer.decoder = decoders.Metaspace(
        replacement="▁", prepend_scheme="always", split=False
    )

    trainer = trainers.BpeTrainer(
        vocab_size=vocab_size,
        special_tokens=SPECIAL_TOKENS,
        min_frequency=2,  # ignore pairs seen only once
        show_progress=False,
    )
    tokenizer.train_from_iterator(list(train.en) + list(train.ru), trainer)
    return tokenizer


VOCAB_SIZE = 16_000

start = time.perf_counter()
tokenizer = build_tokenizer(VOCAB_SIZE)
seconds = round(time.perf_counter() - start, 1)
print("vocabulary of", tokenizer.get_vocab_size(), "trained in", seconds, "s")
print(tokenizer.encode(RU_EXAMPLE).tokens)

vocabulary of 16000 trained in 19.3 s
['▁И', 'сс', 'ледо', 'ватель', 'ница', '▁сказала', ',', '▁что', '▁вы', 'мот', 'алась', '.']

Compare the timings: the Rust trainer builds twice as many symbols in a fraction of the time our Python one needed for the same corpus.

Both see exactly the same words, since we checked normalization and pre-tokenization, so their merges should agree except where the two implementations make different choices: Hugging Face breaks ties between equally frequent pairs differently, and skips pairs seen only once (min_frequency=2). The saved tokenizer lists its merges in order; compare the first thousand with ours:

saved = json.loads(tokenizer.to_str())

hf_merges = []
for merge in saved["model"]["merges"]:
    if isinstance(merge, str):  # older versions of tokenizers store a merge as "a b"
        merge = merge.split(" ")
    hf_merges.append(tuple(merge))

shared = set(hf_merges[:1000]) & set(merges[:1000])
print(len(shared), "of the first 1000 merges are the same in both")

first_difference = 0
while hf_merges[first_difference] == merges[first_difference]:
    first_difference += 1
print("the lists first differ at merge", first_difference + 1)
print("Hugging Face merged", hf_merges[first_difference])

Almost all of the first thousand merges are the same. Why does the first difference happen? Rebuild the corpus as both trainers saw it at that moment: replaying the merges that came before it, with our encode_word, gives every word’s spelling at that step, and pair_counts gives the frequencies.

earlier_ranks = {}
for rank, pair in enumerate(merges[:first_difference]):
    earlier_ranks[pair] = rank

corpus_at_that_step = {}
for word, freq in all_words.items():
    spelling = tuple(encode_word("".join(word), earlier_ranks))
    corpus_at_that_step[spelling] = freq

counts_then = pair_counts(corpus_at_that_step)
theirs, ours = hf_merges[first_difference], merges[first_difference]
print("Hugging Face's pair:", theirs, "occurred", counts_then[theirs], "times")
print("our pair:", ours, "occurred", counts_then[ours], "times")

Hugging Face's pair: ('р', 'ы') occurred 11268 times
our pair: ('▁го', 'вори') occurred 11268 times

A tie: both pairs were equally frequent, and the two implementations break ties differently. Same algorithm, same data, a different rule for a coin toss.

The tokenizer is now self-contained. Feed it raw, unnormalized text, and decoding returns the normalized sentence:

ids = tokenizer.encode(messy).ids

print(ids)
print(repr(tokenizer.decode(ids)))
assert tokenizer.decode(ids) == normalize(messy)

6. How many tokens?

Why 16 000 symbols, and not 8 000 or the 200 000 of GPT-4o? A bigger vocabulary makes sequences shorter, but it isn’t free. The first layer of the model is an embedding table, one learned vector per token:

\[\text{embedding parameters} = \lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert \cdot d_{\text{model}},\]

and the last layer is the same size again, because at every output position the model scores every token in the vocabulary. Worse, a rare token gets few training examples, so its row is learned poorly.

The most famous case is  SolidGoldMagikarp: a Reddit username that was frequent enough in the text GPT-2’s tokenizer was built from to become a token of its own, but that, it seems, almost never occurred in the text the models were then trained on.

In 2023, Rumbelow and Watkins found that GPT-3 models, which share that tokenizer, couldn’t even repeat the word back and answered with unrelated ones. The token is still there:

show_tokens(llm_tokenizers["GPT-2 (2019)"], [" SolidGoldMagikarp"])

So we measure both sides: the average number of tokens per validation sentence for several vocabulary sizes, and the size of the embedding table for the model of lesson 2, whose vectors have \(d_{\text{model}} = 256\) numbers.

def tokens_per_sentence(tokenizer, sentences):
    encodings = tokenizer.encode_batch(list(sentences), add_special_tokens=False)
    lengths = [len(encoding.ids) for encoding in encodings]
    return np.mean(lengths)


D_MODEL = 256
VOCAB_SIZES = [2_000, 4_000, 8_000, 16_000, 32_000]

rows = []
for size in VOCAB_SIZES:
    candidate = build_tokenizer(size)
    rows.append(
        {
            "vocabulary": size,
            "embedding parameters": size * D_MODEL,
            "English tokens": tokens_per_sentence(candidate, valid.en),
            "Russian tokens": tokens_per_sentence(candidate, valid.ru),
        }
    )

sweep = pd.DataFrame(rows)

Each doubling of the vocabulary saves fewer tokens than the previous one, while the embedding table doubles every time. We keep 16 000 symbols.

Compare the last two rows of the table: going to 32 000 would save less than a token per sentence in either language, and double an embedding table that already holds millions of parameters, a sizeable share of a small translation model.

Models with billions of parameters can afford 200 000 tokens, because next to the rest of the model even a huge embedding table is small. Ours can’t.

The token tax, revisited

Back to where we started, with our tokenizer next to the five from section 1. This time we count tokens on the whole validation set rather than on one sentence:

contenders = dict(llm_tokenizers)
contenders["Ours (this lesson)"] = tokenizer

rows = []
for name, candidate in contenders.items():
    rows.append(
        {
            "model": name,
            "vocabulary": candidate.get_vocab_size(),
            "English": tokens_per_sentence(candidate, valid.en),
            "Russian": tokens_per_sentence(candidate, valid.ru),
        }
    )
validation_counts = pd.DataFrame(rows)
plot_token_counts(validation_counts, "Average tokens per validation sentence")

On Russian, our tokenizer needs fewer tokens than every model in the chart, GPT-4o included, with a vocabulary a fraction of the size. That’s not because we out-engineered OpenAI.

Our tokenizer was trained on exactly this kind of text in exactly these two languages; theirs has to serve code, math and dozens of languages at once.

On English we’re slightly worse than all of them, which is the honest price of sharing 16 000 symbols between two languages. A tokenizer is a decision about what to be good at, and for a translator that reads English and writes Russian this one is right.

And the word from section 1, cut by GPT-4o and by ours:

gpt4o_ids = gpt4o.encode(" недопонимание").ids
gpt4o_pieces = [gpt4o.decode([token_id]) for token_id in gpt4o_ids]
our_pieces = tokenizer.encode("недопонимание").tokens

token_chips([gpt4o_pieces, our_pieces], labels=["GPT-4o", "ours"])
plt.show()

Save and publish

The tokenizer is one JSON file. Saving it and loading it back must give the same tokens:

TOKENIZER_PATH = WORK_DIR / "tokenizer.json"
tokenizer.save(str(TOKENIZER_PATH))

reloaded = Tokenizer.from_file(str(TOKENIZER_PATH))
assert reloaded.encode(RU_EXAMPLE).ids == tokenizer.encode(RU_EXAMPLE).ids

The next lessons download the tokenizer and the three splits from the Hugging Face Hub, so that every lesson can start on its own. The course’s copies are published from this notebook.

To publish your own, set the environment variable TFS_HUB_USER to your Hugging Face username and add a write token as the HF_TOKEN secret (Kaggle: Add-ons → Secrets; Colab: the key icon in the sidebar).

Every repository on the Hub needs a card that says what it holds, where it comes from and how it was made. The dataset’s card:

DATASET_CARD = f"""---
license: cc-by-2.0
language: [en, ru]
task_categories: [translation]
---
# Tatoeba English–Russian, cleaned and split without leaks

Built in lesson 1 of the course "Transformers: from scratch to production":
https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch

- train and validation: sentence-transformers/parallel-sentences-tatoeba (en-ru),
  revision `{TRAIN_REVISION[:7]}`
- test: Tatoeba Translation Challenge eng-rus test set (Tiedemann, 2020)
- NFKC normalization, combining marks removed, straight quotes, one dash
- training pairs sharing a sentence fingerprint with the test set removed
- validation split by connected components of the translation graph,
  so no sentence occurs in both

Sentences from [Tatoeba](https://tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

| split | pairs |
|---|---|
| train | {len(train)} |
| validation | {len(valid)} |
| test | {len(test)} |
"""

And the tokenizer’s, with the three lines it takes to use it:

TOKENIZER_CARD = f"""---
license: cc-by-2.0
language: [en, ru]
tags: [tokenizer, bpe]
datasets: [xmarva/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru]
---
# BPE tokenizer for English and Russian, {tokenizer.get_vocab_size()} tokens

Built in lesson 1 of the course "Transformers: from scratch to production":
https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch

- byte-pair encoding over characters, trained with Hugging Face `tokenizers` on the training
  split of xmarva/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru, both languages together
- owns its normalization: NFKC, combining marks removed, straight quotes, one dash
- words keep the space in front of them as `▁`
- special tokens `<pad>`, `<unk>`, `<bos>`, `<eos>` with ids 0 to 3

```python
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from tokenizers import Tokenizer

path = hf_hub_download("xmarva/tfs-bpe-en-ru-16k", "tokenizer.json")
tokenizer = Tokenizer.from_file(path)
```

Trained on sentences from [Tatoeba](https://tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
"""

HUB_USER = os.environ.get("TFS_HUB_USER")
hf_token = env.secret("HF_TOKEN")

if HUB_USER and hf_token:
    from huggingface_hub import HfApi

    api = HfApi(token=hf_token)
    data_repo = f"{HUB_USER}/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru"
    tokenizer_repo = f"{HUB_USER}/tfs-bpe-en-ru-16k"

    api.create_repo(data_repo, repo_type="dataset", exist_ok=True)
    for name in splits:
        api.upload_file(
            path_or_fileobj=str(DATA_DIR / f"{name}.parquet"),
            path_in_repo=f"data/{name}.parquet",
            repo_id=data_repo,
            repo_type="dataset",
        )
    api.upload_file(
        path_or_fileobj=DATASET_CARD.encode(),
        path_in_repo="README.md",
        repo_id=data_repo,
        repo_type="dataset",
    )

    api.create_repo(tokenizer_repo, exist_ok=True)
    api.upload_file(
        path_or_fileobj=str(TOKENIZER_PATH),
        path_in_repo="tokenizer.json",
        repo_id=tokenizer_repo,
    )
    api.upload_file(
        path_or_fileobj=TOKENIZER_CARD.encode(),
        path_in_repo="README.md",
        repo_id=tokenizer_repo,
    )
    print("published", data_repo, "and", tokenizer_repo)
else:
    print("not publishing; lesson 2 downloads the course's copies:")
    print("xmarva/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru and xmarva/tfs-bpe-en-ru-16k")

not publishing; lesson 2 downloads the course's copies:
xmarva/tfs-tatoeba-en-ru and xmarva/tfs-bpe-en-ru-16k

References

  1. Tarjan, R. E. (1975). Efficiency of a good but not linear set union algorithm. Journal of the ACM, 22(2). ↩
  2. Gage, P. (1994). A new algorithm for data compression. The C Users Journal, 12(2).
  3. Sennrich, R., Haddow, B., Birch, A. (2016). Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units. ACL.
  4. Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., Sutskever, I. (2019). Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners. OpenAI. GPT-2 and its byte-level BPE.
  5. Kudo, T., Richardson, J. (2018). SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer. EMNLP.
  6. Petrov, A., La Malfa, E., Torr, P., Bibi, A. (2023). Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages. NeurIPS.
  7. Rumbelow, J., Watkins, M. (2023). SolidGoldMagikarp (plus, prompt generation). LessWrong.
  8. OpenAI (2023). GPT-4 Technical Report. Appendix C on contamination.
  9. Tiedemann, J. (2020). The Tatoeba Translation Challenge. WMT.
  10. Heaps, H. S. (1978). Information Retrieval: Computational and Theoretical Aspects. Academic Press.
  11. Unicode Standard Annex #15: Unicode Normalization Forms.
  12. tiktoken, OpenAI’s tokenizers, and the Hugging Face Tokenizers documentation.
entry.summary: What GPT-4o actually receives when you type, why Russian costs more tokens than English, and byte-pair encoding written from scratch.

entry.title: Damasio’s somatic marker hypothesis: the body in decision-making

link.title: Damasio’s somatic marker hypothesis: the body in decision-making

entry.content:
Elliot had been, in Antonio Damasio’s words, “a good husband and father, had a job with a business firm, and had been a role model for younger siblings and colleagues.” Then a tumour the size of a small orange grew above his eye sockets and pressed on both frontal lobes from below.

Surgeons removed it together with the damaged tissue of the lower, middle part of the frontal lobes. Elliot recovered. His IQ was “in the superior range”, his scores on a standard personality inventory were normal, and he had “a flawless memory for his life story” (Damasio, 1994, pp. 35–44).

And he could no longer run his life. At work, given documents to sort, “he might spend a whole afternoon deliberating on which principle of categorization should be applied: Should it be date, size of document, pertinence to the case, or another?

The flow of work was stopped” (p. 36). He lost his job, then his savings in a doomed business venture, then his marriage; a second marriage, which his family opposed, also ended in divorce (p. 37).

In one test, a psychologist on Damasio’s team asked him to come up with ways to act in social dilemmas. Elliot produced a long list of reasonable options, smiled, and added: “And after all this, I still wouldn’t know what to do!” (p. 49).

Damasio summed up Elliot’s condition in six words: “to know but not to feel” (p. 45). His book Descartes’ Error (1994) built a theory on that phrase.

Emotion, it says, is not the enemy of good decisions but part of the machinery that makes them, and the part that was missing in Elliot was a signal from the body. This post goes through the theory, the experiment that made it famous, the experiments that challenged it, and what is left.

Two patients

Elliot was not the first patient with this kind of damage to become famous.

On 13 September 1848, near Cavendish, Vermont, a railway foreman named Phineas Gage was packing explosive into a drill hole when the charge went off and drove his tamping iron, “three feet, seven inches in length, one and one quarter inch in diameter”, weighing 13¼ pounds, through his left cheek and out of the top of his head[1].

He survived and was talking within minutes. His physician, John Harlow, later described the change: Gage became “fitful, irreverent, indulging at times in the grossest profanity”, so that “his friends and acquaintances said he was ‘no longer Gage’“[2].

Gage is the textbook case of the frontal lobes and personality, and the textbook version is too simple in two ways. First, he recovered more than it suggests.

By Harlow’s own account he worked in a livery stable and then spent nearly eight years in Chile driving stagecoaches, six horses and a heavy load, a job that demands planning and reliability; the historian Malcolm Macmillan, who spent decades on the case, concluded that he “eventually made a surprisingly good psychosocial adaptation to his injury”[3].

Second, his damage may not have been what Damasio’s case needed. In 1994 Hanna Damasio and colleagues reconstructed the path of the iron from measurements of the skull and concluded that it damaged the ventromedial prefrontal cortex on both sides[4].

Later reconstructions from CT scans of the skull itself found the damage limited to the left frontal lobe[5, 6].

Elliot is better documented. In the research literature he is patient EVR, an accountant at a home-building firm, whose “‘measurable’ intelligence was superior, and he was therefore considered a ‘malingerer’” before anyone understood what had happened to him[7].

The region at the centre of the story is the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), the lower, inner surface of the frontal lobes, just above the eyes:

The hypothesis

Damasio’s question was what the vmPFC contributes that IQ tests do not measure. His answer is the somatic marker hypothesis[8].

When we consider an option, the brain does not only compute its consequences. It also re-evokes the bodily state that similar situations produced in the past: a tightening, a flicker of something like fear or relief. That state marks the option.

A bad marker works as “an alarm signal”, a good one as “an incentive signal”, and when the process runs below awareness it is a “biasing signal” that tilts the choice before reasoning finishes.

The vmPFC, on this view, stores the links between kinds of situations and the bodily states they led to, and without it a person can still reason about options but nothing makes one of them feel worse than another. Elliot’s afternoon spent choosing a filing principle is what deciding looks like when every option weighs the same.

The word somatic, from the Greek sōma, body, is literal, but not in the way it is often retold. The signals do not have to travel to the body and back. Damasio describes two routes:

In the body loop, the situation changes the state of the body, heart rate, breathing, the gut, the skin’s sweating, and the somatosensory cortex and the insula register the change.

In the as-if body loop, the vmPFC signals those cortical maps directly and they adopt the pattern the body would have produced, “the body being bypassed”.

Damasio thought the second route is the usual one: “in most circumstances an ‘as if’ body loop is engaged instead, and the body, that is the periphery, is bypassed entirely.”
